questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with crushing substernal chest pain for 90 minutes. ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF. Which coronary artery is most likely occluded?
questions.explanation: ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF represents an inferior STEMI, which is most commonly caused by occlusion of the right coronary artery (RCA). The RCA supplies the inferior wall of the left ventricle in most patients. Reciprocal ST depression is often seen in leads I and aVL. Urgent revascularization with primary PCI is the treatment of choice within 90 minutes of first medical contact.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with chest pain has an initial troponin I of 0.02 ng/mL (normal <0.04) and a repeat troponin at 3 hours of 0.03 ng/mL. Her ECG shows T-wave inversions in V4–V6. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation: Unstable angina is characterized by ischemic symptoms (chest pain at rest, new-onset angina, or crescendo angina) without troponin elevation. Both troponin values here are within normal range, ruling out NSTEMI. STEMI requires ST elevation on ECG; this patient has T-wave inversions, not ST elevation. Stable angina occurs predictably with exertion and would not present as acute chest pain with ECG changes at rest.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents with chest pain. ECG reveals deep, symmetric T-wave inversions in leads V2–V4 without ST elevation, and the pain has now resolved. Troponins are negative. Which syndrome does this ECG pattern represent?
questions.explanation: Wellens syndrome describes a specific ECG pattern of deep symmetric (Type B) or biphasic (Type A) T-wave inversions in V2–V4 that occurs in the pain-free interval after an episode of chest pain. It represents critical proximal LAD stenosis and indicates high risk for impending anterior STEMI if untreated. These patients require urgent cardiac catheterization even with negative troponins. Stress testing is contraindicated in Wellens syndrome due to risk of precipitating complete occlusion.

questions.question: A patient with known heart failure has an ejection fraction of 35%. Which of the following medication classes has NOT been shown to reduce mortality in HFrEF?
questions.explanation: Digoxin reduces hospitalizations in HFrEF but has not been shown to reduce mortality (DIG trial). ACE inhibitors (and ARBs/ARNIs as alternatives) reduce mortality in HFrEF through neurohormonal blockade. Beta-blockers (specifically carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, and bisoprolol) have robust mortality benefit in HFrEF. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone also reduce mortality in HFrEF (RALES and EPHESUS trials).

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with HFrEF (EF 28%) is on maximally tolerated doses of lisinopril and carvedilol. His BNP is 850 pg/mL and he remains NYHA Class III. Which additional therapy has the strongest evidence for further mortality reduction?
questions.explanation: Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI) demonstrated superior mortality reduction compared to enalapril in the PARADIGM-HF trial and is recommended as a replacement for ACE inhibitor or ARB in symptomatic HFrEF patients who can tolerate it. Lisinopril should be stopped 36 hours before starting sacubitril/valsartan to avoid angioedema. Ivabradine is beneficial in selected patients (sinus rhythm, HR ≥70) but has less mortality benefit than ARNI. Hydralazine/nitrate is a reasonable alternative in patients intolerant to ACE inhibitors or ARBs, particularly in Black patients.

questions.question: A 75-year-old woman with hypertension, obesity, and preserved LV function (EF 60%) presents with exertional dyspnea. Echo shows impaired relaxation and elevated filling pressures. Which medication class has recently been shown to reduce heart failure hospitalizations in HFpEF?
questions.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin and dapagliflozin) have demonstrated reduction in heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death in HFpEF patients in the EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER trials. Unlike HFrEF, ACE inhibitors and beta-blockers have not shown clear mortality benefit in HFpEF. SGLT2 inhibitors are now recommended across the spectrum of heart failure regardless of ejection fraction. Their mechanism in heart failure likely involves volume regulation, natriuresis, and direct myocardial effects.

questions.question: Explain the CHA2DS2-VASc scoring system for atrial fibrillation, including how each component is scored, what total scores indicate about anticoagulation, and preferred anticoagulant choices.
questions.answer: CHA2DS2-VASc assigns points as follows: Congestive heart failure (1), Hypertension (1), Age ≥75 years (2), Diabetes mellitus (1), prior Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease—prior MI, peripheral arterial disease, or aortic plaque (1), Age 65–74 years (1), and female Sex category (1); maximum score is 9. A score of 0 in males (or 1 in females attributable only to sex) indicates low risk and anticoagulation is not recommended. A score ≥2 in males or ≥3 in females indicates high enough stroke risk that oral anticoagulation is recommended. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AFib due to comparable or superior efficacy, lower intracranial hemorrhage rates, and no need for INR monitoring. Warfarin remains preferred for AFib with mechanical heart valves or moderate-to-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis, where DOACs are contraindicated.
questions.explanation: CHA2DS2-VASc assigns points for CHF, Hypertension, Age ≥75 (2pts), Diabetes, prior Stroke/TIA (2pts), Vascular disease, Age 65-74, and female Sex. Scores ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women indicate anticoagulation benefit. DOACs are preferred over warfarin for non-valvular AFib due to favorable efficacy/safety profiles.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with sudden-onset palpitations, heart rate of 180 bpm, and a narrow-complex regular tachycardia on ECG. Vagal maneuvers fail. What is the most appropriate next pharmacologic intervention?
options: C. Adenosine 6 mg IV rapid push
questions.explanation: Adenosine 6 mg given as a rapid IV push followed by saline flush is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for hemodynamically stable SVT (likely AVNRT or AVRT) after failed vagal maneuvers. Adenosine's ultra-short half-life (~10 seconds) transiently blocks the AV node, terminating reentrant circuits. If ineffective, doses of 12 mg can be repeated up to twice. Amiodarone is reserved for refractory or recurrent SVT and ventricular arrhythmias. IV beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers are alternatives but are second-line to adenosine for acute termination.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is found unresponsive. ECG shows a wide-complex tachycardia at 160 bpm. Which feature most supports ventricular tachycardia over SVT with aberrancy?
questions.explanation: AV dissociation (P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently) is pathognomonic for ventricular tachycardia. Other VT criteria include fusion beats, capture beats, QRS duration >140 ms, concordance in precordial leads, and northwest axis deviation. Heart rate, RBBB morphology, and response to vagal maneuvers are not reliable distinguishers. The Brugada and Vereckei algorithms use ECG morphology to differentiate VT from SVT with aberrancy. When in doubt, treat as VT—it is more dangerous and more common in patients with structural heart disease.

questions.question: A 78-year-old woman presents with exertional syncope, angina, and dyspnea. Auscultation reveals a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids. Echo shows a mean gradient of 48 mmHg and valve area of 0.7 cm². What is the most appropriate intervention?
options: A. Medical management with ACE inhibitors
C. Aortic valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter)
questions.explanation: This patient has severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (mean gradient >40 mmHg, valve area <1.0 cm²) with all three classic symptoms: syncope, angina, and heart failure (dyspnea). Once symptomatic, severe AS carries a very poor prognosis without intervention (average survival 2–3 years with syncope, 3–5 years with angina, 1–2 years with heart failure). Aortic valve replacement—surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVR) depending on operative risk—is the definitive treatment. Medical therapy does not alter the natural history of AS, and ACE inhibitors may precipitate hypotension.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with fever, sharp pleuritic chest pain that improves when leaning forward, and a pericardial friction rub. ECG shows diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation with PR depression in multiple leads. Which therapy is first-line?
questions.explanation: Acute pericarditis is treated with aspirin (or NSAIDs) plus colchicine for 3 months, based on the COPE and ICAP trials showing colchicine reduces recurrence by 50%. Corticosteroids are reserved for refractory cases, connective tissue disease-related pericarditis, or contraindications to NSAIDs—they increase the risk of recurrence and should not be used first-line. Pericardiocentesis is indicated for cardiac tamponade, not uncomplicated pericarditis. The ECG findings (diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation, PR depression) and pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward are classic features.

questions.question: A patient with a pericardial effusion develops hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds. Pulsus paradoxus is 18 mmHg. Which hemodynamic finding is most characteristic of cardiac tamponade on right heart catheterization?
options: A. Elevated right atrial pressure with prominent Y descent
B. Equalization of diastolic pressures across all four chambers
C. Kussmaul sign (JVP increase with inspiration)
D. Preserved cardiac output with elevated wedge pressure
questions.explanation: Cardiac tamponade is characterized by equalization of diastolic pressures (right atrial pressure = right ventricular diastolic pressure = pulmonary artery diastolic pressure = pulmonary capillary wedge pressure), typically in the range of 15–20 mmHg, reflecting compression of all cardiac chambers by the pericardial fluid. Tamponade classically shows a blunted or absent Y descent (unlike constrictive pericarditis which shows prominent Y descent). Kussmaul sign is seen in constrictive pericarditis, not typically tamponade. Beck's triad—hypotension, elevated JVP, and muffled heart sounds—is the clinical hallmark.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presents with BP 220/130 mmHg, altered mental status, and papilledema. Describe how you would manage this patient, including BP targets, choice of agents, and the physiologic rationale for your approach.
questions.answer: This presentation is a hypertensive emergency with hypertensive encephalopathy, requiring immediate IV antihypertensive therapy in an ICU setting with continuous blood pressure monitoring. The initial goal is to reduce mean arterial pressure (MAP) by no more than 25% within the first hour—over-aggressive lowering risks cerebral, coronary, and renal ischemia by overwhelming the loss of normal autoregulation that occurs with chronic hypertension. Over the next 2–6 hours, BP can be further reduced toward 160/100 mmHg if the patient is stable, then normalized over the following 24–48 hours. Preferred IV agents include nicardipine (titratable calcium channel blocker), labetalol (alpha and beta blockade), or clevidipine; sodium nitroprusside is reserved for cases requiring rapid precise control (e.g., aortic dissection) given its cyanide toxicity risk with prolonged use. Aortic dissection requires a systolic BP target of <120 mmHg within 20 minutes using labetalol or esmolol plus nitroprusside. Oral agents are inappropriate here given the need for rapid, titratable control.
questions.explanation: Hypertensive emergency is defined by severe BP elevation (typically >180/120) with acute target organ damage, distinguishing it from urgency (no end-organ damage). IV agents (nicardipine, labetalol, clevidipine) are used to lower MAP by ~25% in the first hour to avoid ischemia from overly rapid reduction. Aortic dissection and ischemic stroke require specific BP targets.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents with exertional chest pain and near-syncope. Exam reveals a systolic ejection murmur that increases with Valsalva maneuver and decreases with squatting. Echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
questions.explanation: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is treated first-line with beta-blockers to reduce heart rate, increase diastolic filling time, and decrease LVOT obstruction. Negative inotropes reduce the dynamic obstruction caused by systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (amlodipine) and vasodilators (hydralazine, nitrates) are contraindicated as they worsen LVOT obstruction by reducing afterload and preload. Digoxin is also contraindicated as its positive inotropy worsens obstruction. The murmur increasing with Valsalva (decreased preload) and decreasing with squatting (increased preload) is pathognomonic for dynamic LVOT obstruction.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents 2 days after a highly emotionally stressful event with chest pain and dyspnea. Echo reveals apical ballooning with preserved basal function. Coronary angiography shows no obstructive coronary artery disease. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (also called stress cardiomyopathy or apical ballooning syndrome) is characterized by transient apical wall motion abnormalities with preserved basal function following emotional or physical stress, predominantly in postmenopausal women. Coronary angiography shows no culprit lesion, distinguishing it from ACS. The apical ballooning pattern resembles a Japanese octopus trap (tako-tsubo), giving the syndrome its name. The condition is generally reversible within weeks, with supportive management. Catecholamine surge is implicated in the pathophysiology.

questions.question: Describe the ECG criteria for diagnosing STEMI and explain the significance of a new left bundle branch block (LBBB) in the setting of chest pain.
questions.answer: STEMI is diagnosed on ECG by new ST elevation ≥1 mm in two or more contiguous limb leads, or ≥2 mm in two contiguous precordial leads (V1–V4), or ≥2 mm in leads V1–V3 with LBBB (using Sgarbossa criteria). The territory of ST elevation identifies the culprit artery: inferior (II, III, aVF) → RCA; anterior (V1–V4) → LAD; lateral (I, aVL, V5–V6) → circumflex; posterior STEMI shows tall R waves and ST depression in V1–V2. A new LBBB in the setting of ischemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent because LBBB obscures the underlying ST changes and is often caused by a large proximal LAD occlusion; it independently carries a poor prognosis. The Sgarbossa criteria (concordant ST elevation, excessive discordant ST elevation) can identify ischemia superimposed on LBBB. All STEMI and STEMI-equivalent presentations should trigger immediate activation of the catheterization laboratory for primary PCI.
questions.explanation: STEMI is diagnosed by ≥1mm ST elevation in ≥2 contiguous limb leads or ≥2mm in precordial leads, or new LBBB. Lead groupings localize the infarct: II/III/aVF (inferior, RCA), V1-V4 (anterior, LAD), I/aVL (lateral, LCx). Posterior STEMI shows ST depression in V1-V3 with tall R waves. Reciprocal changes in opposite leads support the diagnosis.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF).
questions.answer: ADHF occurs when compensatory mechanisms fail and cardiac output is insufficient to meet metabolic demands, leading to elevated filling pressures and fluid redistribution into the lungs and periphery. Clinically, patients present with dyspnea (orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea), peripheral edema, elevated JVP, crackles on lung exam, and elevated BNP/NT-proBNP. The immediate management focuses on decongestion: IV loop diuretics (furosemide) are first-line for volume overload, with a starting IV dose at least equal to the patient's outpatient oral dose. Oxygen and noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) improve oxygenation and reduce preload. Vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nitroprusside) can be added for patients with high systemic vascular resistance and preserved blood pressure. Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) are reserved for low-output states with end-organ hypoperfusion. Once stabilized, optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) should be ensured before discharge.
questions.explanation: ADHF results from elevated filling pressures causing pulmonary and systemic congestion; reduced cardiac output in cardiogenic shock causes hypoperfusion. The Forrester classification guides therapy based on cardiac output and pulmonary wedge pressure. IV diuretics are first-line for congestion; vasodilators reduce afterload; inotropes (dobutamine) are reserved for low-output states.

questions.question: Describe the NYHA functional classification of heart failure and its clinical and prognostic utility.
questions.answer: The NYHA classification categorizes heart failure patients into four functional classes based on symptom severity with activity: Class I—no symptoms with ordinary activity; Class II—slight limitation, comfortable at rest, symptoms with moderate exertion; Class III—marked limitation, comfortable at rest, symptoms with minimal exertion; Class IV—symptoms at rest or with any physical activity. This classification guides therapeutic decisions: GDMT is indicated for all symptomatic patients (Class II–IV), device therapy (ICD, CRT) is typically considered for those remaining Class II–IV despite optimization, and advanced therapies (LVAD, transplant) are considered for refractory Class III–IV patients. Higher NYHA class correlates with worse prognosis, higher BNP levels, and greater mortality risk. The classification is also used as an eligibility criterion and endpoint in clinical trials.
questions.explanation: NYHA Class I has no symptoms with ordinary activity; Class II has slight limitation; Class III has marked limitation; Class IV has symptoms at rest. Higher NYHA class correlates with worse prognosis and guides therapy intensification. GDMT (ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blockers, MRAs, SGLT2i) is indicated for HFrEF regardless of symptoms.

questions.question: Discuss the rate control versus rhythm control strategy in atrial fibrillation, including when each approach is preferred.
questions.answer: Rate control aims to reduce ventricular response rate (typically <110 bpm at rest) using AV nodal blocking agents such as beta-blockers, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil), or digoxin without attempting to restore sinus rhythm. Rhythm control restores and maintains sinus rhythm through cardioversion (electrical or pharmacologic) and/or antiarrhythmic drugs (flecainide, propafenone for structurally normal hearts; amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide for structural heart disease), or catheter ablation. The AFFIRM trial showed no mortality difference between strategies, but recent data (EAST-AFNET 4 trial) suggest early rhythm control in newly diagnosed AFib reduces cardiovascular outcomes. Rate control is preferred in older, asymptomatic patients with persistent AFib, while rhythm control is preferred in younger, highly symptomatic patients, those with HFrEF (CASTLE-AF trial showed ablation improves outcomes), and those with AFib <1 year duration. Anticoagulation decisions are based on CHA2DS2-VASc score regardless of rate vs. rhythm strategy.
questions.explanation: Rate control targets resting HR <80 bpm using beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs, or digoxin. Rhythm control with antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, flecainide, sotalol) or cardioversion/ablation may be preferred in younger, symptomatic patients or those with HFrEF. The AFFIRM trial showed no mortality benefit of rhythm over rate control, but the EAST-AFNET trial showed early rhythm control improved outcomes.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease is found to have mitral stenosis. Describe the pathophysiology, key physical exam findings, and indications for intervention.
questions.answer: Rheumatic mitral stenosis results from inflammatory scarring of the mitral leaflets and subvalvular apparatus, causing leaflet thickening, fusion of the commissures, and restriction of valve opening—producing a funnel-shaped mitral valve with reduced orifice area. The elevated left atrial pressure that results causes dyspnea, pulmonary hypertension, hemoptysis, and atrial fibrillation; severe MS can cause right heart failure. Key exam findings include an opening snap (high-pitched early diastolic sound), a low-pitched rumbling mid-diastolic murmur best heard at the apex with the patient in left lateral decubitus, and presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm. The shorter the S2-to-opening snap interval, the more severe the stenosis. Valve area <1.5 cm² defines severe MS. Intervention—percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC) or surgical mitral valve replacement—is indicated for symptomatic severe MS or asymptomatic severe MS with new AFib, pulmonary hypertension (PASP >50 mmHg), or planned pregnancy.
questions.explanation: Severe mitral stenosis is defined by MVA <1.0 cm² or mean gradient >10 mmHg. Symptoms include dyspnea, AFib, and pulmonary hypertension. Percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (PMBC) is the preferred intervention for suitable anatomy (Wilkins score ≤8); mitral valve replacement is reserved for unsuitable anatomy or significant MR.

questions.question: Describe the clinical features, hemodynamic hallmarks, and management of constrictive pericarditis, distinguishing it from cardiac tamponade.
questions.answer: Constrictive pericarditis occurs when a thickened, fibrotic, or calcified pericardium impairs diastolic filling, leading to elevated and equalized diastolic pressures in all chambers. Causes include prior cardiac surgery, radiation therapy, viral pericarditis, and tuberculosis (common in endemic areas). Patients present with signs of right heart failure: elevated JVP with prominent X and Y descents (the Y descent is particularly deep, unlike tamponade where Y descent is absent), Kussmaul sign (paradoxical rise in JVP with inspiration), pericardial knock in early diastole, and peripheral edema. CT or MRI showing pericardial thickening (>4 mm) supports the diagnosis, though 20% have normal thickness. In contrast, tamponade shows absent Y descent, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg, and does not exhibit Kussmaul sign. Cardiac catheterization in constrictive pericarditis reveals equalized diastolic pressures and discordant ventricular pressure changes with respiration (ventricular interdependence). Definitive treatment is surgical pericardiectomy, though anti-inflammatory therapy may be tried first for subacute cases.
questions.explanation: Constrictive pericarditis causes equalization of diastolic pressures across all chambers on right heart catheterization. Kussmaul's sign (JVP rise with inspiration), pericardial knock, and ventricular interdependence distinguish it from tamponade. CT/MRI shows pericardial thickening >4mm. Pericardiectomy is definitive treatment for refractory cases.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology and clinical management of hypertensive emergency, distinguishing it from hypertensive urgency.
questions.answer: Hypertensive emergency is defined as severely elevated blood pressure (typically >180/120 mmHg) with evidence of acute target organ damage, including hypertensive encephalopathy, acute kidney injury, aortic dissection, pulmonary edema, eclampsia, or unstable angina/STEMI. The pathophysiology involves loss of normal pressure-natriuresis, fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, and end-organ ischemia from hypoperfusion despite high pressure. Management requires IV antihypertensives (nicardipine, labetalol, clevidipine, or sodium nitroprusside for aortic dissection) with blood pressure monitoring in an ICU setting; the goal is to lower MAP by no more than 25% in the first hour to avoid watershed ischemia. Hypertensive urgency, in contrast, is severely elevated BP without acute end-organ damage; it is managed with oral antihypertensives (amlodipine, lisinopril, or short-acting labetalol) over 24–48 hours and does not require hospitalization or IV therapy. Distinguishing the two relies entirely on evidence of end-organ injury, not the absolute blood pressure value.
questions.explanation: Hypertensive emergency requires IV therapy to lower MAP by 25% in the first hour, then to 160/100 over 2-6 hours. Agents include nicardipine (most versatile), labetalol (safe in pregnancy), and nitroprusside (risk of cyanide toxicity). Exceptions: ischemic stroke (do not treat unless BP >220/120 or thrombolytics planned), aortic dissection (target SBP <120 immediately).

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy (EF 22%) develops sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia at 180 bpm with hemodynamic instability. What is the immediate treatment?
options: A. Adenosine 6 mg IV rapid push
questions.explanation: Hemodynamically unstable sustained ventricular tachycardia requires immediate synchronized DC cardioversion regardless of other factors. Adenosine is effective only for SVT and has no role in VT. Amiodarone is appropriate for hemodynamically stable VT or post-cardioversion maintenance, but when a patient is unstable (hypotension, altered consciousness, pulmonary edema), cardioversion takes priority. Verapamil is absolutely contraindicated in wide-complex tachycardia thought to be VT, as it can precipitate cardiovascular collapse. The synchronized mode ensures the shock is delivered on the R wave to avoid triggering VF.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with chronic aortic regurgitation is asymptomatic. Which echocardiographic finding indicates the need for surgical intervention even in the absence of symptoms?
options: A. Aortic regurgitant jet width/LVOT ratio of 45%
B. Left ventricular end-systolic diameter (LVESD) of 52 mm
D. Effective regurgitant orifice area of 0.25 cm²
questions.explanation: In chronic aortic regurgitation, surgery is indicated in asymptomatic patients when left ventricular end-systolic dimension (LVESD) is ≥50 mm (or ≥25 mm/m² body surface area) or when LVEF drops below 55%, as these thresholds predict irreversible LV dysfunction if surgery is delayed. The regurgitant jet width/LVOT ratio reflects severity (≥65% = severe) but is not itself a surgical trigger. Pressure half-time <200 ms indicates severe AR (shorter PHT = faster equalization of pressure = more severe regurgitation). An EROA ≥0.30 cm² characterizes severe AR but alone does not mandate surgery in asymptomatic patients.

questions.question: Describe the key features of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), including common causes, clinical presentation, and management principles.
questions.answer: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by LV or biventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction (reduced EF) in the absence of abnormal loading conditions (hypertension, valvular disease) sufficient to account for the degree of impairment. Common causes include idiopathic (most common), ischemic, viral myocarditis (Coxsackie B, parvovirus B19), alcohol, peripartum state, chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab), and genetic mutations (titin gene most common familial cause). Patients present with progressive dyspnea, exercise intolerance, lower extremity edema, and may have thromboembolic events due to low-flow state; physical exam reveals displaced PMI, S3 gallop, elevated JVP, and mitral regurgitation murmur from annular dilation. Management follows standard HFrEF guidelines: quadruple GDMT with ACEi/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitor; ICD implantation for EF ≤35% despite ≥3 months of optimal medical therapy; CRT for EF ≤35% with LBBB and QRS ≥150 ms; and advanced therapies (LVAD, cardiac transplantation) for refractory disease.
questions.explanation: DCM is characterized by left ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction (EF <40%). Common causes include idiopathic (most common), viral myocarditis, alcohol, peripartum, doxorubicin toxicity, and hereditary (TTN, LMNA mutations). Management includes GDMT (ACEi, beta-blockers, MRA, SGLT2i), ICD for primary prevention (EF <35%), and CRT for LBBB with QRS >150ms.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with stable angina undergoes coronary angiography showing a 60% stenosis of the LAD. Which measurement would best guide the decision to perform PCI on this lesion?
questions.explanation: Fractional flow reserve (FFR) measures the hemodynamic significance of a coronary stenosis by comparing pressure distal to the lesion versus aortic pressure during maximal hyperemia. An FFR ≤0.80 indicates a hemodynamically significant lesion that benefits from revascularization; values >0.80 favor medical therapy. The DEFER and FAME trials demonstrated that FFR-guided PCI improves outcomes and reduces unnecessary interventions compared to angiography alone. IVUS and OCT provide anatomic information but do not assess physiologic significance.

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic man has triple-vessel coronary artery disease with a SYNTAX score of 28. Which revascularization strategy is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The SYNTAX score quantifies anatomic complexity of coronary artery disease; scores >22 indicate complex disease where CABG is preferred over PCI. The SYNTAX trial showed that patients with high SYNTAX scores (>22-32) treated with CABG had significantly lower rates of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events compared to PCI. In diabetic patients with multivessel disease, CABG is additionally supported by the FREEDOM trial, which demonstrated superior outcomes over PCI regardless of SYNTAX score. Medical therapy alone is insufficient for symptomatic triple-vessel disease with viable myocardium.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with hypertension and hyperlipidemia has a 10-year ASCVD risk of 12%. She has an LDL of 145 mg/dL. According to ACC/AHA guidelines, what is the most appropriate management?
options: A. Lifestyle modification alone for 3 months before reassessing
questions.explanation: ACC/AHA guidelines recommend statin therapy for primary prevention in patients with 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5%. For patients with intermediate risk (7.5-20%), moderate-intensity statin therapy is the standard recommendation, with high-intensity statin reserved for those with risk ≥20% or additional risk-enhancing factors. This patient's 10-year risk of 12% places her in the intermediate category, making moderate-intensity statin the appropriate choice. Risk-enhancing factors (family history, chronic kidney disease, elevated CRP, coronary artery calcium) can shift decision-making toward more intensive therapy.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man on high-intensity statin therapy develops diffuse myalgia with a creatine kinase (CK) level of 4,500 U/L (normal <200). His LDL remains at 95 mg/dL on rosuvastatin 40 mg. What is the best next step?
options: A. Continue statin and add coenzyme Q10
B. Switch to a lower-intensity statin
C. Discontinue statin and add a PCSK9 inhibitor
D. Check TSH and continue current statin
questions.explanation: A CK elevation >10 times the upper limit of normal with myalgia constitutes statin-associated myopathy, requiring statin discontinuation to prevent rhabdomyolysis. PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) are indicated for patients who are statin-intolerant or cannot achieve target LDL on maximally tolerated statin therapy. Hypothyroidism can exacerbate statin myopathy, so checking TSH is advisable, but the immediate priority is stopping the offending agent. Coenzyme Q10 supplementation has not been proven effective for statin myopathy in randomized trials.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of action of PCSK9 inhibitors and describe the patient populations for whom they are indicated according to current ACC/AHA guidelines.
questions.answer: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) is a serine protease that binds to LDL receptors on hepatocytes and promotes their lysosomal degradation, thereby reducing hepatic LDL uptake and raising circulating LDL levels. Monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9 (evolocumab, alirocumab) prevent PCSK9 from binding to LDL receptors, increasing receptor recycling to the cell surface and dramatically lowering LDL by 50-60% beyond statin therapy. According to ACC/AHA guidelines, PCSK9 inhibitors are indicated for patients with clinical ASCVD who cannot achieve adequate LDL reduction on maximally tolerated statin therapy, patients with heterozygous or homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and patients with statin intolerance requiring LDL lowering. The FOURIER and ODYSSEY OUTCOMES trials demonstrated that PCSK9 inhibitors reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk patients, providing the evidence base for their class I indication in very high-risk ASCVD.
questions.explanation: PCSK9 (proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9) is a serine protease that binds to LDL receptors on hepatocytes and promotes their lysosomal degradation, thereby reducing hepatic LDL uptake and raising circulating LDL levels.  Monoclonal antibodies against PCSK9 (evolocumab, alirocumab) prevent PCSK9 from binding to LDL receptors, increasing receptor recycling to the cell surface and dramatically lowering LDL by 50-60% beyond statin therapy.  According to ACC/AHA guidelines, PCSK9 inhibitors are indicated for patients with clinical ASCVD who cannot achieve adequate LDL reduction on maximally tolerated statin therapy, patients with heterozygous or homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, and patients with statin intolerance requiring LDL lowering.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with chest pain. His high-sensitivity troponin I is 0.08 ng/mL (URL 0.026 ng/mL) at presentation and rises to 0.21 ng/mL at 3 hours. Compare troponin I vs. troponin T and CK-MB as cardiac biomarkers, and explain the clinical significance of the rising pattern.
questions.answer: Cardiac troponin I (cTnI) and troponin T (cTnT) are structural proteins of the contractile apparatus released into the bloodstream following cardiomyocyte injury; both have high sensitivity and specificity for myocardial damage, though some cTnT assays can weakly detect skeletal muscle TnT isoforms in conditions like myopathy or renal failure, giving cTnI a slight specificity advantage. High-sensitivity troponin assays (hs-cTn) detect concentrations 10-100 times lower than conventional assays, enabling earlier detection of MI and accelerated rule-in/rule-out protocols (0h/1h or 0h/2h algorithms). CK-MB was previously the standard biomarker and still has utility in detecting reinfarction (rapid return to baseline after MI allows detection of a second event) and in cardiac surgery monitoring, but it is inferior to hs-cTn in sensitivity and cardiac specificity. A rising (delta) pattern—defined by ACC/AHA as an absolute change meeting assay-specific thresholds over serial measurements—is critical for distinguishing acute myocardial injury from chronic stable elevation, which can occur in heart failure, CKD, pulmonary embolism, myocarditis, or sepsis; this patient's rise from 0.08 to 0.21 ng/mL over 3 hours is diagnostic of acute myocardial injury consistent with NSTEMI.

questions.question: Compare BNP and NT-proBNP as biomarkers for heart failure diagnosis, including their biochemistry, half-lives, reference ranges, and factors that affect interpretation.
questions.answer: BNP (B-type natriuretic peptide) and NT-proBNP (N-terminal pro-BNP) are both cleavage products of proBNP, which is synthesized and released by ventricular myocytes in response to wall stress and volume overload; BNP is the biologically active C-terminal fragment while NT-proBNP is the inactive N-terminal fragment. BNP has a half-life of approximately 20 minutes whereas NT-proBNP has a half-life of 60-120 minutes, resulting in NT-proBNP circulating at concentrations approximately 5-10 times higher than BNP for equivalent degrees of heart failure. Diagnostic thresholds differ: for acute dyspnea, BNP >100 pg/mL and NT-proBNP >300 pg/mL suggest heart failure, while age-stratified NT-proBNP cutoffs (450/<50 years, 900/50-75 years, 1800/>75 years pg/mL) improve specificity. Several factors affect interpretation: obesity significantly reduces both BNP and NT-proBNP levels (reducing sensitivity in obese patients), renal impairment elevates NT-proBNP more than BNP (due to renal clearance of NT-proBNP), and neprilysin inhibitors (sacubitril/valsartan) elevate BNP by inhibiting its degradation while NT-proBNP remains unaffected, making NT-proBNP the preferred monitoring marker in patients on sacubitril/valsartan.

questions.question: Describe the ECG features and clinical significance of the three types of second-degree AV block: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach), Mobitz Type II, and 2:1 AV block.
questions.answer: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach) shows progressive PR interval lengthening with each beat until a P wave is not conducted (dropped QRS), then the cycle resets; this reflects fatigue of AV nodal conduction and is usually benign, often due to increased vagal tone, inferior MI, or drug toxicity. Mobitz Type II shows a constant PR interval with sudden non-conduction of a P wave without prior PR prolongation; this reflects infranodal (His-Purkinje) disease and carries a significant risk of progression to complete heart block, often requiring pacemaker implantation. A 2:1 AV block (every other P wave conducts) cannot be classified as Mobitz I or II based on ECG alone since no consecutive conducted beats occur; narrow QRS suggests AV nodal level (more benign, Mobitz I-like), while wide QRS suggests infranodal disease (Mobitz II-like, higher risk). Management hinges on the level of block, symptoms, and hemodynamic stability, with infranodal disease almost always requiring permanent pacing.

questions.question: A 78-year-old man is found to have complete heart block with a ventricular escape rate of 38 bpm and hypotension. He is asymptomatic at rest but becomes dizzy with minimal exertion. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: C. Temporary transvenous pacing followed by permanent pacemaker
D. Isoproterenol infusion as definitive therapy
questions.explanation: Third-degree (complete) AV block with hemodynamic compromise and symptoms is a Class I indication for permanent pacemaker implantation. A temporary transvenous pacemaker should be placed urgently to stabilize the patient while preparing for permanent device implantation. Atropine is given IV (not orally) as a temporizing measure for symptomatic bradycardia at the AV nodal level, but is often ineffective for infranodal complete heart block. Isoproterenol can increase escape rate but is not definitive therapy and has significant side effects including proarrhythmia. Observation alone is inappropriate given hypotension and exertional symptoms.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman experiences recurrent syncope preceded by warmth, nausea, and diaphoresis, typically when standing in crowds. Cardiac workup is negative. Which test is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation—prodromal symptoms (warmth, nausea, diaphoresis), triggering by orthostatic stress in crowded environments, and normal cardiac workup—is classic for vasovagal syncope. The tilt-table test is the standard provocative test for neurocardiogenic (vasovagal) syncope; it induces orthostatic stress by tilting the patient head-up at 60-70 degrees, with or without pharmacologic provocation (nitroglycerin or isoproterenol). A Holter monitor is useful for arrhythmia detection but won't diagnose vasovagal syncope. An implantable loop recorder is reserved for unexplained recurrent syncope after non-invasive testing is unrevealing. Exercise stress testing evaluates for exertional syncope or ischemia-related arrhythmias.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man develops syncope after standing from a chair. His blood pressure drops from 142/88 mmHg supine to 108/68 mmHg after 3 minutes of standing. Discuss the definition, common causes, and management of orthostatic hypotension.
questions.answer: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing from a supine or seated position, as in this patient. Common causes include volume depletion (dehydration, hemorrhage), medications (antihypertensives, alpha-blockers, diuretics, tricyclic antidepressants, dopaminergic agents), autonomic neuropathy (diabetic, Parkinson's disease, multiple system atrophy), adrenal insufficiency, and prolonged bed rest. Initial management includes removing or reducing offending medications, increasing fluid and salt intake (2-3 L water and 10 g salt daily unless contraindicated), and non-pharmacologic measures such as compression stockings, head-of-bed elevation, and physical countermaneuvers (leg crossing, squatting). Pharmacologic therapy with fludrocortisone (volume expansion) or midodrine (alpha-1 agonist) is reserved for refractory cases, with droxidopa an option for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic mitral valve develops fever, a new pansystolic murmur, and Janeway lesions. Blood cultures grow Streptococcus viridans. Echocardiography shows a perivalvular abscess. What is the most important implication of the perivalvular abscess finding?
options: A. It confirms the need for at least 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy
B. It indicates metastatic infection to the liver
C. It predicts a high likelihood of requiring surgical intervention
D. It mandates addition of rifampin to the antibiotic regimen
questions.explanation: Perivalvular abscess is a serious complication of infective endocarditis (IE) and is associated with high rates of surgical intervention due to risks of valve dehiscence, fistula formation, complete heart block (from extension to the conduction system), and treatment failure with antibiotics alone. It is one of the major indications for surgical valve replacement in IE, along with heart failure, persistent bacteremia, large/mobile vegetations, and certain resistant organisms. Complete heart block on ECG in a patient with IE should raise strong suspicion for perivalvular abscess extending to the AV node. While prolonged antibiotics (4-6 weeks) are standard for prosthetic valve IE, the abscess specifically drives surgical decision-making.

questions.question: A 60-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back. BP is 180/100 in the right arm and 145/88 in the left arm. CXR shows a widened mediastinum. Which imaging modality is preferred for definitive diagnosis?
options: B. CT angiography of the chest with contrast
questions.explanation: CT angiography (CTA) of the chest with intravenous contrast is the preferred initial imaging for suspected aortic dissection due to its rapid acquisition, widespread availability, high sensitivity (>95%) and specificity (>95%), and ability to delineate the extent of dissection, involvement of branch vessels, and complications. MRI has comparable accuracy but is slower and less practical in an acute emergency. Transthoracic echocardiography can identify proximal aortic dissection and pericardial effusion but misses distal dissections; transesophageal echocardiography is more sensitive but invasive. Aortography was the historical gold standard but has largely been replaced by CTA due to its invasiveness and time requirements.

questions.question: Describe the DeBakey and Stanford classification systems for aortic dissection and explain how classification guides management.
questions.answer: The DeBakey classification divides dissections into three types: Type I originates in the ascending aorta and extends to the descending aorta or beyond; Type II is confined to the ascending aorta; Type III originates in the descending aorta (IIIa limited to thoracic, IIIb extending to abdominal aorta). The simpler Stanford classification groups dissections as Type A (involving the ascending aorta, regardless of origin) or Type B (not involving the ascending aorta, originating distal to the left subclavian artery). Stanford Type A dissection requires emergent surgical repair because of life-threatening complications including aortic regurgitation, pericardial tamponade, coronary artery involvement (causing MI), and stroke; surgical mortality is ~25% but far exceeds the near-100% mortality of untreated Type A. Stanford Type B dissection is managed medically with aggressive blood pressure and heart rate control (target SBP 100-120 mmHg, HR <60 bpm) using IV beta-blockers and vasodilators, with endovascular repair (TEVAR) reserved for complicated cases involving end-organ ischemia, rupture, or refractory pain.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes reports calf pain after walking one block that resolves with rest. His ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 0.62 bilaterally. What does this ABI value indicate?
questions.explanation: The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the ratio of ankle systolic BP to brachial systolic BP; normal values are 1.0-1.4. An ABI of 0.91-0.99 is borderline, 0.61-0.90 indicates mild-to-moderate PAD, 0.41-0.60 indicates moderate-to-severe PAD, and ≤0.40 indicates severe PAD or critical limb ischemia. This patient's ABI of 0.62 falls in the moderate PAD category, consistent with intermittent claudication. Critical limb ischemia is defined by rest pain, non-healing ulcers, or gangrene, typically associated with ABI ≤0.40 or ankle pressures <50 mmHg. Notably, falsely elevated ABI (>1.40) can occur in diabetics due to medial calcification causing arterial incompressibility.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with known peripheral arterial disease develops rest pain in his right foot with a non-healing ulcer on the great toe. His ABI is 0.35. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: C. Urgent vascular surgery referral for revascularization
questions.explanation: This patient has critical limb ischemia (CLI), defined by rest pain and tissue loss (non-healing ulcer) with a severely reduced ABI of 0.35. CLI represents an arterial insufficiency emergency with high risk of limb loss; urgent revascularization (surgical bypass or endovascular intervention) is required to salvage the limb. Supervised exercise programs and cilostazol are appropriate for intermittent claudication (functional limitation without tissue threat), not CLI. Compression stockings are used for venous insufficiency and are contraindicated in significant arterial disease as they may worsen perfusion. The Rutherford classification categories 4-6 (rest pain, minor tissue loss, major tissue loss) all require urgent revascularization evaluation.

questions.question: A cardiologist orders a stress echocardiogram rather than a nuclear stress test for a 58-year-old woman with exertional chest pain and a normal resting ECG. Compare the two modalities and explain the advantages of stress echocardiography.
questions.answer: Both stress echocardiography and nuclear stress testing (myocardial perfusion imaging, MPI) assess for inducible ischemia, but they differ in their mechanisms and advantages. Stress echocardiography detects new or worsening wall motion abnormalities during stress (exercise or pharmacologic), directly imaging myocardial contractile function, while nuclear MPI uses radiotracers (technetium-99m sestamibi or thallium-201) to map perfusion defects as surrogates for ischemia. Stress echo advantages include no ionizing radiation, lower cost, ability to evaluate valvular function and hemodynamic response simultaneously, and higher specificity (~85-90% vs ~75-85% for nuclear). Nuclear MPI has slightly higher sensitivity (~85-90% vs ~80-85% for echo) and is less operator-dependent, making it preferable when image quality is expected to be poor (obesity, COPD, poor acoustic window). In a woman with normal resting ECG and good exercise capacity, stress echo is preferred to avoid radiation exposure while gaining valvular and diastolic function information.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with dyspnea and suspected cardiac sarcoidosis is referred for advanced cardiac imaging. Which modality provides the best assessment of myocardial fibrosis and infiltrative disease?
options: A. Transthoracic echocardiography with strain imaging
C. Cardiac MRI with gadolinium late enhancement
questions.explanation: Cardiac MRI (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) is the gold standard for characterizing myocardial tissue, including fibrosis, infiltration, inflammation, and necrosis. In cardiac sarcoidosis, LGE shows a patchy, non-ischemic pattern (typically mid-myocardial or epicardial) that does not follow a coronary distribution, distinguishing it from ischemic cardiomyopathy. CMR can also assess myocardial edema (T2-weighted imaging), function, and perfusion. Echocardiography with strain imaging is sensitive for subclinical dysfunction but cannot characterize tissue composition. Cardiac CT excels at coronary anatomy and calcification but has limited soft-tissue characterization. Nuclear perfusion imaging assesses flow but does not characterize myocardial tissue architecture.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with progressive dyspnea undergoes right heart catheterization showing mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of 30 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 8 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) of 4.5 Wood units. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Left heart disease-associated pulmonary hypertension (Group 2)
questions.explanation: The 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines redefined pulmonary hypertension as mPAP >20 mmHg (previously >25 mmHg). Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, Group 1) is characterized by pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension: elevated mPAP >20 mmHg, PCWP ≤15 mmHg (confirming pre-capillary origin), and PVR >2 Wood units (confirming increased pulmonary vascular resistance). This patient's mPAP of 30 mmHg, PCWP of 8 mmHg, and PVR of 4.5 Wood units fulfill PAH criteria. Group 2 (left heart disease) would show elevated PCWP (>15 mmHg). Chronic thromboembolic PH (Group 4) has the same hemodynamic profile as PAH but requires V/Q scan and CT-PA to identify chronic thromboembolic disease.

questions.question: Describe the WHO functional classification for pulmonary hypertension and explain its clinical utility in guiding therapy.
questions.answer: The WHO functional classification (adapted from the NYHA classification) stratifies pulmonary hypertension patients into four classes based on symptoms and activity limitation: Class I has no symptoms with ordinary activity; Class II has slight limitation of physical activity with symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, near syncope) on ordinary exertion but comfortable at rest; Class III has marked limitation with symptoms on less-than-ordinary activity but comfortable at rest; Class IV has inability to carry out any physical activity without symptoms, with dyspnea and fatigue even at rest, and signs of right heart failure. WHO functional class is the single most important prognostic predictor in PAH and is the cornerstone of treatment algorithms in ESC/ERS and ACC/AHA guidelines. Class II-III patients are eligible for oral therapies (endothelin receptor antagonists like ambrisentan/macitentan, PDE-5 inhibitors like sildenafil/tadalafil, sGC stimulators like riociguat), while Class IV patients or those with rapid progression may require intravenous prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol) and urgent consideration for lung transplantation. Serial assessment of functional class guides treatment escalation and identifies responders.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman taking azithromycin and fluconazole for a vaginal infection develops palpitations. Her ECG shows a QTc of 520 ms. Which arrhythmia is she at greatest risk for?
questions.explanation: Torsades de pointes (TdP) is a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia specifically associated with QT prolongation; it appears as a characteristic twisting of the QRS complexes around the isoelectric baseline and can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Both azithromycin and fluconazole independently prolong the QT interval; their combination significantly increases TdP risk, particularly with a QTc >500 ms. Risk factors for drug-induced QT prolongation include female sex, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, bradycardia, structural heart disease, and congenital long QT syndrome. Immediate management includes discontinuing offending drugs, correcting electrolytes (potassium >4.0 mEq/L, magnesium >2.0 mEq/L), and for recurrent TdP, IV magnesium or temporary overdrive pacing to shorten the QT interval.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man collapses during a basketball game. He is resuscitated with an AED. His ECG shows a prolonged QTc of 490 ms. His father died suddenly at age 35. Genetic testing reveals a KCNQ1 mutation. Which statement is correct about congenital long QT syndrome?
options: A. LQT1 (KCNQ1 mutation) is associated with arrhythmias triggered by auditory stimuli
B. LQT1 events are most commonly triggered by exercise, especially swimming
C. LQT2 (KCNH2 mutation) carries a better prognosis than LQT1
D. Beta-blockers are contraindicated in congenital long QT syndrome
questions.explanation: LQT1 (KCNQ1 mutation, IKs channel deficiency) is the most common form of congenital LQTS and is characteristically triggered by exercise, particularly swimming, due to adrenergic stimulation during exertion. LQT2 (KCNH2 mutation, IKr channel deficiency) is triggered by sudden auditory stimuli (alarm clocks, phone ringing) and emotional stress. LQT3 (SCN5A mutation, sodium channel gain-of-function) events often occur at rest or during sleep. Beta-blockers are the cornerstone of therapy for LQT1 and LQT2, significantly reducing the risk of syncope and sudden cardiac death; they are particularly effective in LQT1. LQT2 has a worse prognosis than LQT1 in terms of clinical events despite similar QTc prolongation.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man presents with atrial fibrillation of uncertain duration (possibly >48 hours). He has a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3. Describe the two evidence-based strategies for safe cardioversion and the role of anticoagulation in each.
questions.answer: The 48-hour rule and TEE-guided cardioversion are the two standard strategies for safe electrical or pharmacologic cardioversion of atrial fibrillation. The conventional strategy requires therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before cardioversion (with warfarin INR 2-3 or a DOAC) and for at least 4 weeks after, based on the risk of atrial thrombus formation and post-cardioversion atrial stunning that persists even after restoration of sinus rhythm. The TEE-guided strategy involves performing transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion, allowing earlier cardioversion without 3 weeks of pre-procedure anticoagulation; anticoagulation must still be continued for at least 4 weeks post-cardioversion due to atrial stunning. For patients with AFib clearly of <48 hours duration, the risk of pre-formed thrombus is very low and cardioversion can proceed after heparin anticoagulation, followed by 4 weeks of anticoagulation. This patient's CHA2DS2-VASc of 3 indicates a high thromboembolic risk, mandating long-term anticoagulation (not just peri-cardioversion) with a DOAC as first-line therapy.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with no prior cardiac history undergoes an exercise stress test for pre-operative clearance. He exercises for 8 minutes on the Bruce protocol, achieving 90% of his maximum predicted heart rate without symptoms. There are 2 mm horizontal ST depressions in leads V4-V6 at peak exercise that resolve within 2 minutes of recovery. How should this test be interpreted?
options: A. Normal stress test; no further workup needed
B. Positive (abnormal) stress test suggesting inducible ischemia
C. Inconclusive test due to inadequate heart rate response
D. Duke treadmill score indicating very low risk
questions.explanation: A positive exercise stress test is defined by ≥1 mm horizontal or downsloping ST depression (or elevation in non-Q leads) at ≥60-80 ms after the J point during or after exercise. This patient shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in multiple leads, which is a clearly positive response. ST changes of this magnitude in multiple leads are associated with high sensitivity and specificity for significant coronary artery disease. The Duke Treadmill Score (exercise time – 5×ST deviation – 4×angina index) helps risk-stratify positive tests, but the magnitude of ST change here (2 mm, multiple leads) places this patient in a high-risk category warranting coronary angiography evaluation. Achieving 90% predicted heart rate confirms an adequate test.

questions.question: Explain the mechanism of action of statins, their classification by intensity, and the major adverse effects that clinicians must monitor.
questions.answer: Statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors) competitively inhibit the rate-limiting step in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, reducing intracellular cholesterol levels; this upregulates hepatic LDL receptor expression, increasing LDL clearance from the circulation and lowering plasma LDL by 30-55% depending on agent and dose. High-intensity statins (atorvastatin 40-80 mg, rosuvastatin 20-40 mg) reduce LDL by ≥50%; moderate-intensity (atorvastatin 10-20 mg, rosuvastatin 5-10 mg, simvastatin 20-40 mg, pravastatin 40-80 mg) reduce LDL by 30-50%; low-intensity (simvastatin 10 mg, pravastatin 10-20 mg, lovastatin 20 mg) reduce LDL by <30%. The most clinically important adverse effects are statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS), ranging from myalgia (most common, ~5-10%) to myopathy (CK >10x ULN) to rare but life-threatening rhabdomyolysis; risk is increased by drug interactions via CYP3A4 (simvastatin, lovastatin with azole antifungals, macrolides, cyclosporine), hypothyroidism, and high-dose therapy. Hepatotoxicity (clinically significant transaminase elevation >3x ULN) occurs in <1% of patients and is generally reversible; baseline and symptomatic liver function monitoring is recommended. Statins modestly increase fasting glucose and new-onset diabetes risk (~10% increase), which does not outweigh cardiovascular benefits in high-risk patients.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pallor, and pica (craving ice). Labs show Hgb 8.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, serum ferritin 4 ng/mL, and TIBC elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: C. Transfusion of packed red blood cells
questions.explanation: This patient has classic iron deficiency anemia: microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin (the most sensitive marker of iron stores) and elevated TIBC. Oral ferrous sulfate is first-line therapy for iron deficiency anemia in a stable, non-critically ill patient. Pica, particularly pagophagia (ice craving), is a classic symptom. Reticulocyte count should rise within 1 week, and hemoglobin should normalize over 1–2 months with continued therapy.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol use presents with macrocytic anemia (MCV 112 fL), glossitis, and peripheral smear showing hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes). Serum B12 is low. What is the underlying mechanism of his anemia?
options: A. Decreased intrinsic factor production leading to B12 malabsorption
B. Impaired DNA synthesis due to deficiency of a thymidylate synthesis cofactor
C. Increased red cell destruction by splenic macrophages
D. Suppression of erythropoiesis by chronic alcohol toxicity alone
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is essential as a cofactor for methionine synthase, which regenerates tetrahydrofolate (THF) needed for thymidylate synthesis and DNA replication. Deficiency leads to impaired DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells, causing megaloblastic anemia with hypersegmented neutrophils (5+ lobes in >5% of PMNs). Although alcohol directly suppresses marrow, hypersegmented neutrophils specifically indicate a megaloblastic etiology. Intrinsic factor deficiency causes pernicious anemia, a separate entity; in alcohol-associated deficiency, the mechanism is nutritional depletion.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is found to have hemolytic anemia with a positive direct Coombs test (DAT). Her LDH is elevated, haptoglobin is low, and peripheral smear shows spherocytes. Which diagnosis best fits this picture?
questions.explanation: A positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs) detects IgG antibodies or complement on the red cell surface, confirming immune-mediated hemolysis — the hallmark of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA). Spherocytes form because antibody-coated membranes are partially phagocytosed by splenic macrophages, leaving a smaller, spherical cell. Hereditary spherocytosis also causes spherocytes but is Coombs-negative. G6PD deficiency causes oxidative hemolysis with bite cells and a negative DAT. TTP presents with thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, and neurologic symptoms.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man with known sickle cell disease presents with severe chest pain, fever (38.8°C), new pulmonary infiltrates on CXR, and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air. What is the most immediately life-saving intervention?
questions.explanation: This patient has acute chest syndrome (ACS), defined as new pulmonary infiltrate with fever and/or respiratory symptoms in a sickle cell patient. ACS is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease and requires urgent exchange transfusion to rapidly reduce HbS percentage below 30% while maintaining adequate hemoglobin. Exchange transfusion (rather than simple transfusion) avoids hyperviscosity. Supportive measures include oxygen, bronchodilators, and incentive spirometry. Hydroxyurea is used for long-term prevention of crises, not acute management.

questions.question: Hemoglobin electrophoresis in a patient with microcytic anemia shows elevated HbA2 (4.8%) and elevated HbF (3.5%), with decreased HbA. This pattern is most consistent with which diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassemia trait (minor) is characterized by elevated HbA2 (>3.5%) and often elevated HbF, with decreased HbA — this is the diagnostic electrophoresis pattern. Beta-chain underproduction leads to relative excess of delta and gamma chains, which form HbA2 (α2δ2) and HbF (α2γ2) respectively. Alpha-thalassemia trait causes similar microcytosis but with normal HbA2, because alpha chains are needed for all hemoglobin types. Hemoglobin H disease (3-gene alpha deletion) shows HbH on electrophoresis.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with headache, plethora, pruritus after hot showers, and splenomegaly. CBC shows Hgb 20 g/dL, Hct 62%, WBC 13,000, and platelets 520,000. Which mutation is most likely present?
questions.explanation: Polycythemia vera (PV) presents with panmyelosis (elevated RBCs, WBCs, and platelets), splenomegaly, and characteristic aquagenic pruritus due to histamine release from increased basophils. The JAK2 V617F mutation is found in >95% of PV cases and is a WHO diagnostic criterion. This gain-of-function mutation causes constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signaling pathway, driving cytokine-independent erythroid proliferation. BCR-ABL is the hallmark of CML. FLT3-ITD is associated with AML. CALR mutations are found in JAK2-negative essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss, massive splenomegaly, and a WBC of 180,000/µL with the full spectrum of myeloid maturation on smear (myeloblasts <5%, many myelocytes and metamyelocytes). Philadelphia chromosome is detected. Which therapy is first-line?
options: D. Allogeneic stem cell transplant upfront
questions.explanation: This is chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) in chronic phase, defined by the BCR-ABL fusion gene from the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome. Imatinib, a BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), is established first-line therapy and achieves major cytogenetic remission in >80% of patients. TKIs have dramatically improved prognosis; allogeneic transplant is now reserved for blast crisis or TKI failure. The 7+3 induction regimen is for AML. Hydroxyurea may be used temporarily for cytoreduction but is not definitive treatment.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man is found incidentally to have lymphocytosis of 52,000/µL on routine CBC. Peripheral smear shows small, mature-appearing lymphocytes and many smudge cells. Flow cytometry shows CD5+, CD19+, CD23+ B cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most common adult leukemia and classically presents with asymptomatic lymphocytosis in elderly patients. Smudge (smear) cells result from fragile CLL lymphocytes rupturing during smear preparation and are pathognomonic. The immunophenotype CD5+/CD19+/CD23+ B cells is diagnostic of CLL. Hairy cell leukemia shows CD103+ B cells with cytoplasmic projections and causes pancytopenia, not lymphocytosis. Mantle cell lymphoma is also CD5+ but CD23- and carries t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a mediastinal mass, fever, drenching night sweats, and 12 lb weight loss over 2 months. Biopsy shows large binucleate cells with prominent 'owl-eye' nucleoli surrounded by a background of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Which regimen is standard first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Reed-Sternberg (RS) cells — large binucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli — are the pathognomonic finding of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (HL). B symptoms (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss) indicate systemic disease. ABVD is the standard first-line chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. CHOP and R-CHOP are used for non-Hodgkin lymphomas. RS cells are CD30+ and CD15+ but CD20-, which is why rituximab (anti-CD20) is not part of standard HL treatment.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with back pain, fatigue, and hypercalcemia. SPEP shows an M-spike in the gamma region. Urine protein electrophoresis reveals Bence Jones proteins. Skeletal survey shows multiple punched-out lytic lesions. Bone marrow biopsy shows 40% plasma cells. Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of his hypercalcemia?
options: A. PTH-related protein secretion by plasma cells
B. Osteoclast activation via RANKL secreted by myeloma cells
C. Ectopic calcitriol production by myeloma cells
D. Parathyroid adenoma as an incidental comorbidity
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma causes hypercalcemia through osteoclast activation. Myeloma cells and the bone marrow microenvironment produce RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand), which activates osteoclasts and suppresses osteoblasts, causing osteolytic lesions and calcium release. This is distinct from PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia of malignancy seen in solid tumors and from ectopic calcitriol production in granulomatous diseases. The CRAB criteria (hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions) define myeloma end-organ damage.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man with hemophilia A presents with a painful, swollen knee after minor trauma. His aPTT is prolonged; PT and platelet count are normal. Factor VIII activity is 2%. Which product should be administered?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by deficiency of factor VIII, presenting with hemarthroses, muscle hematomas, and prolonged aPTT with normal PT. Recombinant factor VIII concentrate is the treatment of choice for acute bleeding and is preferred over FFP due to precision dosing, lower infection risk, and absence of volume overload. Recombinant factor IX is used for hemophilia B (Christmas disease). Vitamin K corrects vitamin K-dependent factor deficiencies (II, VII, IX, X) and would not help here.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with septic shock develops oozing from IV sites, petechiae, and hematuria. Labs: platelets 28,000/µL, PT 22 sec, aPTT 68 sec, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL, D-dimer markedly elevated, schistocytes on smear. Which diagnosis best explains this picture?
questions.explanation: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characterized by simultaneous widespread clotting and bleeding due to massive coagulation activation. Classic lab findings include thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen (consumed), markedly elevated D-dimer (fibrin degradation products), and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes. Sepsis is the most common trigger. TTP also causes thrombocytopenia and schistocytes but features normal PT/aPTT and normal or elevated fibrinogen. HIT causes thrombocytopenia with thrombosis but does not prolong PT/aPTT or reduce fibrinogen.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child presents with pallor, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly. CBC shows WBC 95,000/µL with 90% lymphoblasts. Flow cytometry shows TdT+, CD10+, CD19+ cells. Cytogenetics reveal t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 fusion. What is the expected prognosis?
options: A. Poor; requires immediate allogeneic stem cell transplant in first remission
B. Favorable; associated with >90% long-term survival with standard chemotherapy
C. Intermediate; standard chemotherapy achieves remission but relapse is common
D. Poor; associated with Philadelphia chromosome-like signaling features
questions.explanation: B-cell ALL with t(12;21) creating the ETV6-RUNX1 (TEL-AML1) fusion is the most common cytogenetic abnormality in pediatric ALL (~25% of cases) and confers a favorable prognosis with >90% long-term survival with standard chemotherapy. TdT (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase) positivity is characteristic of lymphoblasts; CD10 (CALLA) and CD19 confirm B-lineage. The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) in ALL is high-risk and requires TKI addition plus consideration of transplant in first remission.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presents with acute leukemia. Peripheral smear shows blasts with rod-shaped cytoplasmic inclusions. He develops fever, prolonged PT/aPTT, and low fibrinogen shortly after starting standard induction chemotherapy. Which treatment is essential to add immediately?
questions.explanation: Auer rods (fused primary granules) in myeloid blasts combined with DIC is the classic presentation of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, AML-M3), caused by t(15;17) PML-RARA fusion. The DIC is driven by granule contents released from promyelocytes and worsens with standard chemotherapy. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) induces differentiation of the abnormal promyelocytes, rapidly improving the coagulopathy, and should be started immediately upon clinical suspicion without waiting for cytogenetic confirmation. ATRA plus arsenic trioxide is curative in >90% of APL cases.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has normocytic anemia (Hgb 9.8 g/dL). Serum iron is low, TIBC is low, ferritin is elevated at 320 ng/mL, and reticulocyte count is inappropriately low. Which mechanism best explains her anemia?
options: B. Hepcidin-mediated sequestration of iron in macrophages
C. Folate deficiency due to methotrexate therapy
D. Pure red cell aplasia from parvovirus B19 infection
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic disease (ACD)/anemia of inflammation is characterized by low serum iron, low TIBC (unlike iron deficiency, where TIBC is elevated), and elevated ferritin (an acute-phase reactant). The key mediator is hepcidin, produced by the liver in response to IL-6 and other inflammatory cytokines. Hepcidin degrades ferroportin on macrophages and enterocytes, trapping iron intracellularly and making it unavailable for erythropoiesis — a functional iron deficiency despite adequate total body iron stores. This explains the low serum iron with elevated ferritin.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology, clinical features, and major complications of sickle cell disease, including the mechanism by which hydroxyurea reduces crises.
questions.answer: Sickle cell disease is caused by a missense mutation (Glu→Val at beta-globin position 6) producing HbS. Under hypoxia, acidosis, or dehydration, HbS polymerizes into rigid fibers that distort red cells into sickle shapes, causing vascular occlusion, hemolysis, and ischemic organ damage. Clinically, patients suffer vaso-occlusive pain crises (from marrow and tissue ischemia), acute chest syndrome (new pulmonary infiltrates with hypoxia and fever — the leading cause of death), stroke, splenic sequestration crises, and priapism. Chronic complications include autosplenectomy with susceptibility to encapsulated organisms (Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae), avascular necrosis of the femoral head, sickle nephropathy, and proliferative retinopathy. Hydroxyurea increases fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2) production by activating gamma-globin gene expression through nitric oxide-mediated and cytotoxic mechanisms; HbF inhibits HbS polymerization, reducing sickling, crisis frequency, and acute chest syndrome episodes.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man is diagnosed with polycythemia vera. Explain the diagnostic criteria, the primary risk of this disease, and the rationale for therapeutic phlebotomy and cytoreductive therapy.
questions.answer: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm diagnosed by WHO criteria requiring elevated hematocrit (>49% in men, >48% in women), hypercellular bone marrow with trilineage hyperplasia (panmyelosis), and a JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation present in >95% of cases; serum erythropoietin is characteristically low or suppressed, distinguishing PV from secondary erythrocytosis. The primary morbidity and mortality risk is thrombosis — both arterial (stroke, MI) and venous (DVT/PE, Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic vein thrombosis) — driven by hyperviscosity and platelet dysfunction. Therapeutic phlebotomy targeting Hct <45% reduces blood viscosity and is first-line for all patients; this target was validated in the CYTO-PV trial showing a significantly lower thrombosis rate. Cytoreductive therapy with hydroxyurea (first-line) or ruxolitinib (for hydroxyurea-refractory or intolerant disease) is added for high-risk patients (age >60 or prior thrombotic event) to control myeloproliferation; low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily is recommended for all patients without contraindication to reduce arterial thrombosis risk.

questions.question: Compare and contrast alpha-thalassemia and beta-thalassemia in terms of genetics, pathophysiology, clinical severity spectrum, and key laboratory findings.
questions.answer: Both thalassemias result from reduced globin chain synthesis causing microcytic, hypochromic anemia with target cells and basophilic stippling, but they differ in genetics and severity. Alpha-thalassemia results from deletion of 1–4 alpha-globin genes (chromosome 16): 1-gene deletion is a silent carrier (normal labs), 2-gene deletion causes alpha-thalassemia trait (mild microcytosis, normal HbA2), 3-gene deletion causes HbH disease (moderate hemolytic anemia; excess beta chains form HbH = β4 tetramers), and 4-gene deletion causes hydrops fetalis (incompatible with life, HbBart = γ4 predominates). Beta-thalassemia results from point mutations in the beta-globin gene (chromosome 11): beta-thalassemia trait shows mild microcytosis with elevated HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis (diagnostic); beta-thalassemia intermedia causes moderate anemia with splenomegaly and some transfusion dependence; beta-thalassemia major (Cooley's anemia) presents in infancy with severe transfusion-dependent anemia, massive hepatosplenomegaly, extramedullary hematopoiesis ('hair-on-end' skull X-ray), and iron overload from repeated transfusions. Beta-thalassemia trait is distinguished from iron deficiency by normal ferritin and elevated HbA2.

questions.question: Explain the CRAB criteria for multiple myeloma, why an M-spike appears on SPEP, and how Bence Jones proteinuria develops and causes renal injury.
questions.answer: The CRAB criteria define myeloma end-organ damage: hyperCalcemia (calcium >11 mg/dL), Renal insufficiency (creatinine >2 mg/dL or CrCl <40 mL/min), Anemia (Hgb <10 g/dL), and Bone lesions (lytic lesions or severe osteoporosis with fractures). The M-spike on serum protein electrophoresis reflects secretion of a monoclonal immunoglobulin by a single neoplastic plasma cell clone; because every cell in the clone produces identical protein with identical charge, it migrates as a single sharp band rather than the broad polyclonal gamma region seen in normal reactive states. Bence Jones proteins are free immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) that, due to their small size (~22 kDa), pass freely through the glomerular filtration barrier and appear in urine. In renal tubules, free light chains are endocytosed and directly toxic to proximal tubular cells, causing tubular dysfunction (Fanconi syndrome); they also precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal tubule to form obstructive casts (myeloma cast nephropathy or light chain cast nephropathy), leading to progressive renal failure that may require dialysis.

questions.question: Describe von Willebrand disease: how it differs clinically from hemophilia, the role of the ristocetin cofactor assay in diagnosis, and the treatment approach for the most common subtype.
questions.answer: Von Willebrand disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor (vWF), which mediates platelet adhesion to subendothelium and stabilizes factor VIII in circulation. Unlike hemophilias (which impair secondary hemostasis causing deep tissue bleeds such as hemarthroses and retroperitoneal hematomas), vWD presents with mucocutaneous bleeding — easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after dental extractions — reflecting its primary role in platelet plug formation. Laboratory findings include prolonged bleeding time/PFA-100, and in severe cases a mildly prolonged aPTT due to low factor VIII; platelet count is normal. The ristocetin cofactor assay measures the ability of patient plasma vWF to agglutinate formalin-fixed platelets in the presence of ristocetin, an antibiotic that induces conformational change in vWF and mimics its collagen-binding; reduced agglutination confirms vWF dysfunction and distinguishes vWD from hemophilia. Type 1 vWD (quantitative partial deficiency, ~75–80% of cases) is treated with desmopressin (DDAVP), which triggers release of endogenous vWF from Weibel-Palade bodies in endothelial cells; severe disease or type 3 (complete absence) requires vWF concentrate.
