questions.question: A patient develops pancytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular marrow with >70% fat and markedly reduced hematopoietic cells. Describe the pathophysiology of aplastic anemia, how it is distinguished from other causes of pancytopenia, and its treatment approach.
questions.answer: Aplastic anemia results from destruction or suppression of hematopoietic stem cells, most commonly by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes producing interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha that drive Fas-mediated apoptosis of stem cells; most cases are idiopathic, but triggers include medications (chloramphenicol, sulfonamides), viral infections (EBV, hepatitis), and toxins. The hypocellular 'fatty' marrow on biopsy distinguishes aplastic anemia from other causes of pancytopenia such as myelodysplastic syndrome (hypercellular or normocellular with dysplasia and ringed sideroblasts), acute leukemia (hypercellular with blasts), megaloblastic anemia (hypercellular with megaloblastic changes), and bone marrow infiltration by lymphoma or solid tumor. Distinguishing peripheral features include absence of splenomegaly, no blasts in peripheral blood, and a very low absolute reticulocyte count. For treatment, young patients with severe aplastic anemia who have a matched sibling donor undergo allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which is curative. Patients without a suitable donor or older patients receive immunosuppressive therapy with horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) plus cyclosporine, targeting the autoreactive T cells; eltrombopag (a thrombopoietin receptor agonist) is now added upfront to improve response rates and depth.

questions.question: Describe Richter transformation in CLL: what it is, how it presents clinically, its prognosis, and how it is diagnosed.
questions.answer: Richter transformation (RT) is the development of an aggressive lymphoma — most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL, ~80–95% of cases) or, rarely, classical Hodgkin lymphoma (~5%) — arising from an underlying CLL clone through clonal evolution with acquisition of additional genomic hits such as TP53 mutation, CDKN2A deletion, or MYC rearrangement. It occurs in approximately 5–10% of CLL patients over their lifetime. Clinically, RT should be suspected when a CLL patient develops rapidly enlarging lymph nodes (often discordant, with one region growing disproportionately), constitutional B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss), markedly elevated LDH, and hypercalcemia — features atypical of stable CLL progression. PET-CT typically shows markedly increased FDG uptake (SUVmax >5) in the transformed nodal region, and biopsy of the most metabolically active node is essential for diagnosis, showing DLBCL histology on excisional biopsy. Prognosis is poor, with a median overall survival of 6–12 months; treatment is intensive chemoimmunotherapy (e.g., R-CHOP) followed by consolidative allogeneic stem cell transplant in eligible patients who achieve remission.

questions.question: A patient is diagnosed with follicular lymphoma. Explain the molecular basis of follicular lymphoma, its typical clinical behavior, and the rationale for 'watch and wait' vs. initiating treatment.
questions.answer: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is an indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising from germinal center B cells; its molecular hallmark is t(14;18)(q32;q21), juxtaposing the BCL2 gene (chromosome 18) with the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer (chromosome 14), causing constitutive BCL-2 anti-apoptotic protein overexpression that prevents normal germinal center apoptosis and allows clonal B-cell accumulation. Clinically, FL presents with painless waxing-and-waning lymphadenopathy, is typically disseminated (stage III–IV) at diagnosis, and follows an indolent course with median survival of 10–15 years; however, it is generally not curable with standard chemoimmunotherapy due to persistent minimal residual disease and recurrence. The 'watch and wait' (active surveillance) approach is appropriate for asymptomatic patients with low tumor burden because treatment in this setting has not been shown to improve overall survival and delays toxicity; some patients remain stable or even demonstrate spontaneous regression for years. Treatment — typically bendamustine-rituximab or R-CHOP — is initiated for high tumor burden or symptomatic disease, defined by GELF criteria: bulky disease >7 cm, >3 nodal sites each >3 cm, B symptoms, organ compromise, cytopenias, or significant serous effusion.

questions.question: Describe Burkitt lymphoma: its molecular pathogenesis, clinical presentation subtypes, hallmark histologic findings, and key management considerations.
questions.answer: Burkitt lymphoma (BL) is a highly aggressive B-cell NHL driven by translocations activating the MYC oncogene — most commonly t(8;14), placing MYC under the IgH enhancer, or less commonly t(8;22) or t(2;8) — leading to uncontrolled proliferation with a doubling time of approximately 24 hours and a Ki-67 proliferation index near 100%. Three clinical subtypes exist: endemic (African) BL, strongly associated with EBV infection and presenting as jaw/facial bone tumors in children; sporadic (Western) BL, presenting as abdominal tumors at the ileocecal region with ascites and bowel obstruction; and immunodeficiency-associated BL, seen in HIV-positive patients. Histologically, BL shows a 'starry sky' pattern — sheets of monomorphic medium-sized lymphoblasts (dark sky) interspersed with tingible body macrophages phagocytizing apoptotic debris (pale stars). Management requires immediate, intensive multi-agent chemotherapy (e.g., R-CODOX-M/IVAC or DA-EPOCH-R), as delays of even days lead to disease progression. Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is a critical concern due to the massive cell death induced by chemotherapy; prophylaxis with aggressive IV hydration, allopurinol or rasburicase (for high-risk patients), and close monitoring of uric acid, potassium, phosphate, and creatinine is mandatory.

questions.question: Describe mantle cell lymphoma: its molecular hallmark, typical clinical presentation, how it is distinguished from CLL on flow cytometry, and the significance of blastoid transformation.
questions.answer: Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) is an aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma caused by t(11;14)(q13;q32), which places the CCND1 gene (encoding cyclin D1) under the immunoglobulin heavy chain enhancer, resulting in constitutive cyclin D1 overexpression that drives cell cycle progression from G1 to S phase and uncontrolled proliferation. Clinically, MCL typically presents in older men (median age ~65) with advanced-stage disease: generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, bone marrow involvement, and often peripheral blood involvement (leukemic phase); GI tract involvement (lymphomatous polyposis) is a characteristic feature. On flow cytometry, MCL is CD5+/CD19+/CD20+ but CD23-negative and FMC7-positive, distinguishing it from CLL (which is CD5+/CD23+/FMC7-negative); cyclin D1 immunohistochemistry or SOX11 staining confirms MCL. Blastoid transformation is a morphologic variant with blastoid or pleomorphic large cells, very high Ki-67 (>50–90%), and markedly elevated LDH; it signals aggressive clinical behavior with rapid nodal enlargement and carries a poor prognosis, requiring intensive salvage regimens and consideration of allogeneic stem cell transplantation in eligible patients.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with petechiae and a platelet count of 8,000/µL. She has no splenomegaly, normal PT/PTT, and no systemic illness. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), where autoantibodies target platelet surface glycoproteins leading to accelerated splenic destruction. First-line treatment is corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day), which suppress antibody production and reduce phagocytosis. IVIG is an alternative for rapid platelet rise (e.g., prior to surgery or severe bleeding). Platelet transfusion is generally avoided as transfused platelets are rapidly destroyed; rituximab and splenectomy are reserved for refractory cases.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man develops severe thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, fever, renal failure, and neurologic changes 5 days after starting a new medication. ADAMTS13 activity is less than 10%. What is the most critical next step?
options: C. Fresh frozen plasma infusion only
questions.explanation: This pentad (thrombocytopenia, MAHA, fever, renal failure, neurologic changes) with ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). ADAMTS13 deficiency leads to accumulation of ultra-large vWF multimers, causing platelet aggregation and microvascular thrombosis. Plasma exchange (plasmapheresis) is the cornerstone of treatment, simultaneously removing the inhibitory antibody against ADAMTS13 and replenishing the enzyme. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated as it can worsen microvascular thrombosis.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with a history of unfractionated heparin therapy 8 days ago develops a new DVT and his platelet count has dropped from 220,000 to 85,000/µL. His 4T score is 6. Which anticoagulant should be started?
questions.explanation: A 4T score of 6 indicates high probability of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), an immune-mediated disorder caused by antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes. All heparin products (including LMWH) must be immediately discontinued. The direct thrombin inhibitor argatroban is the preferred alternative anticoagulant, especially in patients with renal insufficiency. Warfarin should not be started alone due to risk of warfarin-induced skin necrosis from protein C depletion; it can be overlapped with a direct thrombin inhibitor only once platelets recover above 150,000/µL.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with left leg swelling and pain. She scores 3 on the Wells DVT criteria. D-dimer is 1,200 ng/mL. Duplex ultrasound confirms proximal DVT. She is otherwise healthy with no prior clots. Which anticoagulation regimen is preferred for initial treatment?
options: A. Unfractionated heparin infusion for 5 days followed by warfarin
B. Rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily for 21 days then 20 mg daily
C. Low-molecular-weight heparin for 3 months then stop
D. Warfarin initiated without bridging anticoagulation
questions.explanation: Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as rivaroxaban are preferred for initial and long-term treatment of DVT due to ease of use, no monitoring requirement, and comparable efficacy and safety to LMWH/warfarin. Rivaroxaban follows a specific dosing protocol: 15 mg BID for 21 days (loading phase), then 20 mg daily for maintenance. Warfarin requires bridging anticoagulation because it initially causes a prothrombotic state by depleting protein C and S before therapeutic anticoagulation is achieved. LMWH alone for 3 months is an option but less convenient than oral therapy for most patients.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man has a PE confirmed by CT-PA. He has a history of recurrent unprovoked DVT. Hypercoagulable workup shows a heterozygous Factor V Leiden mutation. How long should anticoagulation be continued?
questions.explanation: Recurrent unprovoked venous thromboembolism (VTE) is a strong indication for indefinite anticoagulation, as the risk of recurrence exceeds 30% at 5 years without treatment. Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited thrombophilia, causing resistance to activated protein C and increasing thrombotic risk. Even for a first unprovoked VTE with Factor V Leiden, indefinite therapy is recommended by most guidelines. The combination of a recurrent unprovoked event and confirmed thrombophilia makes indefinite anticoagulation clearly appropriate and guideline-supported.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman has three pregnancy losses and recurrent arterial thromboses. Labs show lupus anticoagulant positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart, anticardiolipin IgG elevated, and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I IgG elevated. What is the best long-term anticoagulation strategy?
questions.explanation: This patient has triple-positive antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), the highest-risk serologic profile, confirmed by two positive tests 12 weeks apart per Sapporo criteria. Warfarin with target INR 2.0–3.0 remains the standard of care for APS with thrombosis. DOACs (e.g., rivaroxaban) have been shown in the TRAPS trial to be inferior to warfarin in triple-positive APS, with higher rates of recurrent thrombosis. Aspirin alone is insufficient for venous or arterial thrombosis in APS; higher INR targets (3.0–4.0) are not routinely superior and increase bleeding risk without added benefit.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man is found to have macrocytic anemia with ring sideroblasts comprising 25% of erythroid precursors on bone marrow biopsy. Cytogenetics are normal. IPSS-R score places him in the intermediate-risk category. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
options: C. Sideroblastic anemia due to lead poisoning
questions.explanation: Ring sideroblasts (erythroid precursors with perinuclear iron deposits encircling at least one-third of the nucleus) are the hallmark of MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS), formerly RARS. SF3B1 mutations are present in over 80% of cases and are associated with a relatively favorable prognosis. 5q- syndrome is characterized by isolated del(5q) cytogenetics and responds to lenalidomide, which is not present here. Lead poisoning causes basophilic stippling and acquired sideroblastic anemia but is not classified as MDS. Aplastic anemia features a hypocellular marrow without ring sideroblasts.

questions.question: A 65-year-old woman with MDS and isolated del(5q) has transfusion-dependent anemia. She has a normal or elevated platelet count and hypolobulated megakaryocytes on marrow biopsy. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: 5q- syndrome is a distinct MDS subtype defined by isolated deletion of chromosome 5q, presenting with macrocytic anemia, relative thrombocytosis, and characteristic hypolobulated megakaryocytes. Lenalidomide is highly effective in 5q- syndrome, achieving transfusion independence in approximately 67% of patients and cytogenetic remission in many. It works by targeting the haploinsufficiency of RPS14 (ribosomal protein S14) on chromosome 5q. Azacitidine is used for higher-risk MDS; allogeneic SCT is reserved for high-risk disease or young patients with suitable donors.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with severe pancytopenia. Bone marrow biopsy shows markedly hypocellular marrow (<10% cellularity) with fat replacement. Flow cytometry reveals a PNH clone in 15% of red blood cells. He has an HLA-matched sibling. What is the best treatment?
questions.explanation: Severe aplastic anemia (SAA) in a young patient with a matched sibling donor is best treated with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), which offers the highest chance of cure (~80% long-term survival). Immunosuppression with horse ATG plus cyclosporine is preferred for patients without a matched donor or those who are older or have significant comorbidities. The presence of a PNH clone is common in aplastic anemia and does not change the primary treatment approach. Eculizumab targets complement and is used for symptomatic PNH hemolysis but does not address the underlying aplasia.

questions.question: During a blood transfusion, a patient develops fever (temperature rise >1°C), chills, and malaise without hypotension or hemolysis. The direct antiglobulin test on the transfused unit is negative. What is the most likely reaction?
questions.explanation: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR) is the most common transfusion reaction, caused by recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte HLA antigens or by cytokines that accumulate in stored blood products. It presents with fever and chills without evidence of hemolysis or respiratory compromise. Pre-medicating with acetaminophen and using leukoreduced blood products reduces incidence. Acute hemolytic reactions involve ABO incompatibility with fever, back pain, hemoglobinuria, and hemodynamic instability. TRALI presents with new hypoxia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within 6 hours of transfusion.

questions.question: A patient receiving a blood transfusion suddenly develops fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and hypotension. The direct antiglobulin test is positive. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: A. Slow the transfusion rate and give diphenhydramine
B. Stop the transfusion, administer IV fluids, and verify clerical records
D. Give furosemide to prevent renal failure
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (AHTR), most commonly caused by ABO incompatibility due to clerical error. Intravascular hemolysis triggers complement activation, cytokine release, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The immediate action is to stop the transfusion, maintain IV access with normal saline for renal protection, and verify blood type compatibility by checking patient identification and blood bank records. The blood bank must be notified immediately and a direct antiglobulin test and repeat blood type performed on both the recipient and the remaining donor unit.

questions.question: A hospitalized patient has a prolonged PTT but a normal PT. A mixing study corrects the PTT to normal. What is the most likely explanation?
options: C. Factor VIII, IX, XI, or XII deficiency
questions.explanation: An isolated prolonged PTT tests the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII) and common pathway factors. A mixing study adds normal plasma 1:1 with patient plasma; if the PTT corrects, it indicates a factor deficiency because the added normal plasma supplies the missing factor. If the PTT does not correct, an inhibitor (such as lupus anticoagulant or acquired factor VIII inhibitor) is present. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs both PT and PTT as it affects factors II, VII, IX, and X. Lupus anticoagulant characteristically causes a non-correcting PTT despite its paradoxically prothrombotic clinical effect in vivo.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man with Burkitt lymphoma begins chemotherapy. Two days later, his labs show potassium 6.8 mEq/L, phosphorus 7.2 mg/dL, calcium 6.8 mg/dL, uric acid 14 mg/dL, and creatinine 3.1 mg/dL. Which treatment is most effective for rapidly lowering the elevated uric acid?
questions.explanation: This patient has established tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) with hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and acute kidney injury. Rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) is preferred over allopurinol in this setting because it actively converts existing uric acid to the more soluble allantoin, rapidly reducing uric acid levels within hours. Allopurinol only prevents new uric acid synthesis by inhibiting xanthine oxidase and does not lower existing uric acid levels. Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency due to risk of hemolytic anemia from hydrogen peroxide accumulation. Hemodialysis is reserved for refractory electrolyte abnormalities or severe oliguria.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents with fatigue, weight loss, and visual blurring. Labs show IgM paraprotein of 4.2 g/dL, Hgb 8.9 g/dL, and serum viscosity of 6.5 cP (normal <1.8 cP). Bone marrow shows lymphoplasmacytic infiltration. What is the most urgent intervention?
questions.explanation: Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) is characterized by IgM paraproteinemia arising from a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma infiltrating the marrow. IgM is a large pentameric molecule that remains predominantly intravascular, leading to hyperviscosity syndrome (visual changes, headache, neurologic symptoms, epistaxis) at relatively lower concentrations compared to IgG or IgA. Plasmapheresis rapidly reduces serum IgM and viscosity, providing immediate symptomatic relief and is the urgent intervention for symptomatic hyperviscosity. Definitive chemotherapy (rituximab-based regimens or ibrutinib) addresses the underlying disease but acts too slowly to manage acute hyperviscosity crisis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with a history of asthma and chronic sinusitis presents with new peripheral eosinophilia (eosinophil count 4,500/µL), mononeuritis multiplex, and skin nodules. MPO-ANCA is positive. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?
options: C. Parasitic infection with tissue invasion
questions.explanation: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome, is an ANCA-associated vasculitis characterized by the triad of asthma, eosinophilia, and granulomatous vasculitis. MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA) positivity is found in approximately 40% of cases and correlates with vasculitic manifestations including mononeuritis multiplex and glomerulonephritis. Treatment involves high-dose corticosteroids for induction, with cyclophosphamide or mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) for refractory or severe cases. Idiopathic HES lacks the asthma and sinusitis history with ANCA positivity; parasitic infections typically do not cause ANCA-associated vasculitis or peripheral neuropathy.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology, diagnostic approach using the 4T score, and management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
questions.answer: HIT is an immune-mediated adverse drug reaction in which IgG antibodies form against heparin-platelet factor 4 (PF4) complexes, activating platelets and endothelial cells to generate thrombin and create a paradoxical prothrombotic state despite thrombocytopenia. The 4T scoring system (Thrombocytopenia magnitude, Timing of platelet fall at 5–10 days, Thrombosis or skin necrosis, other causes of Thrombocytopenia) stratifies pre-test probability; a score of 0–3 is low probability, 4–5 intermediate, and 6–8 high. Laboratory confirmation uses the heparin-PF4 ELISA (high sensitivity, good initial screen) followed by the serotonin release assay (SRA, gold standard with >95% specificity). All heparin products must be immediately discontinued, and a non-heparin anticoagulant—argatroban (direct thrombin inhibitor, preferred in hepatic-sparing patients) or bivalirudin—initiated due to 30–50% thrombosis risk. Warfarin should not be started until the platelet count recovers above 150,000/µL to avoid warfarin-induced venous limb gangrene from precipitous protein C depletion.

questions.question: Explain the Wells criteria for pulmonary embolism and how the PERC rule is applied in clinical practice to minimize unnecessary imaging.
questions.answer: The Wells PE score assigns weighted points: clinical signs of DVT (3 points), alternative diagnosis less likely than PE (3), heart rate >100 bpm (1.5), immobilization or surgery within 4 weeks (1.5), prior DVT or PE (1.5), hemoptysis (1), and active malignancy (1); a score ≤4 indicates low/intermediate probability and >4 indicates high probability. In patients deemed low probability (pretest probability <15%), the PERC rule can rule out PE without D-dimer testing if all eight criteria are absent: age <50, heart rate <100, SpO2 ≥95%, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no recent surgery or trauma, no prior DVT/PE, and no exogenous estrogen use. When all PERC criteria are met in a low-probability patient, the post-test probability falls below 2%, safely avoiding CT-PA and D-dimer testing. For PERC-positive but low-probability patients, a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer effectively excludes PE without imaging. High-probability patients should proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiography regardless of D-dimer result.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with recurrent spontaneous abortions and a DVT. Describe the diagnostic criteria and management of antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
questions.answer: APS is diagnosed by the combination of clinical criteria (vascular thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity including ≥3 unexplained miscarriages <10 weeks, ≥1 fetal death ≥10 weeks, or premature birth <34 weeks due to preeclampsia/placental insufficiency) and laboratory criteria confirmed on two occasions at least 12 weeks apart. The three laboratory tests are lupus anticoagulant (most predictive of thrombosis), anticardiolipin antibodies IgG/IgM (≥40 GPL/MPL or >99th percentile), and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I antibodies IgG/IgM (>99th percentile). Triple positivity (all three tests positive) confers the highest thrombotic risk and warrants warfarin with target INR 2.0–3.0 rather than DOACs, based on the TRAPS trial demonstrating inferiority of rivaroxaban in this group. Obstetric APS without prior thrombosis is managed with low-dose aspirin plus prophylactic LMWH throughout pregnancy. Catastrophic APS, featuring multi-organ microvascular thrombosis, requires simultaneous anticoagulation, high-dose corticosteroids, plasma exchange, and IVIG.

questions.question: Describe the clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of aplastic anemia, including its pathophysiologic relationship to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).
questions.answer: Aplastic anemia is characterized by pancytopenia (anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) due to immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells by autoreactive T-lymphocytes, leading to bone marrow failure. Diagnosis requires bone marrow biopsy showing hypocellularity (<25% cellularity, or <50% with <30% hematopoietic cells) with fat replacement, after excluding other causes such as myelodysplasia, leukemia, or nutritional deficiencies. PNH clones (cells lacking GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins CD55 and CD59) are detected by flow cytometry in 20–50% of aplastic anemia patients, because GPI-deficient HSCs escape immune attack and expand selectively in the autoimmune environment; patients with large PNH clones are at risk for hemolytic crises and venous thrombosis. Treatment depends on donor availability: allogeneic HSCT is curative (~80% long-term survival) and preferred for younger patients (<40 years) with matched sibling donors; horse ATG plus cyclosporine (with or without eltrombopag) is used when transplant is not feasible. Eculizumab, a monoclonal antibody blocking complement C5, effectively treats PNH-associated hemolysis and thrombosis but does not correct the underlying aplasia.

questions.question: Describe the approach to evaluating a patient with an isolated prolonged PT and normal PTT, including the differential diagnosis and key confirmatory steps.
questions.answer: An isolated prolonged PT (with normal PTT) indicates dysfunction of the extrinsic pathway, specifically factor VII deficiency or inhibition, since factor VII is the only clotting factor exclusive to the extrinsic pathway and has the shortest half-life (~4–6 hours) among all coagulation factors. The most common cause is early vitamin K deficiency or warfarin therapy, which preferentially reduces factor VII before factors II, IX, and X are significantly depleted, making the PT more sensitive than the PTT in early deficiency states. Liver disease can cause isolated PT prolongation in early stages before global synthetic dysfunction develops. Rare causes include congenital factor VII deficiency or an acquired factor VII inhibitor. A mixing study is the next key step: correction of the PT with normal plasma indicates a factor deficiency, while non-correction suggests an inhibitor. Specific factor VII activity assay, vitamin K levels, and liver function tests confirm the diagnosis and direct treatment.

questions.question: Outline the prevention and management of tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) in a patient about to begin chemotherapy for high-grade lymphoma.
questions.answer: TLS occurs when rapid cell lysis releases intracellular contents, causing hyperuricemia, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, and secondary hypocalcemia, which can precipitate cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and acute kidney injury. Risk stratification guides prophylaxis: high-risk patients (e.g., Burkitt lymphoma, high LDH, bulky disease, high WBC) receive rasburicase prior to chemotherapy, while intermediate-risk patients receive allopurinol (which blocks xanthine oxidase to prevent new uric acid formation but does not reduce existing levels). Aggressive IV hydration (2–3 L/m²/day of isotonic saline) to maintain urine output above 80–100 mL/hr is the cornerstone of prevention, reducing precipitation of urate and phosphate crystals in renal tubules. Electrolytes should be monitored every 4–6 hours; hyperkalemia may require sodium polystyrene sulfonate, insulin-glucose, or dialysis, while hyperphosphatemia is managed with dietary restriction and oral phosphate binders. Hypocalcemia should only be treated if symptomatic (tetany, seizures, arrhythmias) because calcium supplementation in the setting of elevated phosphorus promotes calcium-phosphate precipitation and worsens renal injury. Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency because the hydrogen peroxide byproduct of urate oxidation causes hemolytic anemia.

questions.question: What are the indications for IVC filter placement, and what are the risks associated with their long-term use?
questions.answer: Inferior vena cava (IVC) filters are indicated when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated in a patient with established DVT or PE—for example, active intracranial hemorrhage, recent neurosurgery, or severe thrombocytopenia with active bleeding—or when there is documented failure of adequate anticoagulation despite therapeutic levels. IVC filters reduce the risk of PE but do not treat the underlying thrombosis and are not a substitute for anticoagulation. Long-term risks include IVC thrombosis (up to 20%), filter migration or fracture with potential cardiac embolization, caval penetration, and paradoxically increased risk of recurrent DVT (demonstrated in the PREPIC trial), though short-term PE risk is reduced. Retrievable filters should be removed as soon as anticoagulation becomes safe, typically within the manufacturer-specified retrieval window, since permanent filters carry substantially higher complication rates over time. Anticoagulation should be reinitiated as soon as the contraindication resolves, even in patients with an IVC filter in place.

questions.question: Describe the clinical presentation, pathophysiology, and management of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI), and explain how it is distinguished from transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO).
questions.answer: TRALI presents within 6 hours of transfusion with acute hypoxia (PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg or SpO2 <90% on room air), new bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, and no evidence of pre-existing acute lung injury before transfusion; it is caused by donor anti-HLA or anti-neutrophil antibodies that activate recipient neutrophils, damaging pulmonary capillary endothelium and causing noncardiogenic pulmonary edema. TACO, by contrast, results from fluid overload and presents with hypertension, elevated BNP (typically >250 pg/mL), cardiomegaly, and bilateral infiltrates reflecting cardiogenic pulmonary edema; it responds to diuretics. Management of TRALI is supportive: immediately stop the transfusion, administer supplemental oxygen, and use mechanical ventilation with lung-protective strategy if needed; diuretics are ineffective and potentially harmful. The blood bank should be notified to quarantine the implicated donor unit for antibody testing and perform recipient leukocyte antigen typing. TRALI carries a fatality rate of 5–10% and remains one of the leading causes of transfusion-related mortality in developed countries.

questions.question: Describe hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES): definition, diagnostic workup, potential organ complications, and treatment approach.
questions.answer: Hypereosinophilic syndrome is defined by persistent eosinophilia above 1,500/µL for more than 6 months with evidence of eosinophil-mediated end-organ damage, after thorough exclusion of secondary causes including parasitic infections, atopic disease, drug reactions, EGPA, and eosinophilia-associated malignancies. Workup includes bone marrow biopsy with cytogenetics, FISH for the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene (found in ~15% of HES, predominantly in males, markedly sensitive to imatinib), T-cell receptor clonality studies to identify lymphocytic-variant HES, and serum tryptase (elevated in myeloid HES). Organ damage most critically affects the heart (endomyocardial fibrosis, Löffler endocarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, mural thrombus), peripheral nervous system (mononeuritis multiplex), skin (urticaria, angioedema, erythroderma), and lungs (infiltrates, effusions). Treatment is subtype-driven: PDGFRA-rearranged HES responds dramatically to low-dose imatinib (100 mg/day) and is first-line; corticosteroids are first-line for lymphocytic-variant and idiopathic HES; mepolizumab (anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody) is effective for steroid-dependent or refractory cases. All patients with cardiac involvement require echocardiography and anticoagulation given the high thrombotic risk from intracardiac thrombus.

questions.question: A patient with known protein C deficiency is started on warfarin for a DVT without heparin bridge anticoagulation and develops warfarin-induced skin necrosis. Explain the pathophysiology, prevention, and treatment of this complication.
questions.answer: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis occurs in patients with underlying protein C (or protein S) deficiency because protein C is a vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant with a very short half-life (~8 hours), far shorter than the procoagulant factors II and X. When warfarin is initiated without heparin bridging, protein C levels fall rapidly first, creating a transient hypercoagulable window before adequate inhibition of factors II and X is achieved; this leads to dermal microvascular thrombosis and infarction in fat-rich areas such as the buttocks, breasts, and thighs. Prevention requires overlapping therapeutic heparin (or another anticoagulant) until the INR has been supratherapeutic (>2) for at least two consecutive days before heparin is discontinued, ensuring procoagulant factors are depleted before the anticoagulant bridge is removed. Treatment involves immediately stopping warfarin, administering vitamin K to partially restore vitamin K-dependent factors, infusing fresh frozen plasma or protein C concentrate to replenish protein C, and continuing a non-warfarin anticoagulant to maintain thrombosis protection. The same complication can occur in protein S deficiency and, rarely, in patients without known deficiency who receive large loading doses of warfarin.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presents with fever, productive cough, and confusion. His BUN is 24 mg/dL, respiratory rate is 28/min, and blood pressure is 88/60 mmHg. Using the CURB-65 score, which management is most appropriate?
options: A. Outpatient treatment with oral amoxicillin
B. Outpatient treatment with oral azithromycin
C. Inpatient treatment with consideration of ICU admission
D. Inpatient treatment on general medical ward only
questions.explanation: This patient scores 4 on CURB-65 (Confusion, BUN >19, RR ≥30, BP <90 systolic or ≤60 diastolic, Age ≥65). A CURB-65 score of 3–5 indicates severe CAP with high 30-day mortality risk and warrants inpatient treatment with consideration of ICU-level care. Scores of 0–1 support outpatient management, while a score of 2 suggests inpatient admission on a general ward.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man who recently stayed at a hotel develops fever, dry cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray shows a lobar infiltrate. Which diagnostic test is most useful for rapidly confirming the likely causative organism?
options: A. Sputum Gram stain and culture
D. Blood culture with extended incubation
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for Legionella pneumophila pneumonia, suggested by hotel exposure (contaminated water source), GI symptoms, and neurologic involvement. The Legionella urinary antigen test is rapid, highly specific, and detects serogroup 1 (the most common cause). Cold agglutinins are associated with Mycoplasma pneumoniae, not Legionella. Sputum and blood cultures can grow Legionella but are slow and less sensitive.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman develops fever and purulent sputum 7 days after being intubated in the ICU. Tracheal aspirate grows Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which antibiotic regimen is most appropriate for ventilator-associated pneumonia in this setting?
questions.explanation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa requires antipseudomonal coverage. Piperacillin-tazobactam is a broad-spectrum beta-lactam with antipseudomonal activity, and combination with an aminoglycoside (tobramycin) provides synergistic coverage and reduces resistance emergence. Azithromycin/ceftriaxone covers CAP organisms but lacks reliable antipseudomonal activity. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and levofloxacin alone are insufficient for Pseudomonas VAP in critically ill patients.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder is found unconscious and later develops fever with a chest X-ray showing a right lower lobe infiltrate with a cavity. Which organism is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia in alcoholics predisposes to infection with gram-negative organisms, and Klebsiella pneumoniae classically causes a necrotizing, cavitary pneumonia in immunocompromised or alcoholic patients, with the characteristic 'bulging fissure' sign. Streptococcus pneumoniae causes lobar pneumonia without typical cavitation. Legionella and Mycoplasma cause atypical pneumonia without cavitation.

questions.question: A 32-year-old immigrant from Southeast Asia has a positive QuantiFERON-TB Gold test. He is asymptomatic with a normal chest X-ray. Which statement best describes his condition and management?
options: A. He has active tuberculosis and requires four-drug therapy immediately
B. He has latent TB infection and should receive treatment to prevent reactivation
C. A positive IGRA in a BCG-vaccinated individual always represents a false positive
D. No treatment is needed because he is asymptomatic with a normal chest X-ray
questions.explanation: A positive IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold) with a normal chest X-ray and no symptoms indicates latent TB infection (LTBI). Unlike the TST, IGRAs are not affected by prior BCG vaccination, making them preferred in BCG-vaccinated individuals. Treatment of LTBI (e.g., 9 months of isoniazid or 3 months of isoniazid plus rifapentine) significantly reduces the risk of progression to active TB. Untreated LTBI carries a lifetime reactivation risk of approximately 5–10%.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 45 cells/µL) presents with painless progressive visual loss in his left eye. Fundoscopy reveals perivascular hemorrhages and exudates in a 'pizza pie' pattern. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: B. Intravenous ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir
questions.explanation: The clinical picture describes CMV retinitis, which occurs in HIV patients with CD4 counts below 50 cells/µL. The 'pizza pie' appearance refers to the characteristic fundoscopic finding of hemorrhages and exudates along retinal vessels. Treatment is with IV ganciclovir or oral valganciclovir; the choice depends on disease severity and proximity to the macula. TMP-SMX is used for PCP prophylaxis, and pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine treats CNS toxoplasmosis.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman with HIV has a CD4 count of 180 cells/µL. She has no prior opportunistic infections and is currently not on antiretroviral therapy. Which prophylactic medication should be started immediately?
questions.explanation: PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia) prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is indicated when CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL. This patient's CD4 of 180 meets the threshold for TMP-SMX prophylaxis. Azithromycin for MAC prophylaxis is indicated at CD4 <50 cells/µL, fluconazole prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in the US, and CMV prophylaxis with ganciclovir is not standard practice. ART initiation is also essential regardless of CD4 count.

questions.question: According to Sepsis-3 definitions, which combination best defines septic shock?
options: A. SIRS criteria plus suspected infection
B. Organ dysfunction with SOFA score increase ≥2 points
C. Vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and serum lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation
D. Hypotension with SBP <90 mmHg plus fever and suspected infection
questions.explanation: Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as a subset of sepsis in which vasopressors are required to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥65 mmHg AND the serum lactate remains >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, indicating profound circulatory and cellular metabolic abnormalities. Sepsis itself is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction with a SOFA score increase ≥2. SIRS criteria were part of older Sepsis-1/2 definitions and are no longer used in Sepsis-3.

questions.question: A 26-year-old IV drug user presents with fever, chills, and a new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Which echocardiographic finding would satisfy a Major Duke Criterion for infective endocarditis?
options: A. Mild tricuspid regurgitation without vegetation
B. Oscillating intracardiac mass on the tricuspid valve leaflet
D. Splinter hemorrhages on nail beds
questions.explanation: The Modified Duke Criteria for infective endocarditis include Major Criteria (positive blood cultures with typical organisms or echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement) and Minor Criteria. An oscillating intracardiac mass consistent with a vegetation on echocardiography is a Major Criterion. Elevated inflammatory markers are not part of the criteria, splinter hemorrhages are vascular phenomena (Minor Criterion), and mild regurgitation without vegetation does not satisfy a Major Criterion.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man with a prosthetic aortic valve develops infective endocarditis. Blood cultures are negative after 5 days of incubation. Which organisms should be considered as a cause of culture-negative endocarditis?
options: A. Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes
B. HACEK organisms, Brucella, Coxiella burnetii, and Bartonella
C. Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae
D. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter baumannii
questions.explanation: Culture-negative endocarditis is most often caused by fastidious or intracellular organisms. HACEK organisms (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella) are slow-growing gram-negative rods associated with endocarditis, particularly in patients with poor dentition. Coxiella burnetii (Q fever), Bartonella species, and Brucella are intracellular organisms requiring special serologic testing or prolonged incubation for detection. S. aureus grows readily in standard blood cultures and is rarely the cause of culture-negative endocarditis.

questions.question: A 19-year-old college student presents with sudden fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. CSF analysis reveals WBC 1,200 cells/µL (90% neutrophils), glucose 28 mg/dL (serum glucose 90 mg/dL), and protein 220 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen?
options: B. Ceftriaxone plus vancomycin plus dexamethasone
questions.explanation: The CSF profile (high WBC with neutrophil predominance, low glucose, high protein) is consistent with bacterial meningitis. Empiric treatment includes ceftriaxone (to cover Neisseria meningitidis and Streptococcus pneumoniae) plus vancomycin (to cover ceftriaxone-resistant S. pneumoniae). Dexamethasone given before or with the first antibiotic dose reduces neurologic complications — especially hearing loss — by blunting the inflammatory cytokine response. Ampicillin is added in patients >50 years or immunocompromised for Listeria coverage; acyclovir is added if HSV encephalitis is also suspected.

questions.question: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man (CD4 count 65 cells/µL) presents with headache, fever, and altered mental status. CSF India ink preparation reveals encapsulated yeast. What is the treatment of choice for the induction phase?
options: A. Oral fluconazole 400 mg daily alone
B. Liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks
questions.explanation: The India ink preparation showing encapsulated yeast in CSF is diagnostic of cryptococcal meningitis caused by Cryptococcus neoformans. The three-phase treatment approach begins with induction therapy using liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine for at least 2 weeks. This is followed by consolidation with fluconazole for 8 weeks, then maintenance/suppressive fluconazole 200 mg daily until CD4 >200 on ART. Fluconazole monotherapy is inferior to amphotericin-based induction and is associated with higher early mortality.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with AIDS (CD4 count 55 cells/µL) presents with a new-onset seizure. MRI brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions with surrounding edema in the basal ganglia. What is the most likely diagnosis and first-line treatment?
options: A. Primary CNS lymphoma; high-dose methotrexate
B. Brain abscess from Staphylococcus aureus; IV vancomycin
C. Cerebral toxoplasmosis; pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin
questions.explanation: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia of an AIDS patient with CD4 <100 is the classic presentation of cerebral toxoplasmosis caused by Toxoplasma gondii reactivation. First-line treatment is pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin (leucovorin prevents bone marrow suppression from pyrimethamine). If the patient does not improve after 10–14 days of empiric therapy, brain biopsy should be considered to rule out CNS lymphoma. Primary CNS lymphoma also causes ring-enhancing lesions but is typically solitary and associated with a positive EBV PCR in the CSF.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. His CD4 count is 350 cells/µL and his viral load is 45,000 copies/mL. He has no opportunistic infections. When should antiretroviral therapy (ART) be initiated?
options: A. Immediately, regardless of CD4 count or symptoms
B. When CD4 count falls below 200 cells/µL
C. Only after an AIDS-defining illness develops
D. When viral load exceeds 100,000 copies/mL
questions.explanation: Current guidelines (DHHS, WHO) recommend initiating ART in all HIV-positive individuals regardless of CD4 count, viral load, or symptoms. Early ART initiation reduces AIDS-defining events, lowers mortality, decreases HIV transmission to sexual partners, and reduces non-AIDS comorbidities (cardiovascular, renal, hepatic). The START trial demonstrated clear clinical benefit of early ART even at CD4 counts above 500 cells/µL. There is no CD4 or viral load threshold at which ART should be withheld in a patient ready and willing to take it.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. Susceptibility testing eventually confirms sensitivity to all first-line agents. Which regimen is the standard treatment?
options: A. Isoniazid plus rifampin for 6 months
B. Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months
D. Rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and streptomycin for 6 months
questions.explanation: The standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB is the RIPE regimen: 2 months of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol (intensive phase), followed by 4 months of Rifampin and Isoniazid (continuation phase) — totaling 6 months. Ethambutol can be stopped once susceptibility to isoniazid and rifampin is confirmed. Isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months is used only for latent TB, not active disease. All four drugs in the intensive phase rapidly reduce bacterial load and prevent the emergence of resistance.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology and clinical differences between primary tuberculosis and reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis, including the typical radiographic findings for each.
questions.answer: Primary tuberculosis occurs when a previously unexposed host inhales Mycobacterium tuberculosis droplets, leading to a localized lower or middle lobe parenchymal infiltrate (Ghon focus) combined with hilar lymphadenopathy — together forming a Ghon complex. The immune system typically contains the infection through granuloma formation, and most primary infections resolve without symptoms; however, hematogenous spread can cause miliary TB or extrapulmonary disease, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. Reactivation tuberculosis occurs when dormant bacilli in old granulomas — most commonly in the apical and posterior segments of the upper lobes (where oxygen tension is highest) — reactivate, typically in the setting of immunosuppression (HIV, corticosteroids, malnutrition, or aging). Radiographically, primary TB shows lower or middle lobe consolidation with ipsilateral hilar adenopathy, while reactivation TB shows upper lobe fibrocavitary disease, apical scarring, and cavities that may contain air-fluid levels. Miliary TB, a form of disseminated hematogenous disease, shows a characteristic 'millet seed' pattern of diffuse 1–3 mm nodules throughout both lung fields on chest X-ray.

questions.question: Compare the interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) and tuberculin skin test (TST) for diagnosing latent TB infection, including advantages and limitations of each.
questions.answer: Both the IGRA (e.g., QuantiFERON-TB Gold) and TST detect immune sensitization to M. tuberculosis antigens, but they differ in important ways. The TST involves intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD) with induration read at 48–72 hours; it is inexpensive but requires two healthcare visits and is subject to reader variability. The IGRA is a single blood draw that measures interferon-gamma release from sensitized T-cells in response to TB-specific antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10), with results available within 24 hours and no return visit required. The key advantage of IGRA over TST is that it is not confounded by prior BCG vaccination, making it far more specific in BCG-vaccinated populations common in high-prevalence countries. Both tests can be falsely negative in immunocompromised patients (e.g., advanced HIV) due to impaired cell-mediated immunity, and neither test distinguishes latent from active TB — current guidelines favor IGRA over TST for most situations, particularly in BCG-vaccinated individuals.

questions.question: Explain the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis, the concept of organ dysfunction as measured by the SOFA score, and the key early management steps in a patient presenting with suspected sepsis.
questions.answer: Sepsis-3 (2016) defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalized as a suspected or confirmed infection plus an acute increase in SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score of ≥2 points from baseline. The SOFA score evaluates six organ systems: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 ratio), coagulation (platelets), hepatic (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP or vasopressor requirement), neurologic (Glasgow Coma Scale), and renal (creatinine or urine output), with higher scores indicating greater dysfunction. Early management follows the 'Hour-1 Bundle': measure lactate (repeat if initial lactate ≥2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L, and apply vasopressors (norepinephrine is first-line) to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg if unresponsive to fluids. Source control — identification and removal or drainage of the infectious source (e.g., abscess drainage, removal of infected catheter) — is a critical component that should not be delayed.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with poor dentition develops fever, a new mitral regurgitation murmur, and multiple splinter hemorrhages. Describe the Modified Duke Criteria for diagnosing infective endocarditis and how they apply to this case.
questions.answer: The Modified Duke Criteria classify infective endocarditis as Definite (2 Major, or 1 Major + 3 Minor, or 5 Minor criteria), Possible (1 Major + 1 Minor, or 3 Minor criteria), or Rejected. Major Criteria include: (1) positive blood cultures with typical organisms (S. viridans, S. bovis, HACEK organisms, S. aureus, or enterococcus without another primary focus) — either two separate cultures, persistently positive cultures, or a single positive for Coxiella burnetii; and (2) echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement such as an oscillating vegetation, abscess, prosthetic valve dehiscence, or new valvular regurgitation. Minor Criteria include: predisposing heart condition or IV drug use, fever ≥38°C, vascular phenomena (arterial emboli, Janeway lesions, splinter hemorrhages), immunologic phenomena (Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor), and microbiologic evidence not meeting Major Criteria. In this patient: poor dentition is a predisposing condition (Minor), fever is Minor, splinter hemorrhages are vascular phenomena (Minor), and blood cultures and echocardiography are needed — S. viridans bacteremia would be Major, and a vegetation on echo would be a second Major Criterion, confirming Definite endocarditis.

questions.question: Describe the CSF findings that differentiate bacterial meningitis from viral (aseptic) meningitis, and explain the rationale for empiric dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis.
questions.answer: In bacterial meningitis, CSF typically shows markedly elevated WBC (often >1000 cells/µL) with neutrophil predominance (>80%), significantly low glucose (<45 mg/dL or CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4), and elevated protein (>150–200 mg/dL), reflecting bacterial destruction of the blood-brain barrier and glucose consumption by bacteria and leukocytes. Viral (aseptic) meningitis shows a milder pleocytosis (typically 10–500 cells/µL) with lymphocytic predominance, normal or mildly low glucose, and mildly elevated protein — early viral meningitis may briefly show neutrophil predominance before shifting to lymphocytes. Dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days) is given before or with the first antibiotic dose because it suppresses the cytokine-mediated inflammatory cascade triggered by bacterial cell wall lysis from antibiotics; this inflammatory surge causes much of the neurologic damage including hearing loss and cerebral edema. Evidence is strongest for benefit in S. pneumoniae meningitis in adults, where dexamethasone reduces mortality and hearing loss, and dexamethasone should be discontinued if a non-pneumococcal organism is identified in adults.

questions.question: Explain the CDC staging of HIV disease, define AIDS, and list the major opportunistic infections categorized by CD4 count thresholds.
questions.answer: The CDC classifies HIV disease into three stages based on CD4 count: Stage 1 (CD4 ≥500 cells/µL), Stage 2 (CD4 200–499 cells/µL), and Stage 3/AIDS (CD4 <200 cells/µL OR the presence of an AIDS-defining condition regardless of CD4 count). AIDS-defining conditions include specific opportunistic infections and AIDS-defining malignancies (Kaposi sarcoma, primary CNS lymphoma, invasive cervical cancer). The CD4 count is the primary determinant of susceptibility to specific opportunistic infections: at CD4 <200, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) and mucocutaneous candidiasis become common; at CD4 <100, cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcal meningitis, and esophageal candidiasis occur; at CD4 <50, disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infection and CMV retinitis/colitis are prominent risks. Prophylaxis thresholds mirror these: TMP-SMX at CD4 <200 for PCP, and azithromycin at CD4 <50 for MAC; ART initiation and sustained viral suppression allow CD4 recovery and permit eventual discontinuation of prophylaxis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with HIV asks about her antiretroviral medications. Describe the four major ART drug classes, their mechanisms of action, and one key toxicity or clinical consideration for each.
questions.answer: The four major antiretroviral drug classes are: (1) Nucleoside/Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) — e.g., tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir — act as chain terminators by incorporating into viral DNA and blocking reverse transcriptase; tenofovir can cause nephrotoxicity and bone mineral density loss, while abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 testing to avoid a potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction. (2) Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) — e.g., efavirenz, rilpivirine — bind allosterically to reverse transcriptase; efavirenz causes neuropsychiatric side effects (vivid dreams, depression) and is a CYP450 inducer with significant drug interactions. (3) Protease Inhibitors (PIs) — e.g., darunavir, atazanavir (boosted with ritonavir or cobicistat) — block HIV protease from cleaving the viral polyprotein; class toxicities include metabolic syndrome, lipodystrophy, and hyperlipidemia; atazanavir specifically causes benign indirect hyperbilirubinemia and nephrolithiasis. (4) Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) — e.g., dolutegravir, bictegravir — block integration of viral DNA into the host genome; they are generally the best-tolerated class and form the backbone of preferred first-line regimens, though dolutegravir is associated with neural tube defects when taken periconceptionally and should be used with caution in pregnancy planning.

questions.question: Describe miliary tuberculosis: its pathogenesis, clinical presentation, radiographic appearance, and diagnostic approach.
questions.answer: Miliary tuberculosis results from massive hematogenous dissemination of M. tuberculosis seeding multiple organs simultaneously; it occurs most commonly during primary infection in young children, in immunosuppressed individuals (HIV, biologic agents, malnutrition), or as reactivation in the elderly. Clinically, patients present with non-specific constitutional symptoms — prolonged fever, night sweats, weight loss, and malaise — often without prominent respiratory symptoms, which can significantly delay diagnosis; hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and rarely choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy (pathognomonic when present) may be found on examination. The hallmark radiographic finding is a diffuse bilateral 'millet seed' pattern of uniform 1–3 mm nodules throughout both lung fields on chest X-ray; HRCT is more sensitive and can detect this pattern earlier when plain films are equivocal. Diagnosis is challenging because sputum smear may be negative; bronchoscopy with BAL, bone marrow biopsy, or liver biopsy may be required to obtain specimens, and IGRA or TST can be falsely negative due to immunosuppression — cultures remain the gold standard but may take weeks, so empiric treatment is often initiated based on clinical suspicion while awaiting results.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman on high-dose prednisone for polymyalgia rheumatica develops progressive dyspnea, non-productive cough, and fever. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities and LDH is elevated. Discuss PCP in non-HIV immunocompromised patients, including clinical differences from HIV-associated PCP, treatment, and prophylaxis indications.
questions.answer: PCP in non-HIV immunocompromised patients (e.g., those on corticosteroids, biologics, or cytotoxic chemotherapy, or transplant recipients) tends to present more acutely and severely than in HIV patients, with rapid progression to respiratory failure over days rather than weeks, because the inflammatory response is less blunted compared to advanced HIV disease where the immune system is more profoundly suppressed. Classic features include subacute-to-acute onset dyspnea, non-productive cough, fever, and bilateral ground-glass opacities on CT; elevated LDH is a non-specific but useful marker of disease severity and tissue injury. Diagnosis is made by demonstrating Pneumocystis organisms in BAL fluid using methenamine silver staining, direct immunofluorescence, or PCR (the most sensitive method). Treatment is TMP-SMX (15–20 mg/kg/day of the TMP component in divided doses IV or oral) for 21 days; adjunctive corticosteroids are added for moderate-to-severe disease (PaO2 <70 mmHg on room air or A-a gradient >35), extrapolating evidence from HIV trials showing reduced inflammatory deterioration. Prophylaxis with TMP-SMX (one SS or DS tablet daily or 3 times per week) is recommended for non-HIV patients receiving prednisone ≥20 mg/day for ≥1 month, solid organ transplant recipients, and patients on certain immunosuppressive regimens; alternatives for sulfa-intolerant patients include dapsone, atovaquone, or monthly inhaled pentamidine.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man presents with 3 weeks of fever, a new mitral valve vegetation on echocardiography, and blood cultures growing Streptococcus viridans. Discuss the antibiotic treatment for native valve endocarditis due to viridans group streptococci, treatment duration, and indications for surgical intervention.
questions.answer: Viridans group streptococci (e.g., S. sanguinis, S. mutans) are the most common cause of community-acquired native valve endocarditis and are typically associated with poor dentition or recent dental procedures. They are usually penicillin-sensitive, and treatment with IV penicillin G or ceftriaxone for 4 weeks is the standard for native valve endocarditis; a shortened 2-week course of beta-lactam plus gentamicin is an option for uncomplicated cases with highly sensitive strains (MIC ≤0.125 µg/mL) in patients at low risk for aminoglycoside toxicity. Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires a longer course of 6 weeks with addition of gentamicin for at least the first 2 weeks. Blood cultures should be repeated 48–72 hours after starting therapy to confirm clearance of bacteremia, and a follow-up echocardiogram assesses vegetation size and valvular function. Surgical indications include: heart failure due to severe valvular regurgitation or obstruction unresponsive to medical therapy, uncontrolled infection (persistent bacteremia >5–7 days despite appropriate antibiotics, abscess, fistula, or new conduction block), and prevention of systemic embolism (large vegetations >10 mm, especially on the anterior mitral leaflet or with prior embolic events); multidisciplinary endocarditis team consultation (infectious disease, cardiology, cardiac surgery) is strongly recommended for all cases.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presents with mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervical motion tenderness. Nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Which of the following is the recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea?
options: D. Doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 7 days
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone 500mg IM as a single dose is the current CDC-recommended first-line treatment for uncomplicated gonorrhea following rising fluoroquinolone resistance. Due to increasing azithromycin resistance, dual therapy with azithromycin is no longer routinely recommended unless chlamydia co-infection is not excluded. Ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones are no longer recommended due to widespread resistance. Doxycycline is used to treat co-existing chlamydia but is inadequate monotherapy for gonorrhea.

questions.question: A 32-year-old man is found to have a painless penile ulcer with a clean, indurated base and non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. RPR is reactive at 1:64 and confirmatory treponemal test is positive. This presentation is most consistent with which stage of syphilis?
questions.explanation: The painless, clean-based, indurated ulcer (chancre) with regional non-tender lymphadenopathy is classic for primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Secondary syphilis typically presents with a diffuse maculopapular rash (including palms and soles), condyloma lata, and mucous patches without a primary ulcer. Latent syphilis is asymptomatic by definition. Tertiary syphilis occurs years later with cardiovascular or neurological involvement.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with no prior HSV history presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base on her labia. She is 32 weeks pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: A. No treatment; await spontaneous resolution
B. Acyclovir 400mg orally three times daily
C. Valacyclovir 1g orally twice daily for 10 days
D. Famciclovir 500mg orally twice daily for 7 days
questions.explanation: Acyclovir is the preferred antiviral for HSV in pregnancy based on the most safety data and is FDA category B. For a first-episode genital HSV in pregnancy, acyclovir 400mg three times daily for 7–10 days is standard therapy. Valacyclovir and famciclovir have less safety data in pregnancy and are generally avoided, particularly in the first trimester, though valacyclovir may be used in the second and third trimesters in some guidelines. Suppressive therapy starting at 36 weeks is recommended to reduce the risk of neonatal HSV.

questions.question: A 42-year-old man presents with a 3-day history of fever, severe headache, and a petechial rash that began on his wrists and ankles and spread centrally. He recently returned from a camping trip in the Carolinas. What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?
options: C. Doxycycline 100mg orally or IV twice daily
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) caused by Rickettsia rickettsii, transmitted by Dermacentor ticks in the eastern United States. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for all ages, including children, because the mortality without treatment is high and delay is dangerous. Do not wait for confirmatory serology before treating. Azithromycin has poor activity against Rickettsia; cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones are ineffective. Early empiric doxycycline is life-saving.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man with AIDS (CD4 50 cells/µL) presents with fever, weight loss, and a chest CT showing a right upper lobe nodule with hilar lymphadenopathy. Urine Histoplasma antigen is positive. Which of the following is the recommended induction therapy for severe disseminated histoplasmosis?
options: C. Liposomal amphotericin B 3mg/kg/day for 2 weeks
D. Itraconazole 200mg three times daily for 3 days then twice daily
questions.explanation: For severe or moderately severe disseminated histoplasmosis, liposomal amphotericin B is the recommended induction therapy for 1–2 weeks, followed by step-down to oral itraconazole for maintenance. Fluconazole has poor activity against Histoplasma and is not recommended. Voriconazole is not a standard treatment for histoplasmosis. Itraconazole is used for mild-to-moderate disease and for consolidation/maintenance after amphotericin B induction.

questions.question: A hospitalized patient develops watery diarrhea after 5 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Stool testing shows positive glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) and positive toxin immunoassay. WBC is 18,000/µL and creatinine is 1.8mg/dL (baseline 0.9mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: A. Metronidazole 500mg orally three times daily for 10 days
B. Vancomycin 125mg orally four times daily for 10 days
C. Fidaxomicin 200mg orally twice daily for 10 days
D. Rifaximin 550mg orally three times daily for 14 days
questions.explanation: This patient meets criteria for severe Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) — WBC >15,000/µL and rising creatinine — and fidaxomicin 200mg twice daily for 10 days is preferred over oral vancomycin for non-severe and severe (non-fulminant) CDI based on lower recurrence rates. Metronidazole is no longer recommended as first-line therapy for any severity of CDI due to inferior outcomes. Rifaximin may be used as adjunctive therapy to prevent recurrence but is not first-line induction. Vancomycin remains an acceptable alternative when fidaxomicin is unavailable.

questions.question: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with 3 weeks of right foot pain. X-ray shows periosteal elevation and cortical erosion of the second metatarsal head. MRI confirms osteomyelitis. Blood cultures are negative, but a bone biopsy grows methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). What is the treatment of choice?
options: B. Nafcillin or oxacillin IV for 6 weeks
questions.explanation: For MSSA osteomyelitis, antistaphylococcal penicillins such as nafcillin or oxacillin are the preferred agents because they have superior activity compared to vancomycin against MSSA and achieve better outcomes in staphylococcal infections. The standard treatment duration for hematogenous or contiguous-focus osteomyelitis is 4–6 weeks of parenteral therapy. Vancomycin is reserved for MRSA or penicillin-allergic patients. Daptomycin is inactivated by pulmonary surfactant but is an alternative for MRSA osteomyelitis; TMP-SMX oral step-down may be considered after initial IV therapy.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman returning from sub-Saharan Africa presents with fever, chills, and headache 10 days after return. Peripheral blood smear shows ring-form trophozoites in >5% of red blood cells, some red cells containing multiple rings, and the absence of visible parasites outside red cells. What is the most likely diagnosis and appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: High parasitemia (>5%), multiple rings per red cell, and absence of trophozoites/schizonts outside RBCs are characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum, the most dangerous malaria species. Artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem) or atovaquone-proguanil are first-line for uncomplicated falciparum malaria acquired in chloroquine-resistant regions. Chloroquine resistance is widespread in sub-Saharan Africa, making chloroquine an inappropriate choice. P. vivax and P. ovale cause relapsing malaria and require primaquine to eradicate hypnozoites, but they are not consistent with this smear morphology.

questions.question: A 50-year-old immunocompromised patient with a hematologic malignancy develops fever unresponsive to broad-spectrum antibiotics. CT chest shows a nodule with a 'halo sign.' Serum galactomannan is elevated at 1.8. Which of the following is the most appropriate antifungal therapy?
options: C. Voriconazole 6mg/kg IV every 12 hours for two doses, then 4mg/kg every 12 hours
questions.explanation: The CT halo sign (ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule due to hemorrhagic infarction) in an immunocompromised patient with elevated serum galactomannan is highly suggestive of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. Voriconazole is the first-line treatment for invasive aspergillosis, with superior outcomes compared to amphotericin B demonstrated in clinical trials. Fluconazole has no activity against Aspergillus. Echinocandins (micafungin) may be used for salvage or combination therapy but are not first-line monotherapy. Liposomal amphotericin B is an alternative when voriconazole is not tolerated.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of malar rash, diffuse rash on the trunk, painless oral ulcers, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. He denies any genital ulcers. RPR is reactive at 1:128 and treponemal antibody is positive. Which treatment is indicated?
options: A. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM once
B. Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly for 3 weeks
C. Doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 14 days
D. Ceftriaxone 1g IM daily for 10 days
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with secondary syphilis, characterized by a diffuse rash (often involving palms and soles), mucous membrane lesions (oral ulcers), and lymphadenopathy. Secondary syphilis is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose, the same as primary syphilis. The 3-dose weekly regimen is reserved for late latent syphilis (>1 year duration or unknown duration) and tertiary syphilis. Doxycycline is an alternative only in penicillin-allergic patients. Ceftriaxone is an off-label alternative for non-neurological syphilis.

questions.question: Compare the three major endemic fungal infections — histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, and blastomycosis — in terms of geographic distribution, diagnostic tests, and treatment.
questions.answer: Histoplasma capsulatum is endemic to the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and is acquired by inhaling soil disturbed near bird or bat habitats; urine Histoplasma antigen is the most sensitive diagnostic test, especially for disseminated disease, and treatment uses liposomal amphotericin B for severe cases followed by itraconazole for consolidation and maintenance. Coccidioides immitis/posadasii is endemic to the arid southwestern United States and northern Mexico; diagnosis relies on serology (IgM and IgG via immunodiffusion or complement fixation), with rising complement fixation titers indicating dissemination to meninges, bone, or skin; treatment is fluconazole for most cases, with amphotericin B for severe or disseminated disease. Blastomyces dermatitidis is found in the north-central and southeastern US near waterways; diagnosis is by culture showing broad-based budding yeast or histopathology, and urine antigen testing is available but less sensitive than for histoplasmosis; treatment mirrors histoplasmosis (itraconazole for mild-moderate, liposomal amphotericin B for severe). All three are dimorphic fungi that can cause community-acquired pneumonia mimicking tuberculosis or malignancy in endemic regions, and geographic exposure history is essential for correct diagnosis.

questions.question: A 62-year-old patient with a tunneled central venous catheter develops fever and blood cultures grow Candida albicans. Which of the following management steps is most important in addition to antifungal therapy?
options: A. Transition immediately to oral fluconazole
B. Remove the central venous catheter as soon as possible
C. Obtain a serum (1,3)-β-D-glucan assay to confirm the diagnosis
D. Add an echinocandin to fluconazole for combination therapy
questions.explanation: Candidemia guidelines (IDSA) strongly recommend prompt removal of the central venous catheter when feasible, as catheter removal significantly reduces mortality and duration of candidemia. An echinocandin (e.g., micafungin, caspofungin) is the preferred initial antifungal for candidemia, not fluconazole, due to superior efficacy. Oral step-down to fluconazole is appropriate after clinical improvement and susceptibility confirmation, not at initiation. Combination antifungal therapy is not recommended for routine candidemia. Ophthalmologic examination and echocardiography should also be performed.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 1a infection and compensated cirrhosis is ready to begin treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate regimen?
options: A. Pegylated interferon-alpha plus ribavirin for 48 weeks
C. Sofosbuvir plus ribavirin for 12 weeks
D. Daclatasvir plus asunaprevir for 24 weeks
questions.explanation: Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir (Epclusa) is a pangenotypic regimen effective for all HCV genotypes including genotype 1a, achieving sustained virologic response (SVR) rates >95%, even in patients with compensated cirrhosis. Interferon-based regimens are no longer recommended due to poor tolerability and inferior efficacy. Sofosbuvir monotherapy is insufficient and not recommended. Pangenotypic regimens such as sofosbuvir-velpatasvir or glecaprevir-pibrentasvir have replaced genotype-specific regimens as the standard of care.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman develops fever of 38.9°C, hypotension, and profuse watery diarrhea 10 days after hip arthroplasty. She is oliguric with creatinine 3.2mg/dL. Abdominal CT shows pancolonic wall thickening. Stool GDH and toxin assays are positive. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: A. Fidaxomicin 200mg orally twice daily for 10 days
B. Oral vancomycin 500mg four times daily plus IV metronidazole 500mg every 8 hours
D. Oral vancomycin 125mg four times daily for 10 days
questions.explanation: This patient has fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus/megacolon signs, severe organ dysfunction). IDSA guidelines recommend high-dose oral vancomycin (500mg QID) plus IV metronidazole for fulminant CDI. IV metronidazole is added because it reaches the colon via biliary secretion when ileus may impair oral drug delivery. FMT is indicated for recurrent CDI (typically second or third recurrence) but not as initial therapy for fulminant disease. Fidaxomicin is preferred for non-fulminant CDI but data are limited for fulminant disease, and dose escalation is not standard.

questions.question: A 25-year-old traveler is planning a 3-month trip to rural sub-Saharan Africa where chloroquine-resistant Plasmodium falciparum is endemic. Describe the available chemoprophylaxis options, including dosing schedules, key side effects, and contraindications.
questions.answer: Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone) is a preferred option: taken daily starting 1–2 days before travel, during travel, and for 7 days after; it is well tolerated with mainly GI side effects and is contraindicated in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30 mL/min) and pregnancy. Doxycycline 100 mg daily is equally effective, starting 1–2 days before and continuing for 4 weeks after travel; it is contraindicated in pregnancy and children under 8, and causes photosensitivity and GI upset. Mefloquine 250 mg weekly is effective but requires initiation 2–3 weeks before travel (to assess tolerability) and is continued for 4 weeks after; it carries neuropsychiatric side effects (vivid dreams, anxiety, dizziness) and is contraindicated in patients with seizure disorders or psychiatric illness. Chloroquine is not appropriate for chloroquine-resistant regions. Primaquine can be used as an alternative in special circumstances and also provides causal prophylaxis and terminal prophylaxis against P. vivax/ovale relapse, but G6PD testing is mandatory before use. Choice depends on traveler characteristics, destination-specific resistance patterns, duration of travel, and tolerability.
