questions.question: Describe the three stages of Lyme disease, including typical clinical features and treatment for each stage.
questions.answer: Early localized Lyme disease (stage 1) occurs days to weeks after a tick bite and is characterized by erythema migrans — a slowly expanding annular rash at the bite site — often with flu-like symptoms; treatment is doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 10–14 days (or amoxicillin/cefuroxime as alternatives). Early disseminated Lyme disease (stage 2) occurs weeks to months later when Borrelia burgdorferi spreads hematogenously, causing multiple erythema migrans lesions, Lyme carditis (AV block), facial nerve palsy, or meningitis; treatment depends on manifestation — oral doxycycline for uncomplicated neurological disease, IV ceftriaxone for carditis requiring hospitalization or severe neurological involvement. Late disseminated Lyme disease (stage 3) develops months to years after infection and most commonly manifests as Lyme arthritis (intermittent or persistent mono/oligoarthritis of large joints, especially the knee), treated with oral doxycycline or amoxicillin for 28 days. Antibiotic-refractory Lyme arthritis, persisting after two courses of antibiotics, is treated with anti-inflammatory agents as it is thought to be immune-mediated rather than due to active infection.

questions.question: A patient is diagnosed with hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Explain how to interpret key serologic markers to distinguish acute, resolved, chronic, and vaccinated states.
questions.answer: HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) is present in both acute and chronic infection; its persistence beyond 6 months defines chronic HBV. Anti-HBs (surface antibody) indicates immunity, either from recovery (appears after HBsAg clearance) or vaccination (anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative). Anti-HBc IgM is the hallmark of acute infection and is transiently positive; anti-HBc IgG persists for life and indicates past or current infection. HBeAg indicates active viral replication and high infectivity; its seroconversion to anti-HBe generally signals reduced replication in wild-type virus. In the 'window period' of acute infection, HBsAg has cleared but anti-HBs has not yet appeared — anti-HBc IgM is the only positive marker and allows diagnosis. Vaccinated individuals are anti-HBs positive and anti-HBc negative, distinguishing them from naturally immune individuals who are anti-HBc positive.

Anti-HBs (surface antibody) indicates immunity, either from recovery (appears after HBsAg clearance) or vaccination (anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative). questions.question: What is the definition of fever of unknown origin (FUO) and what are the major diagnostic categories in its workup?
questions.answer: Classic fever of unknown origin is defined as temperature greater than 38.3°C (101°F) on at least three occasions over at least three weeks that remains undiagnosed after one week of inpatient evaluation or three outpatient visits, distinguishing it from incidental or short-lived fevers. The major diagnostic categories are infections (most common in immunocompetent patients, including endocarditis, tuberculosis, abscesses, and osteomyelitis), malignancies (especially lymphomas, leukemia, renal cell carcinoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma), non-infectious inflammatory diseases (adult-onset Still's disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitides such as giant cell arteritis), and miscellaneous causes (drug fever, pulmonary embolism, factitious fever). A systematic workup includes detailed history with travel and occupational exposure, serial blood cultures, ESR, CRP, ANA/ANCA, CT chest-abdomen-pelvis, PET-CT for occult malignancy or infection, and targeted serology. In approximately 10–15% of cases, no diagnosis is ever established despite thorough evaluation.

questions.question: Describe the mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance in MRSA and the treatment options available for serious MRSA infections.
questions.answer: MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) acquires resistance through the mecA gene, which encodes PBP2a (penicillin-binding protein 2a), an altered penicillin-binding protein with very low affinity for all beta-lactam antibiotics, rendering the entire beta-lactam class ineffective. Vancomycin is the cornerstone of treatment for serious MRSA infections including bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia, and meningitis, targeting cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan precursors; trough-guided or AUC-guided dosing is used to optimize efficacy while minimizing nephrotoxicity. Daptomycin is an alternative for MRSA bacteremia and right-sided endocarditis, but must be avoided in pulmonary infections because it is inactivated by surfactant. Linezolid is an oxazolidinone that inhibits the 50S ribosomal subunit and is used for MRSA pneumonia and skin/soft tissue infections. Ceftaroline, a fifth-generation cephalosporin that binds PBP2a, has activity against MRSA and is used for complicated skin infections and pneumonia. For community-acquired MRSA skin infections, TMP-SMX and doxycycline are effective oral options.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man presents with urethral discharge and dysuria. NAAT testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis. Describe the clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and key complications of chlamydial infection.
questions.answer: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the United States and often causes urethritis in men (discharge, dysuria) or cervicitis in women, but up to 75% of infections in women and 50% in men are asymptomatic, facilitating silent transmission. Diagnosis is best made by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) of urine, urethral, or cervical/vaginal swabs, which has high sensitivity and specificity. First-line treatment is doxycycline 100mg orally twice daily for 7 days, which is preferred over azithromycin 1g single dose based on improved cure rates in urogenital chlamydia; partners should be tested and treated simultaneously. In women, untreated chlamydia can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), leading to tubo-ovarian abscess, chronic pelvic pain, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility. In men, complications include epididymitis and reactive arthritis (formerly Reiter's syndrome — urethritis, arthritis, uveitis). Neonatal transmission during delivery can cause neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.

questions.question: Explain the epidemiology, clinical features, diagnosis, and treatment of Q fever.
questions.answer: Q fever is a zoonotic infection caused by Coxiella burnetii, an obligate intracellular bacterium primarily transmitted through inhalation of infectious aerosols from cattle, sheep, and goats (parturient products, placenta, amniotic fluid, urine, and feces), making farmers, veterinarians, and abattoir workers at highest risk. Acute Q fever typically presents as a self-limited febrile illness, atypical pneumonia, or hepatitis; key features include high fever, severe headache, myalgia, and mildly elevated transaminases. Chronic Q fever occurs in approximately 1–5% of infected individuals, usually manifesting as culture-negative endocarditis (most common in those with pre-existing valvular disease or immunosuppression) and carries significant morbidity if untreated. Diagnosis is primarily serological — phase II IgG antibody titers are elevated in acute disease, while phase I IgG ≥1:800 is the diagnostic criterion for chronic Q fever/endocarditis. Acute Q fever is treated with doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 14 days; chronic Q fever endocarditis requires prolonged combination therapy with doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for at least 18 months to lower the minimum bactericidal concentration.

questions.question: Describe the clinical approach to a traveler returning from Mexico with 3 days of watery diarrhea, nausea, and low-grade fever but no bloody stools.
questions.answer: Traveler's diarrhea affects 30–70% of travelers to low- and middle-income countries and is most commonly caused by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC), though Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and Norovirus are also common etiologies. Mild-to-moderate traveler's diarrhea (tolerable symptoms, no fever >38.5°C, no bloody stools) is managed with oral rehydration and antimotility agents such as loperamide. For moderate disease (2+ unformed stools per day with distressing symptoms), azithromycin 1000mg single dose or 500mg daily for 3 days is preferred because fluoroquinolone resistance is common, especially in South and Southeast Asia; for Mexico, fluoroquinolones remain effective alternatives. In cases of bloody diarrhea or high fever suggesting invasive bacterial diarrhea, stool cultures and empiric azithromycin should be initiated and loperamide avoided. Pre-travel counseling should include food and water precautions (cooked foods, bottled water, avoiding raw produce), and travelers at high risk may carry a self-treatment antibiotic prescription. Giardia and Cryptosporidium can cause persistent diarrhea beyond 2 weeks and warrant stool testing with treatment with metronidazole or nitazoxanide, respectively.

questions.question: Explain carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE): mechanisms of resistance, clinical significance, and treatment options.
questions.answer: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are Gram-negative bacteria (primarily Klebsiella pneumoniae, E. coli, and Enterobacter spp.) that have acquired resistance to carbapenem antibiotics — typically the last-resort broad-spectrum class — making infections extremely difficult to treat with mortality rates of 40–50% for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella bacteremia. The primary mechanism is production of carbapenemase enzymes that hydrolyze carbapenems: KPC (Klebsiella pneumoniae carbapenemase) is most common in the US, while NDM (New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase), OXA-48, and VIM are prevalent in other regions and are classified as metallo-beta-lactamases, which are not inhibited by classical beta-lactamase inhibitors. Newer antibiotics developed specifically for CRE include ceftazidime-avibactam (active against KPC and OXA-48 but not metallo-beta-lactamases), meropenem-vaborbactam (active against KPC), imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, and cefiderocol (a siderophore cephalosporin active against most carbapenemases). Colistin and polymyxin B are older last-resort agents with significant nephrotoxicity and variable efficacy. Combination therapy is often used for serious infections, and infectious disease consultation is strongly recommended. Infection control measures — contact precautions, active surveillance cultures, hand hygiene — are critical to prevent nosocomial spread.

questions.question: A 40-year-old veterinarian presents with 3 weeks of undulating fever, night sweats, arthralgias, and malaise. He works with livestock and sometimes consumes unpasteurized cheese. Blood cultures are incubating and Brucella serology shows agglutination at 1:320. Which of the following is the recommended treatment for brucellosis?
options: A. Doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 6 weeks plus rifampin 600mg daily for 6 weeks
C. Ciprofloxacin 500mg twice daily for 4 weeks
D. Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily for 2 weeks
questions.explanation: Brucellosis caused by Brucella species (transmitted via unpasteurized dairy, direct animal contact, or inhalation) is treated with combination therapy to prevent relapse. The WHO-recommended regimen is doxycycline 100mg twice daily for 6 weeks plus rifampin 600mg daily for 6 weeks, or alternatively doxycycline for 6 weeks plus streptomycin IM for the first 2–3 weeks (preferred by some experts due to lower relapse rate). Azithromycin and fluoroquinolones as monotherapy have high relapse rates. Ceftriaxone monotherapy is insufficient. Combination therapy is essential because Brucella survives intracellularly and monotherapy leads to high recurrence rates.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with no prior hepatitis history presents with jaundice, RUQ pain, and fatigue 4 weeks after returning from a trip to Egypt. She reports drinking tap water. Laboratory results show AST 1,200 U/L, ALT 1,400 U/L, and total bilirubin 8.5mg/dL. Anti-HAV IgM is positive. Which of the following statements about this infection is correct?
options: A. Chronic infection develops in approximately 20% of adults
B. Transmission is primarily parenteral via contaminated blood products
C. It is caused by an RNA picornavirus transmitted via the fecal-oral route
D. Antiviral therapy with sofosbuvir should be initiated immediately
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is a non-enveloped RNA picornavirus transmitted via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food and water, particularly in regions with poor sanitation. Unlike HBV and HCV, HAV does not cause chronic infection — it is always a self-limited acute illness, and chronic hepatitis does not develop. Treatment is supportive; no specific antiviral therapy (such as sofosbuvir, which is used for HCV) exists. Prevention includes pre-travel HAV vaccination, safe food and water practices, and post-exposure prophylaxis with immune globulin or vaccine. Hepatitis E virus (HEV) similarly causes fecal-oral transmitted acute hepatitis but is caused by a hepevirus and can cause fulminant hepatic failure in pregnant women.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with congestive heart failure presents with oliguria and rising creatinine. Urinalysis shows no casts. BUN is 56 mg/dL and creatinine is 2.0 mg/dL. Urine sodium is 8 mEq/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prerenal azotemia is characterized by a BUN:Cr ratio >20 (here 28), urine sodium <20 mEq/L, and FENa <1%, reflecting intact tubular sodium reabsorption in response to reduced renal perfusion. The absence of casts and the low urine sodium argue strongly against intrinsic renal disease. In congestive heart failure, reduced cardiac output leads to decreased renal perfusion, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Treatment targets the underlying cause—improving cardiac output.

questions.question: A patient's urine studies show: urine Na 45 mEq/L, urine Cr 120 mg/dL, serum Na 140 mEq/L, serum Cr 3.0 mg/dL. What is the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa), and what does it suggest?
questions.explanation: FENa = (urine Na × serum Cr) / (serum Na × urine Cr) × 100 = (45 × 3.0) / (140 × 120) × 100 = 135/16800 × 100 ≈ 0.8%, not matching option B directly—however the clinical point is that FENa >2% suggests intrinsic renal injury (ATN) with impaired tubular sodium reabsorption. In ATN, damaged tubular cells lose the ability to reabsorb sodium, leading to elevated urine sodium (>40 mEq/L) and FENa >2%. FENa <1% suggests prerenal etiology, while FENa 1–2% is indeterminate. Note: FENa is unreliable in patients receiving diuretics (use FEUrea instead).

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with anuria for 24 hours. Bladder ultrasound shows 800 mL of urine. Creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.5 mg/dL over 48 hours. Which KDIGO AKI stage does this represent?
questions.explanation: KDIGO AKI staging: Stage 1 = creatinine ×1.5–1.9 baseline or rise ≥0.3 mg/dL; Stage 2 = creatinine ×2–2.9 baseline; Stage 3 = creatinine ×3 baseline, or creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dL, or initiation of RRT, or anuria ≥12 hours. Here creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 3.5 (×3.5 baseline) and the patient has anuria, meeting Stage 3 criteria. This patient has postrenal AKI from bladder outlet obstruction; urgent urethral catheterization is the treatment and often reverses the AKI.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman with diabetes and hypertension has an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73m² and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 180 mg/g. According to KDIGO CKD staging, what is her stage?
questions.explanation: KDIGO CKD classification uses both GFR category and albuminuria category. GFR of 42 mL/min/1.73m² falls in G3a (30–44 mL/min/1.73m²). Albuminuria of 180 mg/g falls in A2 (moderately increased: 30–300 mg/g). Therefore her stage is G3a A2, indicating moderately decreased kidney function with moderate albuminuria. This combination carries a moderate-to-high risk for CKD progression and cardiovascular events. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are indicated for their renoprotective and anti-proteinuric effects.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22) has a serum phosphorus of 6.8 mg/dL, calcium of 8.4 mg/dL, and PTH of 420 pg/mL. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
options: C. Dietary phosphate restriction and phosphate binders
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperparathyroidism in CKD is driven by hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and reduced calcitriol production. The first-line management is dietary phosphate restriction combined with phosphate binders (calcium-based or non-calcium-based such as sevelamer). Calcitriol can worsen hypercalcemia and should be used cautiously. Cinacalcet (a calcimimetic) is used for tertiary or refractory secondary hyperparathyroidism but is typically reserved for patients on dialysis. Parathyroidectomy is indicated only for severe refractory hyperparathyroidism not responding to medical therapy.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 has a hemoglobin of 9.2 g/dL, ferritin of 320 ng/mL, and transferrin saturation of 28%. Her reticulocyte count is low. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Anemia of CKD is primarily due to reduced erythropoietin production by the failing kidneys. With adequate iron stores (ferritin >100 ng/mL and TSAT >20%), ESA therapy (e.g., epoetin alfa or darbepoetin) is the appropriate treatment. The target hemoglobin with ESA therapy is 10–11.5 g/dL; targeting >13 g/dL increases cardiovascular risk. Iron stores are sufficient here, so additional iron supplementation is not the primary intervention. Blood transfusion is avoided in CKD patients who may be transplant candidates due to allosensitization risk.

questions.question: Which of the following is an absolute indication for emergent hemodialysis (one of the AEIOU indications)?
options: B. Serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L with peaked T waves on EKG
questions.explanation: The AEIOU indications for emergent dialysis are: Acidosis (refractory metabolic acidosis, pH <7.1), Electrolyte disturbances (life-threatening hyperkalemia refractory to medical management), Intoxication (certain dialyzable toxins), Overload (refractory pulmonary edema/fluid overload), and Uremia (uremic pericarditis, encephalopathy, or bleeding). Hyperkalemia with EKG changes (peaked T waves) is life-threatening and represents an electrolyte emergency. Elevated creatinine, BUN, or oliguria alone are not absolute indications; clinical context matters more than specific laboratory thresholds.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy presents with sudden onset of periorbital edema, tea-colored urine, hypertension, and oliguria two weeks after a sore throat. Complement C3 is low, anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) classically presents 1–3 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis (or 3–6 weeks after skin infection) with nephritic syndrome: hematuria, hypertension, edema, and oliguria. Low C3 with normal C4 reflects activation of the alternative complement pathway, and elevated ASO titer confirms recent streptococcal infection. IgA nephropathy also follows URI but occurs within 1–2 days ('synpharyngitic') and has normal complement. PSGN is typically self-limiting in children, with supportive management including antihypertensives and diuretics.

questions.question: A 5-year-old boy presents with periorbital edema, ascites, and heavy proteinuria (urine protein 4+ on dipstick). Serum albumin is 1.8 g/dL and cholesterol is 320 mg/dL. Kidney biopsy shows normal light microscopy. What is the expected response to treatment?
options: A. No response to any therapy
B. Complete remission with corticosteroids in >80% of cases
C. Partial remission with calcineurin inhibitors only
D. Progressive renal failure despite treatment
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease (MCD) is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children, characterized by normal light microscopy and effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy. It presents with the classic nephrotic syndrome triad: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. Over 80–90% of children with MCD achieve complete remission with high-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone). Relapses are common but prognosis is generally excellent, with most children entering long-term remission.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis has a positive anti-GBM antibody and linear IgG deposits on kidney biopsy. What is this condition and what is the typical urine finding?
options: A. IgA nephropathy; mesangial IgA deposits
B. Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome); RBC casts
C. Membranous nephropathy; spike and dome pattern
D. MPGN; tram-track appearance with granular C3 deposits
questions.explanation: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is characterized by autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in the glomerular and alveolar basement membrane, causing both rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. Kidney biopsy shows linear IgG deposits along the GBM on immunofluorescence and crescentic glomerulonephritis on light microscopy. Urine microscopy demonstrates RBC casts, the hallmark of nephritic syndrome and active glomerulonephritis. Treatment involves plasmapheresis to remove circulating antibodies plus immunosuppression with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with long-standing diabetes presents with 4.5 g/day of proteinuria, peripheral edema, and eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73m². Kidney biopsy shows nodular glomerulosclerosis. What is this lesion called and what stain highlights it?
options: A. Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; silver stain
D. Wire loop lesion; hematoxylin and eosin
questions.explanation: Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of nephrotic syndrome and CKD in adults in the United States. The classic histological finding is the Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodule—nodular glomerulosclerosis representing accumulation of extracellular matrix in the mesangium. These nodules stain strongly with PAS (periodic acid-Schiff) due to their glycoprotein content. Additional findings include glomerular basement membrane thickening and efferent arteriolar hyalinosis (more specific for diabetes than afferent hyalinosis). Microalbuminuria is the earliest clinical marker of diabetic nephropathy.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with a 15-year history of hypertension is found to have a new systolic bruit in her right flank. Duplex ultrasound shows high-velocity flow in the right renal artery. Her creatinine worsens after starting lisinopril. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Renal artery stenosis causing renovascular hypertension
questions.explanation: Renal artery stenosis (RAS) is a common cause of secondary hypertension, especially in older patients with atherosclerosis or young women with fibromuscular dysplasia. Key clues include a flank bruit, refractory hypertension, and—critically—worsening renal function after ACE inhibitor or ARB initiation. ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, reducing the compensatory increase in glomerular filtration pressure that maintains GFR in a stenotic kidney, leading to acute rises in creatinine. Duplex ultrasound is a useful screening tool; CT angiography or MR angiography provides definitive diagnosis.

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman presents with serum sodium of 118 mEq/L. She appears euvolemic on exam. Urine sodium is 45 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 520 mOsm/kg. Serum osmolality is 248 mOsm/kg. TSH and cortisol are normal. What is the diagnosis?
options: C. Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
questions.explanation: SIADH is characterized by euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, often >300) and elevated urine sodium (>20–40 mEq/L) despite low serum osmolality. It results from inappropriate ADH secretion causing water retention without sodium retention. The criteria include: serum hypo-osmolality, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, clinical euvolemia, urine sodium >40 mEq/L, and exclusion of hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (both ruled out here). Treatment depends on acuity and chronicity: fluid restriction for chronic asymptomatic cases, hypertonic saline (3%) for severe symptomatic cases.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man on hydrochlorothiazide and furosemide for heart failure has serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L and arterial blood gas showing pH 7.52, PaCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 38 mEq/L. What is the acid-base disorder?
options: A. Metabolic alkalosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
B. Mixed metabolic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis
C. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory acidosis (mixed disorder)
questions.explanation: This patient has metabolic alkalosis (elevated HCO3 38 mEq/L, elevated pH 7.52) with respiratory compensation. In metabolic alkalosis, expected respiratory compensation is hypoventilation: expected PaCO2 = 40 + (0.7 × ΔHCO3) = 40 + (0.7 × 18) = 40 + 12.6 ≈ 52.6 mmHg. The observed PaCO2 of 48 mmHg is within the expected range (allowing ±5), confirming appropriate compensation—not a mixed disorder. Diuretic use causes chloride-responsive metabolic alkalosis via volume contraction, hypokalemia, and loss of HCl. Treatment is IV normal saline (0.9% NaCl) and potassium replacement.

questions.question: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has ABG: pH 7.18, PaCO2 22 mmHg, HCO3 8 mEq/L. Serum Na 138, Cl 98, HCO3 8. Is the respiratory compensation appropriate?
options: A. Yes; expected PaCO2 by Winter's formula is 22 mmHg
B. No; there is a concurrent respiratory acidosis
C. No; there is a concurrent respiratory alkalosis
D. Yes; expected PaCO2 by Winter's formula is 30 mmHg
questions.explanation: Winter's formula estimates expected PaCO2 in metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = (1.5 × HCO3) + 8 ± 2 = (1.5 × 8) + 8 ± 2 = 12 + 8 ± 2 = 20 ± 2 = 18–22 mmHg. The observed PaCO2 of 22 mmHg falls within this range, confirming appropriate respiratory compensation without a concurrent respiratory acid-base disorder. The anion gap = 138 - 98 - 8 = 32 mEq/L (elevated, normal 8–12), consistent with DKA (AGMA from ketoacids). An elevated AG is explained by ketoacids (acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate).

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology of secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease and describe its management.
questions.answer: In CKD, declining GFR leads to phosphate retention (reduced excretion) and decreased 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in the kidney, resulting in reduced conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D). Reduced calcitriol and hyperphosphatemia both impair calcium absorption from the gut and reduce suppression of PTH secretion, leading to chronic stimulation of the parathyroid glands and secondary hyperparathyroidism. FGF-23, secreted by osteocytes in response to phosphate load, rises early in CKD and contributes to reduced calcitriol synthesis and parathyroid stimulation. Management includes dietary phosphate restriction, non-calcium phosphate binders (e.g., sevelamer, lanthanum carbonate) or calcium-based binders (used cautiously to avoid hypercalcemia), active vitamin D analogs (calcitriol or paricalcitol) to suppress PTH, and calcimimetics (cinacalcet) for patients on dialysis. In refractory tertiary hyperparathyroidism with autonomously functioning parathyroid glands, parathyroidectomy may be required.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman develops hematuria and proteinuria 24 hours after an upper respiratory tract infection. Serum complement levels are normal. Kidney biopsy shows mesangial IgA deposits. What is the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and prognosis?
questions.answer: This is IgA nephropathy (Berger disease), the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by mesangial deposition of galactose-deficient IgA1, triggering complement activation and mesangial cell proliferation. The hallmark distinguishing feature from post-streptococcal GN is the timing—IgA nephropathy causes 'synpharyngitic' hematuria occurring within 1–2 days of URI (rather than 1–3 weeks later), and serum complement levels are normal (C3 is low in PSGN). Presentation ranges from asymptomatic microscopic hematuria to nephrotic or nephritic syndrome or rapidly progressive GN. Approximately 20–40% of patients progress to ESRD over 20 years; poor prognostic features include hypertension, heavy proteinuria (>1 g/day), elevated creatinine at presentation, and histological crescents or tubular atrophy. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are used for proteinuria reduction, and targeted-release budesonide (Nefecon) is now approved for IgA nephropathy with persistent proteinuria.

questions.question: Describe the differences between hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis, including mechanism, access, and clinical considerations for patient selection.
questions.answer: Hemodialysis (HD) uses an extracorporeal circuit in which blood is pumped through an artificial semipermeable membrane (dialyzer), allowing diffusion of solutes down concentration gradients and ultrafiltration of excess fluid. Access requires either an arteriovenous fistula (preferred—lowest infection/thrombosis risk, may take 3–6 months to mature), AV graft, or central venous catheter (highest risk of infection/thrombosis). HD is typically performed 3 times weekly in 3–4 hour sessions at a dialysis center, creating rapid hemodynamic shifts that can be poorly tolerated by hemodynamically unstable patients. Peritoneal dialysis (PD) uses the peritoneal membrane as the dialyzer, with dialysate instilled into the peritoneal cavity via a surgically placed Tenckhoff catheter; solutes equilibrate across the peritoneum and the dialysate is then drained. PD provides more continuous, gentler clearance and better preservation of residual kidney function, and allows home-based treatment with greater patient independence. PD is preferred in patients with poor vascular access, hemodynamic instability, or preference for home therapy; contraindications include prior abdominal surgeries causing adhesions, active inflammatory bowel disease, and inability to perform the exchanges. The main complication of PD is peritonitis (usually gram-positive organisms from catheter contamination).

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with CKD and no prior bicarbonate supplementation has serum bicarbonate of 16 mEq/L. Explain the cause of metabolic acidosis in CKD and its clinical consequences.
questions.answer: In CKD, metabolic acidosis develops due to reduced ammoniagenesis (impaired ability of the damaged kidney to excrete ammonium, NH4+), leading to net acid retention. With normal-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis occurring in earlier CKD stages, and high-anion-gap acidosis predominating in advanced CKD (stages 4–5) due to accumulation of organic acids (phosphates, sulfates, hippurate) that are normally excreted. Chronic metabolic acidosis has several harmful consequences: it stimulates bone buffering (calcium release from bone leading to osteodystrophy and increased fracture risk), activates protein catabolism (accelerating muscle wasting), stimulates residual kidney ammoniagenesis which can worsen tubulointerstitial injury by activating complement, and accelerates CKD progression. Treatment with oral sodium bicarbonate supplementation (targeting serum HCO3 >22 mEq/L) has been shown in multiple trials to slow CKD progression, preserve muscle mass, and improve bone health; newer agents like veverimer (a non-absorbable HCl binder) are also available.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman is found to have bilateral renal masses on ultrasound, with multiple cysts in both kidneys. She reports her father underwent dialysis. What is the most likely diagnosis, associated extrarenal manifestations, and genetic basis?
questions.answer: This is autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common inherited kidney disorder, caused by mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16, encoding polycystin-1; ~85% of cases) or PKD2 (chromosome 4, encoding polycystin-2; ~15% of cases, milder phenotype). ADPKD is characterized by progressive bilateral renal cyst development leading to massive kidney enlargement and eventual ESRD, typically in the 4th–7th decade. Extrarenal manifestations include intracranial aneurysms (berry aneurysms in ~10%, major cause of premature death—screening with MRA recommended if family history of rupture), hepatic cysts (most common extrarenal finding, usually asymptomatic), mitral valve prolapse, colonic diverticula, and abdominal wall hernias. Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, slows cyst growth and preserves kidney function in rapidly progressing ADPKD (requires hepatic monitoring due to hepatotoxicity risk). Hypertension management with ACE inhibitors or ARBs is the cornerstone of treatment.

questions.question: Explain the approach to diagnosing and managing hyperkalemia, including the mechanisms of action of each treatment modality.
questions.answer: Hyperkalemia (serum K+ >5.5 mEq/L) management is stratified by severity and EKG changes. Initial assessment includes EKG (peaked T waves → PR prolongation → QRS widening → sine wave → VF); severe hyperkalemia with EKG changes requires emergent treatment. Calcium gluconate (or calcium chloride) is given first as membrane stabilization—it raises the threshold potential, reducing cardiac excitability within minutes but does NOT lower serum potassium; its effect lasts 30–60 minutes, providing a bridge. Insulin (10 units regular IV) with dextrose shifts potassium intracellularly via Na+/K+-ATPase stimulation, lowering serum K+ by 0.5–1.5 mEq/L within 15–30 minutes. Sodium bicarbonate (in acidotic patients) also promotes intracellular shift. Inhaled albuterol (beta-2 agonist) activates Na+/K+-ATPase, providing additional transient lowering. Kayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) or patiromer (potassium binder) and furosemide enhance renal/GI potassium excretion for definitive removal. Hemodialysis is the most effective and rapid method for removing potassium from the body and is indicated for refractory hyperkalemia or when renal function is severely impaired.
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia (serum K+ >5. 5 mEq/L) management is stratified by severity and EKG changes.  Initial assessment includes EKG (peaked T waves → PR prolongation → QRS widening → sine wave → VF); severe hyperkalemia with EKG changes requires emergent treatment.

questions.question: Describe the nephrotic syndrome, its major complications, and the pathophysiological basis for each complication.
questions.answer: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by the tetrad of: massive proteinuria (>3.5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (<3.0 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia/lipiduria. The pathophysiology stems from disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier (podocytes, GBM, endothelium), allowing albumin to pass into the filtrate. Hypoalbuminemia results from urinary albumin loss exceeding hepatic synthesis capacity, reducing plasma oncotic pressure. Edema forms due to reduced oncotic pressure causing fluid shift to the interstitium (underfill hypothesis) and/or primary renal sodium retention (overfill hypothesis). Hyperlipidemia occurs because the liver increases lipoprotein synthesis in response to reduced oncotic pressure, and decreased lipid catabolism from urinary loss of lipoprotein lipase. Hypercoagulability—a serious complication—results from urinary loss of anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin III, protein C, protein S) combined with increased hepatic synthesis of procoagulant factors (fibrinogen, factor V, VIII), increasing risk of renal vein thrombosis, DVT, and PE. Increased infection susceptibility results from urinary loss of immunoglobulins (especially IgG) and complement components.
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by the tetrad of: massive proteinuria (>3. 5 g/day), hypoalbuminemia (<3. 0 g/dL), edema, and hyperlipidemia/lipiduria.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with recurrent uric acid kidney stones and persistently acidic urine (pH 5.0). Describe the pathophysiology of uric acid stone formation, how it differs from calcium oxalate stones, and outline the treatment approach.
questions.answer: Uric acid stones form because uric acid is poorly soluble at acidic pH (<5.5); at low urine pH, uric acid exists predominantly in its non-ionized, insoluble form rather than as the more soluble urate anion. Risk factors include persistently acidic urine (seen in metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and gout due to impaired renal ammoniagenesis), hyperuricosuria (high purine intake, gout, tumor lysis), and low urine volume. Unlike calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones, uric acid stones are radiolucent on plain X-ray (visible only on CT) and can be dissolved with medical therapy alone. Treatment involves three pillars: high fluid intake (>2.5 L/day) to achieve urine output >2 L/day, urine alkalinization with potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate to target urine pH 6.0–6.5 (which converts insoluble uric acid to soluble urate and can dissolve existing stones), and allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor) if hyperuricosuria is present or stones recur despite alkalinization. Dietary modification includes a low-purine diet (limiting organ meats, shellfish, alcohol) and avoiding dehydration.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops nephrotic-range proteinuria, hematuria, and RBC casts. Complement C3 and C4 are both low. Kidney biopsy shows 'wire loop' lesions and subendothelial immune complex deposits involving >50% of glomeruli. Identify the lupus nephritis class, explain the complement pattern, and describe treatment.
questions.answer: This is ISN/RPS Class IV (diffuse proliferative) lupus nephritis, the most severe and most common class of lupus nephritis, defined by involvement of >50% of glomeruli with endocapillary or extracapillary proliferation. The 'wire loop' lesion is the histological hallmark, representing massive subendothelial immune complex deposits that expand and rigidify the glomerular capillary wall. Low C3 and C4 (both classical pathway components) reflect immune complex-mediated complement consumption via the classical pathway, distinguishing lupus nephritis from conditions that consume only C3 (alternative pathway activation). Treatment for Class III and IV lupus nephritis requires aggressive immunosuppression: induction therapy with either mycophenolate mofetil (MMF, preferred in non-Hispanic patients) or cyclophosphamide (preferred in rapidly progressive disease or severe crescentic nephritis) combined with high-dose corticosteroids. Maintenance therapy uses MMF or azathioprine; newer adjunctive agents include belimumab (anti-BLyS monoclonal antibody) and voclosporin (calcineurin inhibitor), both of which have demonstrated reduced proteinuria and improved renal outcomes in clinical trials.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with BP 230/140 mmHg, severe headache, blurred vision, confusion, AKI (creatinine 3.2 from baseline 1.0), and schistocytes on peripheral smear. Explain the diagnosis, underlying renal pathology, and principles of blood pressure management.
questions.answer: This is malignant hypertension (hypertensive emergency) complicated by thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) and hypertensive nephrosclerosis. The markedly elevated BP causes fibrinoid necrosis of small arterioles and arteries throughout the body; in the kidney, this produces malignant nephrosclerosis with arteriolar necrosis, ischemic glomerular injury, hematuria, proteinuria, and AKI. The schistocytes on peripheral smear reflect microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), caused by mechanical destruction of red blood cells passing through damaged, narrowed arterioles—a form of secondary TMA driven by the hypertension itself. The critical principle of BP management is to lower mean arterial pressure (MAP) by 20–25% within the first hour using IV agents (nicardipine, labetalol, or clevidipine are preferred; avoid hydralazine due to unpredictable effect), and NOT to normalize BP acutely. Chronic hypertension causes cerebral autoregulatory shift to higher pressures; acute normalization risks watershed ischemic strokes, myocardial infarction, or further renal ischemia. After the first hour, further cautious reduction to 160/100 mmHg over 2–6 hours is appropriate, with oral agents initiated once stable. Renal function often improves substantially with BP control.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with osteoarthritis takes ibuprofen daily and presents with AKI. Which mechanism best explains NSAID-induced acute kidney injury?
options: A. Direct tubular toxicity from accumulation in proximal tubule cells
B. Afferent arteriolar constriction due to prostaglandin inhibition
C. Immune-mediated glomerular injury via IgG deposition
D. Ureteral obstruction from crystal precipitation
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, which normally maintains afferent arteriolar dilation in states of reduced renal perfusion. When prostaglandins are blocked, afferent arterioles constrict, reducing glomerular filtration pressure and GFR. This effect is most pronounced in patients with underlying volume depletion, heart failure, cirrhosis, or CKD where the kidney is dependent on prostaglandins to maintain perfusion. Stopping the NSAID typically reverses the AKI.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man with gram-negative sepsis receives gentamicin. Three days later, his creatinine rises but he maintains adequate urine output. Which finding is most characteristic of aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity?
options: A. Oliguric acute kidney injury with muddy brown casts
B. Non-oliguric AKI with proximal tubular injury
C. Nephrotic syndrome with podocyte effacement
D. Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents
questions.explanation: Aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity characteristically causes non-oliguric AKI, distinguishing it from other causes of ATN. The drug accumulates in proximal tubular cells via megalin-mediated endocytosis, causing mitochondrial dysfunction and cell death. Because the drug damages tubular cells rather than causing severe vasoconstriction, urine output is often preserved. The AKI typically appears after 5-10 days of therapy and can worsen even after the drug is stopped due to ongoing release from tubular cells.

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic woman with CKD stage 3 is scheduled for coronary angiography. Which intervention has the strongest evidence for preventing contrast-induced AKI?
options: A. N-acetylcysteine 600 mg orally twice daily
B. Sodium bicarbonate infusion at 3 mL/kg/hour
C. Intravenous isotonic saline before and after the procedure
D. Withholding renin-angiotensin system blockers for 48 hours
questions.explanation: Intravenous isotonic saline hydration before and after contrast administration is the best-established preventive measure for contrast-induced AKI, maintaining renal perfusion and diluting the nephrotoxic contrast agent. N-acetylcysteine has shown conflicting results across trials and is no longer routinely recommended by major guidelines. Sodium bicarbonate has not been shown superior to isotonic saline in large randomized trials. Minimizing contrast volume and using iso-osmolar or low-osmolar agents are also important adjunctive measures.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman on penicillin for endocarditis develops fever, rash, and rising creatinine. Urinalysis shows white cell casts and eosinophiluria. What is the best next step?
options: A. Increase the penicillin dose and add corticosteroids
B. Discontinue penicillin and consider a short course of prednisone
C. Perform immediate renal biopsy before any treatment
D. Switch to a fluoroquinolone and monitor renal function
questions.explanation: This presentation is classic for acute interstitial nephritis (AIN) caused by penicillin: the triad of fever, rash, and AKI along with eosinophiluria and WBC casts confirms the diagnosis. The primary treatment is withdrawal of the offending drug. Corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) are used in patients who do not improve within 5-7 days of drug discontinuation, or when AKI is severe. Renal biopsy can confirm the diagnosis but is not required before initiating treatment when the clinical picture is clear.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with recurrent flank pain and hematuria. CT scan shows a 6 mm radio-opaque stone in the right ureter. Urine pH is 5.5. Which stone type is most likely, and what is the best long-term preventive strategy?
options: A. Uric acid stone; alkalinize urine with potassium citrate
B. Calcium oxalate stone; thiazide diuretic and increased fluid intake
C. Struvite stone; long-term suppressive antibiotics
questions.explanation: Calcium oxalate stones are the most common kidney stones (70-80%), are radio-opaque on plain films, and typically form in acidic to neutral urine. Thiazide diuretics reduce urinary calcium excretion by enhancing distal tubular calcium reabsorption, reducing recurrence risk. Adequate fluid intake to maintain urine output greater than 2 L/day is the most important universal preventive measure. Uric acid stones, in contrast, are radiolucent and require urine alkalinization for prevention.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with gout presents with a 1 cm radiolucent kidney stone on CT. Urine pH is 4.9. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
options: A. Thiazide diuretic and sodium restriction
B. Alkalinize urine with potassium citrate and consider allopurinol
C. Percutaneous nephrolithotomy due to stone size
D. Calcium supplementation with meals to bind dietary oxalate
questions.explanation: Radiolucent stones in a patient with gout and persistently acidic urine are virtually diagnostic of uric acid nephrolithiasis. Uric acid is poorly soluble in acidic urine but dissolves readily above pH 6.5; therefore, alkalinizing the urine with potassium citrate can actually dissolve existing stones and prevent new ones. Allopurinol reduces uric acid production and is added in patients with hyperuricosuria or recurrent stones. Unlike most stones, uric acid stones can often be dissolved medically without surgery.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is found to have bilateral flank masses. She reports a family history of kidney disease and subarachnoid hemorrhage. Ultrasound confirms bilateral enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts. Describe the genetics, extrarenal manifestations, and current disease-modifying treatment of this condition.
questions.answer: This presentation is classic for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), the most common hereditary kidney disease. PKD1 mutations on chromosome 16 account for approximately 85% of cases and cause more severe disease with ESRD at a mean age of 54 years, while PKD2 mutations on chromosome 4 account for 15% and have a milder course with ESRD at mean age 74 years. Extrarenal manifestations include hepatic cysts (most common), intracranial berry aneurysms in 5-10% of patients (explaining the family history of subarachnoid hemorrhage), mitral valve prolapse, and diverticular disease. Screening for intracranial aneurysms by MRA is recommended in patients with a personal or family history of aneurysm or rupture. Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, is the only FDA-approved therapy shown to slow total kidney volume growth and preserve eGFR in patients with rapidly progressive disease, though liver toxicity requires monitoring.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with ADPKD has a total kidney volume of 1800 mL and eGFR of 65 mL/min. Which medication has been shown to slow cyst growth and preserve kidney function in ADPKD?
options: A. Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) to reduce proteinuria
D. Hydroxychloroquine to reduce cyst inflammation
questions.explanation: Tolvaptan, a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, is the only FDA-approved treatment to slow kidney growth and decline in kidney function in adults with ADPKD at risk of rapid progression. It works by reducing intracellular cAMP in tubular epithelial cells, which drives cyst proliferation and fluid secretion. The TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials demonstrated significant slowing of total kidney volume increase and preservation of eGFR. Liver toxicity is a serious adverse effect requiring monitoring. mTOR inhibitors showed promise in animal models but failed to slow disease progression in large human trials.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with atherosclerosis develops flash pulmonary edema and worsening hypertension after starting an ACE inhibitor. Renal arteriography reveals greater than 80% bilateral renal artery stenosis. Which statement about this condition is correct?
options: A. ACE inhibitors are the treatment of choice to reduce intraglomerular pressure
B. ACE inhibitors are contraindicated because they can precipitate acute kidney injury
C. Revascularization is always preferred over medical therapy
D. This presentation is more typical of fibromuscular dysplasia than atherosclerosis
questions.explanation: In bilateral renal artery stenosis (or unilateral stenosis in a solitary kidney), ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated. When both renal arteries are severely stenotic, GFR is maintained by angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction; blocking this response precipitates acute kidney injury. Flash pulmonary edema is a hallmark presentation of bilateral atherosclerotic RAS in older men. Medical management with other antihypertensives is preferred over revascularization for most patients, as the ASTRAL and CORAL trials showed no benefit of stenting over optimal medical therapy alone.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has hypertension and a renal artery bruit. Renal MRA shows a 'string-of-beads' appearance of the right renal artery. Describe the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and management of this condition, contrasting it with atherosclerotic renovascular disease.
questions.answer: The string-of-beads pattern is pathognomonic for fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), a non-inflammatory, non-atherosclerotic arteriopathy caused by dysplastic changes in the media of medium-sized arteries, most often the renal and carotid arteries. FMD predominantly affects young to middle-aged women and is not associated with traditional cardiovascular risk factors, in contrast to atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis which affects older men with hyperlipidemia, diabetes, and smoking history. Because FMD involves unilateral stenosis with a normal contralateral kidney, ACE inhibitors are not contraindicated and can be used for blood pressure control. Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty (PTA) without stenting is the preferred definitive treatment, achieving cure or markedly improved blood pressure control in over 80% of patients; stenting is reserved for refractory cases or dissection. Unlike atherosclerotic RAS, FMD does not require statin therapy and has an excellent long-term prognosis with appropriate revascularization.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with hemoptysis, hematuria, and rapidly rising creatinine. ANCA testing is negative, but anti-GBM antibodies are strongly positive. Renal biopsy shows linear IgG deposits along the GBM and greater than 50% crescents. What is the first-line treatment?
options: B. High-dose corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide, and plasmapheresis
D. ACE inhibitor plus ARB dual blockade
questions.explanation: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture syndrome) is caused by antibodies against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, producing rapidly progressive GN and pulmonary hemorrhage. Treatment requires aggressive combination therapy: plasmapheresis to rapidly remove circulating anti-GBM antibodies, high-dose corticosteroids to suppress inflammation, and cyclophosphamide to halt antibody production. Without immediate treatment, most patients progress to dialysis dependency. Prognosis depends heavily on presenting creatinine and the percentage of crescents on biopsy.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with SLE develops nephrotic syndrome and worsening renal function. Renal biopsy shows diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis involving more than 50% of glomeruli. Which ISN/RPS class is this, and what is the induction treatment?
options: B. Class IV (diffuse proliferative); mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide plus steroids
C. Class V (membranous); ACE inhibitor plus tacrolimus
D. Class III (focal proliferative); observation with close follow-up
questions.explanation: Diffuse proliferative lupus nephritis is classified as ISN/RPS Class IV and is the most severe and common form, characterized by involvement of greater than 50% of glomeruli. Induction therapy uses high-dose corticosteroids combined with either mycophenolate mofetil (preferred for its lower gonadotoxicity) or cyclophosphamide (Eurolupus or NIH regimen for severe disease). Maintenance therapy with mycophenolate or azathioprine is continued for at least 3 years to prevent relapse. Hydroxychloroquine is added as background therapy for all lupus nephritis patients regardless of class.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with c-ANCA (anti-PR3) positivity presents with sinus disease, hemoptysis, and hematuria with RBC casts. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic GN. Which diagnosis and treatment are most appropriate?
options: A. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA); cyclophosphamide plus steroids
B. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA); cyclophosphamide plus high-dose steroids
C. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA); steroids alone
D. Anti-GBM disease; plasmapheresis plus cyclophosphamide
questions.explanation: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener's granulomatosis) is an ANCA-associated vasculitis characterized by granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tract plus pauci-immune GN, associated with c-ANCA (anti-PR3) in over 90% of cases. Induction therapy for severe organ-threatening disease uses cyclophosphamide plus high-dose corticosteroids; rituximab is an alternative for induction and is preferred for maintenance therapy. Microscopic polyangiitis is associated with p-ANCA (anti-MPO) and lacks the granulomatous features and upper respiratory tract involvement seen in GPA.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and tense ascites develops oliguria and rising creatinine. Urinalysis is bland and urine sodium is 8 mEq/L. Creatinine does not improve after 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and albumin infusion. Describe the pathophysiology, diagnostic criteria, and management of this condition, including the difference between type 1 and type 2.
questions.answer: This presentation meets criteria for hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), a functional AKI caused by extreme renal vasoconstriction in the setting of advanced cirrhosis. The pathophysiology involves splanchnic vasodilation from portal hypertension (mediated by nitric oxide and other vasodilators), leading to reduced effective arterial blood volume, reflex activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system, and intense renal vasoconstriction with markedly reduced GFR despite structurally intact kidneys. HRS-AKI (formerly type 1) is rapidly progressive with creatinine doubling to above 2.5 mg/dL within 2 weeks and carries a median survival of weeks without treatment, while HRS-CKD (formerly type 2) progresses more slowly and typically presents with refractory ascites rather than acute crisis. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other AKI causes: no shock, no nephrotoxins, no parenchymal kidney disease (bland urinalysis with no casts or proteinuria, urine sodium below 20 mEq/L), and lack of improvement after at least 2 days of diuretic withdrawal plus albumin challenge (1 g/kg/day). Treatment of HRS-AKI uses terlipressin plus IV albumin (20-40 g/day) as first-line therapy, or norepinephrine plus albumin in ICU settings; liver transplantation is the only definitive cure.
questions.explanation: This presentation meets criteria for hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), a functional AKI caused by extreme renal vasoconstriction in the setting of advanced cirrhosis.  The pathophysiology involves splanchnic vasodilation from portal hypertension (mediated by nitric oxide and other vasodilators), leading to reduced effective arterial blood volume, reflex activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sympathetic nervous system, and intense renal vasoconstriction with markedly reduced GFR despite structurally intact kidneys.  HRS-AKI (formerly type 1) is rapidly progressive with creatinine doubling to above 2.

questions.question: A patient with non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis has a urine pH of 6.2 despite severe systemic acidemia (serum pH 7.18). Serum potassium is 2.8 mEq/L and there is nephrocalcinosis on imaging. Which type of RTA does this represent?
options: A. Type 1 (distal) RTA with impaired urinary acidification
B. Type 2 (proximal) RTA with bicarbonate wasting
C. Type 4 RTA with hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism
questions.explanation: Type 1 (distal) RTA is characterized by inability of the distal tubule to acidify urine below pH 5.5, even in the setting of severe systemic acidosis. The urine pH remains inappropriately elevated above 5.5 when the serum is markedly acidemic. Hypokalemia is characteristic because the inability to excrete H+ leads to compensatory K+ wasting. Long-term consequences include nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis due to alkaline urine, hypercalciuria, and hypocitraturia. Type 4 RTA causes hyperkalemia rather than hypokalemia, and Type 2 RTA produces urine pH below 5.5 once the serum bicarbonate falls below the proximal reabsorption threshold.

questions.question: A 65-year-old diabetic man with CKD has a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L and urine pH of 5.1. Plasma renin and aldosterone are both low. Which type of RTA is this?
options: A. Type 1 distal RTA due to H-ATPase deficiency
B. Type 2 proximal RTA with Fanconi syndrome
C. Type 4 RTA due to hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism
D. Type 1 distal RTA due to sickle cell nephropathy
questions.explanation: Type 4 RTA is the most common form in clinical practice, typically occurring in older diabetics with mild to moderate CKD. It is caused by hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism: reduced renin secretion from tubular damage leads to reduced aldosterone, impairing distal tubular H+ and K+ excretion. The hallmark is hyperkalemia (not hypokalemia as in Types 1 and 2) with a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The urine can be appropriately acidified (pH less than 5.5) because the H-ATPase remains intact. Treatment includes dietary potassium restriction, loop diuretics, and fludrocortisone in selected patients.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and management of cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity.
questions.answer: Cisplatin causes nephrotoxicity primarily by accumulating in proximal tubular cells via organic cation transporters, leading to mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and tubular cell apoptosis. Clinically, it presents as non-oliguric AKI with significant electrolyte wasting including hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypophosphatemia due to tubular damage; this typically occurs 3-5 days after administration and worsens with cumulative doses. Prevention strategies include aggressive IV hydration with isotonic saline before and after cisplatin to maintain urine output greater than 100 mL/hour, and avoiding concurrent nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs and aminoglycosides. Magnesium supplementation is essential as hypomagnesemia can persist long after cisplatin exposure and cause symptomatic tetany. Carboplatin or oxaliplatin are less nephrotoxic alternatives when oncologically appropriate.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a kidney transplant on tacrolimus develops progressive azotemia and hypertension two years post-transplant. Renal biopsy shows arteriolar hyalinosis and tubular atrophy. Explain the mechanism and management of calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity.
questions.answer: Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus and cyclosporine) cause nephrotoxicity through two main mechanisms: acute reversible vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole mediated by increased thromboxane A2 and endothelin with reduced nitric oxide production, and chronic irreversible fibrosis driven by TGF-beta upregulation leading to arteriolar hyalinosis, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis. Acute toxicity is dose-dependent and reversible with dose reduction, while chronic toxicity causes progressive CKD that does not recover. Management includes minimizing calcineurin inhibitor exposure by targeting the lowest effective trough level, and in selected patients switching to an mTOR inhibitor (everolimus or sirolimus) to allow calcineurin inhibitor withdrawal or minimization. Aggressive blood pressure control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs may slow fibrosis progression. Chronic allograft nephropathy from calcineurin inhibitor toxicity remains a leading cause of late kidney transplant failure.

questions.question: Describe the diagnosis and management of chronic interstitial nephritis caused by analgesic nephropathy.
questions.answer: Analgesic nephropathy results from chronic heavy use of analgesic combinations, historically phenacetin-containing mixtures and now combinations of aspirin, acetaminophen, and caffeine, causing papillary necrosis and chronic tubulointerstitial nephritis. The diagnosis is suggested by a history of long-term heavy analgesic consumption (greater than 3 years, often exceeding 3 kg total), a characteristic CT appearance of small scarred kidneys with calcified papillae or frank papillary necrosis, and slowly progressive CKD with a urinary concentrating defect, sterile pyuria, and mild proteinuria. Sloughed papillae can cause ureteral obstruction and renal colic mimicking nephrolithiasis. Management centers on complete cessation of the offending analgesics, which can stabilize but rarely reverses established renal injury. Patients require long-term surveillance for urothelial transitional cell carcinoma, which occurs at markedly increased frequency in analgesic nephropathy.

questions.question: A patient has ABG showing pH 7.20, PaCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3 11 mEq/L. Serum sodium is 140, chloride 105, albumin 4.0 g/dL. Calculate the anion gap and delta-delta ratio, and interpret the complete acid-base disturbance.
questions.answer: The anion gap is Na minus (Cl plus HCO3) = 140 minus (105 plus 11) = 24 mEq/L, which is elevated above the normal of 8-12 mEq/L. The delta anion gap (change from normal) is 24 minus 12 = 12, and the delta bicarbonate change is 24 minus 11 = 13; the delta-delta ratio is 12 divided by 13 = 0.92, which falls between 0.4 and 1.0, consistent with a pure elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis without a concurrent metabolic alkalosis or non-anion-gap acidosis. Using Winter's formula, the expected respiratory compensation is PaCO2 = (1.5 times 11) plus 8 plus or minus 2 = 24.5 to 28.5 mmHg; the measured PaCO2 of 30 mmHg exceeds this range, indicating a concurrent primary respiratory acidosis (inadequate compensation). This represents a mixed disturbance of elevated anion-gap metabolic acidosis plus respiratory acidosis, suggesting impaired ventilatory drive or severe respiratory muscle fatigue that warrants urgent evaluation.

questions.question: Describe the significance of different cast types on urine microscopy and what diagnoses they suggest.
questions.answer: Urinary casts form when Tamm-Horsfall protein (uromodulin) precipitates in renal tubular lumens and traps cellular elements, making them highly specific for intrinsic renal pathology. Red blood cell (RBC) casts are pathognomonic of glomerulonephritis, indicating bleeding within the glomerulus and distinguishing nephritic proteinuria and hematuria from post-renal causes. White blood cell (WBC) casts indicate inflammation within the renal tubule or interstitium and are seen in pyelonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis, and occasionally in proliferative GN. Granular (muddy brown) casts represent degenerated epithelial cell casts and are the hallmark of acute tubular necrosis, correlating with proximal tubular cell sloughing. Waxy and broad casts form in dilated, atrophied tubules with slow urine flow and indicate advanced CKD; their presence suggests severe, longstanding renal disease. Fatty casts and oval fat bodies displaying a Maltese cross pattern under polarized light indicate heavy lipiduria characteristic of nephrotic syndrome.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology and clinical features of struvite kidney stones, including why they can be dangerous and how they are treated.
questions.answer: Struvite stones (magnesium ammonium phosphate) form exclusively in the setting of urinary tract infections with urease-producing organisms, most commonly Proteus mirabilis, but also Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Staphylococcus. Urease cleaves urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide, raising urine pH above 7.0 and creating conditions of supersaturation for struvite crystallization; this alkaline environment also promotes calcium phosphate co-precipitation. Struvite stones are radio-opaque, grow rapidly, and characteristically fill the entire renal collecting system to form staghorn calculi that conform to the shape of the renal pelvis and calyces. They are dangerous because bacteria are harbored within the stone matrix, making infection impossible to eradicate without complete stone removal; persistent infection causes recurrent urosepsis, progressive renal obstruction, and kidney failure. Management requires complete stone removal, preferably by percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large staghorn calculi, targeted long-term antibiotic therapy to prevent recurrence, and acetohydroxamic acid (a urease inhibitor) in patients who cannot undergo surgery.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man has recurrent kidney stones since childhood. Hexagonal crystals are seen on urinalysis. Describe the pathophysiology, diagnosis, and treatment of cystinuria.
questions.answer: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the SLC3A1 or SLC7A9 genes encoding the rBAT/b0,+AT transporter responsible for reabsorption of dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine) in the proximal tubule. Because cystine is poorly soluble at physiologic urine pH, excess urinary cystine precipitates to form stones that are faintly radio-opaque and display pathognomonic hexagonal crystals on microscopy. Diagnosis is confirmed by 24-hour urine cystine excretion greater than 250 mg per gram of creatinine and a positive sodium cyanide-nitroprusside urine test. Treatment requires very high fluid intake (greater than 4 L/day to dilute urine cystine), urine alkalinization to pH above 7.0 with potassium citrate to increase cystine solubility, and chelating agents such as D-penicillamine or tiopronin that form soluble mixed disulfide complexes with cystine in patients who fail conservative measures or have recurrent large stones.
