questions.question: A 32-year-old Black woman presents with bilateral hilar adenopathy on chest X-ray, erythema nodosum on her shins, and bilateral ankle arthritis. She has no fever, weight loss, or pulmonary symptoms. What is the most likely diagnosis and what is the initial treatment?
options: A. Lymphoma; start chemotherapy after biopsy confirmation
B. Tuberculosis; start four-drug anti-tuberculosis therapy
C. Löfgren syndrome (sarcoidosis); NSAIDs and observation
questions.explanation: Löfgren syndrome is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis characterized by the triad of bilateral hilar adenopathy, erythema nodosum, and arthritis/periarthritis, often with fever. It is most common in young women of Northern European or Black African descent and carries an excellent prognosis with spontaneous remission in most cases. Treatment is symptomatic with NSAIDs for joint pain and erythema nodosum; corticosteroids are not required for Löfgren syndrome as it typically resolves on its own. Biopsy is not always necessary when the clinical picture is classic.

questions.question: In a patient with sarcoidosis, an elevated serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level is found. Which statement best describes the clinical utility of serum ACE in sarcoidosis?
options: A. It is diagnostic of sarcoidosis and eliminates the need for biopsy
B. It is elevated in most sarcoidosis patients and correlates with disease activity, but is neither sensitive nor specific enough to diagnose sarcoidosis
C. A normal ACE level rules out active sarcoidosis
D. ACE levels are used to determine when to start corticosteroid therapy
questions.explanation: Serum ACE is produced by epithelioid cells in sarcoid granulomas and is elevated in approximately 60% of patients with active sarcoidosis. However, it has limited diagnostic utility because it is neither sensitive (elevated in only ~60% of cases) nor specific (elevated in other granulomatous diseases such as berylliosis, histoplasmosis, TB, and silicosis, as well as hyperthyroidism and diabetes). ACE levels can be used to monitor disease activity and response to treatment in known sarcoidosis patients, but the diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation of non-caseating granulomas. A normal ACE does not rule out active sarcoidosis.

questions.question: A 48-year-old farmer presents with progressive dyspnea, cough, and low-grade fever that improves when he is away from work. HRCT shows upper-lobe predominant ground-glass opacities, mosaic attenuation, and centrilobular nodules. Describe the diagnosis, pathophysiology, and management.
questions.answer: This presentation is consistent with hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP), formerly called extrinsic allergic alveolitis, caused by inhalation of organic antigens—in a farmer this is most likely thermophilic actinomycetes from moldy hay ("Farmer's lung"). The pathophysiology involves a type III (immune complex) and type IV (delayed hypersensitivity) immune response to inhaled organic antigens, leading to lymphocytic and granulomatous inflammation in the bronchioles and alveoli. Symptoms classically worsen with antigen exposure and improve with removal, and BAL typically shows marked lymphocytosis (>40%) with a reversed CD4/CD8 ratio. Management requires complete antigen avoidance, which is the most important intervention; protective equipment (respirators) and modifications to working practices can help when complete avoidance is impossible. Corticosteroids (prednisone) are used for moderate-to-severe acute disease to hasten symptom resolution, though they do not alter long-term fibrotic progression. Chronic HP with fibrosis carries a poorer prognosis similar to IPF.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman with no prior medical history presents with a right-sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis reveals milky white fluid with triglycerides of 650 mg/dL and cholesterol of 80 mg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis and its most common cause in adults?
options: A. Chylothorax; most commonly caused by lymphoma or thoracic duct trauma
B. Pseudochylothorax; caused by long-standing rheumatoid pleuritis
C. Empyema; caused by anaerobic bacterial infection
D. Hemothorax; caused by thoracic aortic dissection
questions.explanation: A milky pleural fluid with triglycerides >110 mg/dL confirms chylothorax, which results from disruption or obstruction of the thoracic duct, causing lymph (chyle) to accumulate in the pleural space. The most common cause in adults is malignancy, particularly lymphoma (especially non-Hodgkin lymphoma), followed by thoracic duct trauma from surgery or procedures. Pseudochylothorax (cholesterol effusion) occurs in long-standing effusions (rheumatoid arthritis, TB) with cholesterol crystals and elevated cholesterol but normal or low triglycerides. Management of chylothorax includes dietary modifications (low-fat diet with medium-chain triglycerides), drainage, and treatment of the underlying cause.

questions.question: A 67-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 28% predicted, PaO2 55 mmHg on room air at rest) is evaluated in clinic. His hematocrit is 52%. He has no acute illness. Which intervention has been shown to improve survival in this patient?
options: A. Roflumilast to reduce exacerbation frequency
B. Long-term oxygen therapy for ≥15 hours per day
C. High-dose inhaled corticosteroids to reduce inflammation
D. Pulmonary rehabilitation alone without oxygen
questions.explanation: Long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT) for at least 15 hours per day is one of the few interventions proven to improve survival in COPD patients with severe resting hypoxemia (PaO2 ≤55 mmHg, or ≤59 mmHg with evidence of end-organ effects such as polycythemia, cor pulmonale, or pulmonary hypertension). This was established by the NOTT (Nocturnal Oxygen Therapy Trial) and MRC trials. The secondary polycythemia (Hct 52%) in this patient is consistent with chronic hypoxemia. Roflumilast reduces exacerbations but does not improve survival. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves exercise capacity and quality of life but not survival.

questions.question: Explain the PERC (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria) rule, including all eight criteria and how it is appropriately used in clinical practice.
questions.answer: The PERC rule is a clinical decision tool used to exclude PE in low-risk patients without any laboratory testing, including D-dimer. All eight criteria must be absent (PERC-negative) to apply the rule: age <50 years, heart rate <100 bpm, SpO2 ≥95% on room air, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no recent surgery or trauma within 4 weeks requiring hospitalization, no prior DVT or PE, and no hormone use (oral contraceptives, hormone replacement, or estrogenic substances). The PERC rule is only valid when the pre-test probability of PE is low (typically <15%), as assessed by clinical gestalt or a low Wells score; applying PERC to moderate or high pre-test probability patients is inappropriate and may miss PE. When a patient is low pre-test probability and PERC-negative, the probability of PE is reduced to less than 2%, which is below the test-threshold, and no further workup is needed. PERC is most useful in emergency settings to avoid unnecessary D-dimer testing and downstream imaging in low-risk patients.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer presents with progressive dyspnea and a large left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis provides symptomatic relief, but the effusion recurs within 3 weeks. What is the most appropriate definitive management for her recurrent malignant pleural effusion?
options: A. Repeat therapeutic thoracentesis every 2–3 weeks indefinitely
B. Tunneled indwelling pleural catheter (TIPC) for outpatient drainage
C. Chemical pleurodesis with talc at the time of chest tube insertion
D. Either TIPC or talc pleurodesis are appropriate first-line options
questions.explanation: For recurrent malignant pleural effusion, both tunneled indwelling pleural catheter (TIPC) and talc pleurodesis are recommended as equivalent first-line options in national guidelines (BTS, ASCO). TIPC allows outpatient intermittent drainage and is preferred in patients with poor performance status, trapped lung, or short life expectancy. Talc pleurodesis requires hospitalization and chest tube placement but may achieve long-term control without ongoing drainage requirements. The choice should be individualized based on patient performance status, pleural anatomy (whether the lung can re-expand), and patient preference. Repeat thoracentesis alone is appropriate for very limited life expectancy but is not a definitive management strategy.

questions.question: Describe the management of status asthmaticus in the emergency setting, including pharmacological and ventilatory strategies.
questions.answer: Status asthmaticus is defined as severe bronchospasm unresponsive to initial bronchodilator therapy, representing a life-threatening emergency. Initial treatment includes continuous nebulized short-acting beta-agonists (albuterol) and ipratropium, high-dose systemic corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone or oral prednisone) to reduce airway inflammation within 4–6 hours, and supplemental oxygen titrated to SpO2 >93%. Intravenous or inhaled magnesium sulfate is given for severe cases refractory to beta-agonists, as it causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation by blocking calcium entry. Heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) reduces gas density and work of breathing and may be used as a bridge therapy. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP) can be trialed in alert, cooperative patients to reduce respiratory muscle fatigue. Mechanical ventilation is a last resort due to the risk of dynamic hyperinflation (auto-PEEP) and barotrauma; if required, a strategy of low respiratory rate, long expiratory time, and permissive hypercapnia (allowing PaCO2 to rise while maintaining acceptable pH) is used to prevent air trapping. Ketamine and volatile anesthetics have bronchodilatory properties and may be used as adjuncts in refractory cases.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman with a history of dermatomyositis develops progressive exertional dyspnea. HRCT shows bilateral, lower-lobe predominant ground-glass opacities and fine reticulation in a subpleural sparing pattern. Lung biopsy shows temporally homogeneous fibrosis and inflammation without honeycombing. What is the most likely interstitial lung disease pattern?
questions.explanation: Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) is the most common ILD pattern associated with connective tissue diseases, including dermatomyositis, systemic sclerosis, and Sjögren syndrome. HRCT in NSIP shows bilateral, lower-lobe predominant ground-glass opacities and reticulation with subpleural sparing—a key distinguishing feature from UIP (which has subpleural honeycombing). Histologically, NSIP shows temporally homogeneous (uniform) fibrosis and inflammation, contrasting with the temporal heterogeneity and honeycombing of UIP. NSIP generally carries a better prognosis than IPF/UIP and is treated with corticosteroids and immunosuppression.

questions.question: A 58-year-old obese man with hypertension reports loud snoring and witnessed apneas. His STOP-BANG score is 6. Which diagnostic criterion on polysomnography confirms obstructive sleep apnea?
options: C. More than 30 arousals per hour of sleep
D. REM sleep comprising less than 15% of total sleep time
questions.explanation: OSA is diagnosed by polysomnography when the AHI is ≥5 events/hour in the setting of symptoms (e.g., daytime sleepiness, witnessed apneas) or ≥15 events/hour regardless of symptoms. The AHI counts both apneas (complete cessation of airflow ≥10 seconds) and hypopneas. Oxygen desaturation and arousals may accompany OSA but are not the defining diagnostic criterion. CPAP therapy is first-line treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed.

questions.question: Describe obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS): its diagnostic criteria, pathophysiology of chronic hypercapnia, relationship to obstructive sleep apnea, and first-line treatment.
questions.answer: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), historically called Pickwickian syndrome, is defined by three criteria: obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²), awake daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >45 mmHg), and exclusion of other causes of hypoventilation such as COPD, neuromuscular disease, or chest wall deformity. The pathophysiology involves reduced respiratory drive relative to the increased work of breathing imposed by excess chest wall and abdominal fat, blunted central chemoreceptor sensitivity to CO2, and upper airway obstruction during sleep; over time, renal bicarbonate retention compensates for chronic hypercapnia, raising serum bicarbonate above 27 mEq/L. Approximately 90% of OHS patients have coexisting OSA, but OSA alone does not cause OHS — the sustained daytime hypercapnia distinguishes OHS from pure OSA. First-line treatment is positive airway pressure therapy: CPAP is used when OSA predominates, while BiPAP (bilevel PAP) is preferred for those with severe hypercapnia or who fail CPAP, targeting normalization of PaCO2 and resolution of nocturnal hypoventilation.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy (EF 25%) reports orthopnea and is found on polysomnography to have repetitive cycles of hyperpnea followed by apnea with a crescendo-decrescendo pattern. What is the most appropriate initial management of this sleep-disordered breathing?
options: D. Optimization of heart failure therapy
questions.explanation: This patient has Cheyne-Stokes breathing, a form of central sleep apnea associated with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction. The cyclical ventilatory pattern results from prolonged circulation time and hypersensitivity of central chemoreceptors. First-line management is optimization of underlying heart failure (diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, beta-blockers), as improving cardiac output often reduces Cheyne-Stokes breathing. Adaptive servo-ventilation is contraindicated in patients with EF ≤45% based on the SERVE-HF trial, which showed increased cardiovascular mortality.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman with no known cardiac or pulmonary disease presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion. Right heart catheterization shows mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) of 28 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) of 10 mmHg, and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) of 4 Wood units. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: B. Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease (WHO Group 2)
C. Normal hemodynamics — no pulmonary hypertension
D. Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease (WHO Group 3)
questions.explanation: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH, WHO Group 1) is defined by mPAP ≥25 mmHg, PCWP ≤15 mmHg (excluding left heart disease), and PVR >3 Wood units. This patient meets all criteria. WHO Group 2 (left heart disease) requires PCWP >15 mmHg. Right heart catheterization is the gold standard for diagnosing and classifying pulmonary hypertension. Treatment options for Group 1 PAH include PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil), endothelin receptor antagonists (ambrisentan, bosentan), and prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, treprostinil).

questions.question: Describe the pharmacological treatment options for WHO Group 1 pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), including the three main drug classes, their mechanisms, and how treatment is selected.
questions.answer: WHO Group 1 PAH is treated with three classes of pulmonary vasodilators targeting distinct pathways in pulmonary vascular remodeling. Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) such as ambrisentan and bosentan block endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation; bosentan requires liver function monitoring due to hepatotoxicity risk. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE5i) such as sildenafil and tadalafil increase cyclic GMP, promoting vasodilation via the nitric oxide pathway; they are the most commonly used oral agents. Prostacyclin analogues (epoprostenol, treprostinil, iloprost) and the prostacyclin receptor agonist selexipag mimic prostacyclin's vasodilatory and antiproliferative effects; IV epoprostenol is the most potent and is reserved for severe or refractory disease. Treatment selection is guided by WHO functional class: mild-moderate disease (FC II–III) typically begins with oral monotherapy or combination ERA plus PDE5i; severe disease (FC III–IV) often warrants upfront combination therapy or IV prostacyclin. Lung transplantation is considered for patients who progress despite maximal medical therapy.
questions.explanation: WHO Group 1 PAH is treated with three classes of pulmonary vasodilators targeting distinct pathways in pulmonary vascular remodeling.  Endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs) such as ambrisentan and bosentan block endothelin-1-mediated vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation; bosentan requires liver function monitoring due to hepatotoxicity risk. questions.question: A 67-year-old male smoker (50 pack-years) presents with weight loss, hemoptysis, and a 4 cm right upper lobe mass. Biopsy reveals squamous cell carcinoma. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung?
options: B. Hypercalcemia of malignancy via PTHrP
D. Cushing syndrome from ectopic ACTH
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically produces hypercalcemia of malignancy through secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which mimics PTH at its receptor. This is the most characteristic paraneoplastic syndrome of squamous cell carcinoma. SIADH and Cushing syndrome from ectopic ACTH are associated with small cell lung cancer (SCLC). Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is also associated with SCLC. Squamous cell carcinoma is typically centrally located and associated with heavy smoking.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman who never smoked presents with a peripheral lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR exon 19 deletion. What is the preferred first-line systemic therapy?
options: C. Osimertinib (third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor)
D. Surgical resection alone without systemic therapy
questions.explanation: EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (adenocarcinoma) with sensitizing mutations (exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R) is treated with EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Osimertinib is the preferred first-line agent based on the FLAURA trial showing superior progression-free and overall survival compared to earlier-generation TKIs. EGFR mutations are more common in women, never-smokers, and East Asian patients. Chemotherapy and immunotherapy are less effective than targeted therapy in EGFR-mutated disease.

questions.question: Describe the USPSTF recommendations for lung cancer screening with low-dose CT, the evidence base supporting screening, and the criteria for discontinuing screening.
questions.answer: The USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT (LDCT) screening for lung cancer in adults aged 55–80 years who have a ≥30 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years. The recommendation is based primarily on the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), which demonstrated a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality and a 6.7% reduction in all-cause mortality with annual LDCT compared to chest X-ray in high-risk smokers. Screening should be discontinued when the person has not smoked for more than 15 years, reaches age 80, or develops a health problem that substantially limits life expectancy or the ability to undergo curative lung surgery. A positive screen requires structured follow-up using Lung-RADS categories to guide management, ranging from routine annual screening (Lung-RADS 1–2) to short-interval CT, PET scan, or tissue sampling (Lung-RADS 3–4). Shared decision-making is recommended, including counseling about the benefits, harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, radiation exposure), and the importance of continued smoking cessation.
questions.explanation: The USPSTF recommends annual low-dose CT (LDCT) screening for lung cancer in adults aged 55–80 years who have a ≥30 pack-year smoking history and currently smoke or have quit within the past 15 years.  The recommendation is based primarily on the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), which demonstrated a 20% relative reduction in lung cancer mortality and a 6. 7% reduction in all-cause mortality with annual LDCT compared to chest X-ray in high-risk smokers.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with no smoking history is found to have a 9 mm solid solitary pulmonary nodule on CT scan. Per Fleischner Society guidelines, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: B. PET scan to evaluate for malignancy
C. Surgical resection without further imaging
D. No follow-up needed — nodule is too small to be malignant
questions.explanation: Per Fleischner Society guidelines for solid pulmonary nodules, nodules >8 mm warrant PET scan and/or tissue sampling due to higher malignancy probability, regardless of risk category. For a 9 mm nodule, PET scan is appropriate to evaluate metabolic activity; FDG-avid nodules or those with interval growth require tissue sampling or surgical resection. Nodules ≤6 mm in low-risk patients typically require no follow-up. Nodules 6–8 mm in low-risk patients are followed with CT at 6–12 months.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman with severe asthma presents with productive cough, hemoptysis, and recurrent pneumonias. CT chest shows central bronchiectasis with mucus plugging. Total IgE is markedly elevated at 4,500 IU/mL and skin testing is positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus colonization occurring predominantly in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis. Diagnostic criteria include asthma, elevated total IgE (>1,000 IU/mL typically), positive Aspergillus skin test or specific IgE, central bronchiectasis, and peripheral eosinophilia. Treatment includes oral corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and itraconazole as a steroid-sparing agent. Untreated ABPA leads to progressive central bronchiectasis and fibrosis.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man with recurrent sinopulmonary infections since childhood, bronchiectasis, and male infertility is found to have situs inversus on imaging. Nasal nitric oxide is very low. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) with situs inversus constitutes Kartagener syndrome. PCD is caused by structural or functional defects in cilia, leading to impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent sinopulmonary infections progressing to bronchiectasis. Low nasal nitric oxide is a sensitive screening test for PCD. Male infertility results from immotile spermatozoa. Diagnosis is confirmed by electron microscopy of ciliary ultrastructure or genetic testing, and chest physiotherapy is the mainstay of management.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has a sweat chloride of 102 mEq/L and is homozygous for the F508del mutation. Which CFTR modulator regimen is most appropriate?
options: D. No CFTR modulator — treat symptoms only
questions.explanation: F508del is the most common CFTR mutation and causes a folding/processing defect. Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI, brand name Trikafta) is approved for patients ≥6 years with at least one F508del allele and is the most effective triple-combination modulator. ETI markedly improves FEV1, reduces pulmonary exacerbations, and improves sweat chloride and BMI. Ivacaftor monotherapy is effective only for gating mutations (e.g., G551D), not F508del. Sweat chloride >60 mEq/L is diagnostic for CF; 40–60 mEq/L is borderline.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman develops ARDS following septic shock. Her PaO2/FiO2 ratio is 85 mmHg on PEEP of 8 cmH2O. Which ventilator strategy has the strongest mortality benefit in ARDS?
options: A. High tidal volume ventilation (12 mL/kg IBW) to correct hypercapnia
B. Low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg IBW) with plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O
C. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) as first-line
D. Volume-controlled ventilation targeting normocapnia (PaCO2 35–45 mmHg)
questions.explanation: The ARDSNet ARMA trial demonstrated that low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg ideal body weight) with plateau pressure ≤30 cmH2O significantly reduces mortality in ARDS compared to traditional higher tidal volumes (12 mL/kg). This lung-protective strategy limits ventilator-induced lung injury by preventing alveolar overdistension and cyclic atelectrauma. Permissive hypercapnia is acceptable. HFOV did not improve outcomes in the OSCILLATE trial and may cause harm. This patient has severe ARDS (P/F <100) and also qualifies for prone positioning.

questions.question: A patient with severe ARDS (P/F ratio 75) on lung-protective ventilation has refractory hypoxemia. Prone positioning is initiated. What is the recommended minimum duration of prone positioning per session based on the PROSEVA trial?
options: D. Continuous prone positioning without breaks
questions.explanation: The PROSEVA trial demonstrated that prone positioning for ≥16 hours per day significantly reduces 28-day and 90-day mortality in severe ARDS (P/F <150) when combined with lung-protective ventilation. Prone positioning improves V/Q matching by recruiting dependent lung zones, reduces dorsal atelectasis, and improves oxygenation. Most protocols recommend 16-hour prone sessions with brief supine repositioning for procedures and care. Prone positioning is indicated for severe ARDS (P/F <100–150) refractory to optimized ventilator settings.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a prior history of pulmonary tuberculosis presents with sudden onset massive hemoptysis (approximately 700 mL over 6 hours). Flexible bronchoscopy cannot localize or control the bleeding. What is the most appropriate next management step?
options: A. Systemic anticoagulation with heparin infusion
B. Bronchial artery embolization (BAE) by interventional radiology
D. Observation with supplemental oxygen and serial chest X-rays
questions.explanation: Massive hemoptysis (classically >600 mL/24 hours or any life-threatening bleed) requires urgent intervention. In post-tuberculous patients, bleeding often arises from hypertrophied bronchial arteries or Rasmussen aneurysms. Bronchial artery embolization (BAE) by interventional radiology is the preferred treatment when bronchoscopy cannot control bleeding, achieving immediate hemostasis in >80% of cases. Anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated in hemoptysis. If BAE fails or is unavailable, surgical resection may be required. Rigid bronchoscopy is preferred over flexible bronchoscopy for active airway management in massive hemoptysis.

questions.question: Compare and contrast asbestosis and silicosis: describe the radiographic patterns, associated malignancies, and key clinical distinctions between these two occupational pneumoconioses.
questions.answer: Asbestosis causes lower lobe-predominant pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)-like pattern on HRCT, bilateral calcified pleural plaques (pathognomonic of asbestos exposure), and pleural thickening; eggshell hilar calcifications are absent. Silicosis causes upper lobe-predominant nodular fibrosis, with progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) in severe cases, and eggshell calcification of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, which is pathognomonic. In terms of malignancy, asbestos is the leading cause of malignant mesothelioma (pleural or peritoneal) and also synergistically increases lung cancer risk with smoking; notably, mesothelioma risk is not substantially reduced by smoking cessation. Silicosis is not associated with mesothelioma but dramatically increases the risk of tuberculosis reactivation (silicotuberculosis, up to 30-fold), and can be complicated by Caplan syndrome (large necrobiotic nodules in the setting of rheumatoid arthritis). Neither condition responds well to corticosteroids, and both are managed supportively with removal from exposure, pulmonary rehabilitation, and surveillance for complications.
questions.explanation: Asbestosis causes lower lobe-predominant pulmonary fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP)-like pattern on HRCT, bilateral calcified pleural plaques (pathognomonic of asbestos exposure), and pleural thickening; eggshell hilar calcifications are absent.  Silicosis causes upper lobe-predominant nodular fibrosis, with progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) in severe cases, and eggshell calcification of hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, which is pathognomonic.  In terms of malignancy, asbestos is the leading cause of malignant mesothelioma (pleural or peritoneal) and also synergistically increases lung cancer risk with smoking; notably, mesothelioma risk is not substantially reduced by smoking cessation.

questions.question: A 48-year-old sandblaster presents with progressive dyspnea and bilateral upper lobe nodules with eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes on CT scan. He has a tuberculin skin test of 18 mm. What is the most important reason to treat latent TB in this patient?
options: A. Silicosis causes direct immunosuppression increasing TB reactivation risk up to 30-fold
B. Anti-TB medications also slow the progression of silicosis fibrosis
C. Eggshell calcifications indicate active TB requiring immediate treatment
D. Caplan syndrome in silicosis increases susceptibility to atypical mycobacteria only
questions.explanation: Silicosis dramatically increases the risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis), with up to a 30-fold increased risk of TB reactivation compared to the general population, because silica particles impair macrophage function and mycobacterial killing. All patients with silicosis should be tested for latent TB and treated if positive. Eggshell calcifications of hilar nodes are characteristic of silicosis itself and do not indicate active TB. Anti-TB medications have no effect on silicosis progression. Caplan syndrome (large rheumatoid nodules in pneumoconiosis) occurs with silicosis or coal worker's pneumoconiosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old aerospace engineer who worked with beryllium develops progressive dyspnea and bilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy with non-caseating granulomas on lung biopsy. The beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT) is positive. How does management of berylliosis differ from sarcoidosis?
options: A. Berylliosis requires antifungal therapy; sarcoidosis does not
B. Berylliosis requires removal from beryllium exposure as a critical management step; sarcoidosis has no such occupational trigger
C. Berylliosis never requires corticosteroids; sarcoidosis always does
D. Berylliosis spontaneously resolves within 2 years without treatment in most cases
questions.explanation: Berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease) causes non-caseating granulomatous lung disease histologically identical to sarcoidosis, but is caused by sensitization to beryllium particles. The critical distinguishing management step is removal from ongoing beryllium exposure, which is not applicable to sarcoidosis. Diagnosis relies on the positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT), which can be performed on peripheral blood or bronchoalveolar lavage cells. Both conditions may require corticosteroids for symptomatic disease or declining lung function.

questions.question: A 42-year-old non-smoking man of Northern European descent is diagnosed with emphysema predominantly affecting the lower lung lobes. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated. Which genotype confers the highest risk for this condition?
options: A. PiMM genotype with normal AAT levels
B. PiZZ genotype with severely reduced AAT levels
questions.explanation: Alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) should be suspected in patients with early-onset emphysema, lower lobe predominance, and minimal smoking history. The PiZZ genotype results in the lowest AAT serum levels (<15% of normal) and the greatest risk for panacinar emphysema and liver disease (cirrhosis from misfolded Z-protein accumulation in hepatocytes). The PiMM genotype is normal. PiMZ heterozygotes have intermediate levels and intermediate risk. IV augmentation therapy with pooled human AAT is available for PiZZ patients with FEV1 25–65% predicted.

questions.question: Describe the Berlin definition of ARDS, including the three severity categories and the key diagnostic criteria.
questions.answer: The Berlin definition (2012) defines ARDS as acute onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms, bilateral opacities on chest imaging not fully explained by effusions, lobar collapse, or nodules, and respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload. Three severity categories are based on the PaO2/FiO2 (P/F) ratio with a minimum PEEP of 5 cmH2O: mild (P/F 201–300 mmHg), moderate (P/F 101–200 mmHg), and severe (P/F ≤100 mmHg). The Berlin definition removed the term 'acute lung injury' and eliminated the requirement for pulmonary artery catheter measurement of wedge pressure, replacing it with echocardiography or clinical judgment to exclude cardiogenic edema. Higher severity categories correlate with greater mortality, with severe ARDS carrying approximately 45% hospital mortality.

questions.question: Explain the WHO classification of pulmonary hypertension (Groups 1–5), providing one example condition for each group.
questions.answer: WHO Group 1 (pulmonary arterial hypertension, PAH) involves intrinsic pulmonary vascular remodeling with examples including idiopathic PAH, heritable PAH (BMPR2 mutations), and PAH associated with connective tissue disease, HIV, or portopulmonary hypertension. Group 2 (PH due to left heart disease) includes heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction and valvular disease causing elevated left-sided filling pressures. Group 3 (PH due to lung disease and/or hypoxia) includes COPD and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, where hypoxic vasoconstriction and vascular remodeling drive elevated pressures. Group 4 (chronic thromboembolic PH, CTEPH) results from unresolved pulmonary emboli causing mechanical obstruction and is potentially curable with pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE). Group 5 (PH with unclear or multifactorial mechanisms) includes conditions such as sarcoidosis, sickle cell disease, and myeloproliferative disorders where the pathophysiology is complex or poorly defined.

questions.question: A 63-year-old male smoker is found on low-dose CT chest to have a 6 mm solid solitary pulmonary nodule. Describe the Fleischner Society guidelines for management of this nodule and the factors that determine follow-up intensity.
questions.answer: The Fleischner Society 2017 guidelines for solid solitary pulmonary nodules in patients ≥35 years recommend risk-stratified follow-up based on nodule size, morphology, and patient risk factors (smoking history, family history of lung cancer, emphysema, upper lobe location, spiculated margins). For a 6 mm solid nodule in a high-risk patient such as this smoker, optional CT follow-up at 6–12 months is recommended. In a low-risk patient with a 6 mm nodule, no routine follow-up is generally needed per the 2017 update given the very low malignancy probability. Nodules 7–14 mm require CT follow-up at 3–6 months (high-risk) or 6–12 months (low-risk). Nodules >8 mm warrant consideration of PET scan, CT with contrast, or tissue sampling due to higher malignancy probability, with management guided by clinical risk, radiologic features, and patient preference.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology, clinical features, staging, and first-line treatment of small cell lung cancer (SCLC), including its key associated paraneoplastic syndromes.
questions.answer: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor arising from Kulchitsky cells, almost exclusively in heavy smokers, typically presenting as a central hilar mass with extensive mediastinal lymphadenopathy and early hematogenous spread to brain, bone, liver, and adrenal glands. It is staged as limited disease (confined to one hemithorax and regional nodes, treatable within a single radiation port) or extensive disease (beyond one hemithorax, including contralateral nodes or distant metastases). SCLC is highly chemosensitive initially; first-line treatment for extensive disease is etoposide plus carboplatin combined with atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1), based on the IMpower133 trial showing improved overall survival. Paraneoplastic syndromes are common and include SIADH (hyponatremia from ectopic ADH secretion), Cushing syndrome (ectopic ACTH causing hypokalemia and hyperglycemia), and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels causing proximal muscle weakness that paradoxically improves with repeated use, distinguishing it from myasthenia gravis).

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis develops chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa airway colonization. Describe the clinical implications of Pseudomonas colonization in bronchiectasis and the management strategies used to reduce bacterial burden.
questions.answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most clinically significant pathogen colonizing the airways of patients with bronchiectasis and cystic fibrosis, producing a mucoid biofilm that resists eradication and is associated with accelerated lung function decline, increased pulmonary exacerbation frequency, worse quality of life, and higher mortality. Eradication is attempted at the time of initial isolation with inhaled tobramycin or aztreonam combined with oral ciprofloxacin for 4–6 weeks. Once chronic colonization is established (defined as two or more positive cultures over 6 months), long-term suppressive therapy with alternating-month inhaled tobramycin, inhaled aztreonam, or inhaled colistin reduces exacerbations and bacterial density without eradicating the organism. Long-term oral azithromycin provides additional anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory benefits in non-NTM bronchiectasis, reducing exacerbation frequency by approximately 30%. Daily airway clearance techniques — including oscillatory positive expiratory pressure (PEP) devices, high-frequency chest wall oscillation (HFCWO), and autogenic drainage — are the cornerstone of management to mobilize secretions and reduce bacterial load.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology of alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, why emphysema affects the lower lobes preferentially, and the indications for augmentation therapy.
questions.answer: Alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) is a serine protease inhibitor produced primarily by hepatocytes that neutralizes neutrophil elastase in the lung; deficiency allows unopposed elastase-mediated destruction of alveolar walls, causing panacinar emphysema that is most severe at the lung bases. Lower lobe predominance occurs because gravitational blood flow directs more neutrophils to the dependent lung bases, exposing lower lobe alveoli to greater elastase activity in the setting of inadequate AAT protection. The PiZZ genotype leads to misfolded Z-protein that polymerizes and accumulates in hepatocytes, simultaneously causing liver disease (neonatal hepatitis, cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma) and reducing circulating AAT to <11 μmol/L. Augmentation therapy with weekly IV infusions of pooled human AAT is FDA-approved for patients with severe deficiency (serum AAT level <11 μmol/L), PiZZ or null/null genotype, and FEV1 25–80% predicted, with evidence from CT density studies showing slowing of lung density loss. Smoking cessation is the single most important intervention and dramatically reduces the accelerated rate of lung function decline regardless of augmentation therapy.

Lower lobe predominance occurs because gravitational blood flow directs more neutrophils to the dependent lung bases, exposing lower lobe alveoli to greater elastase activity in the setting of inadequate AAT protection. questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation. Her TSH is 12 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0) and free T4 is low. Which diagnosis best fits?
questions.explanation: Primary hypothyroidism is characterized by an elevated TSH with a low free T4, reflecting failure of the thyroid gland itself. Symptoms include fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, and constipation. Central hypothyroidism would show a low or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4. Sick euthyroid syndrome typically presents with low T3 in the context of systemic illness.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, and exophthalmos. Labs show suppressed TSH and elevated free T4. Which antibody is most likely elevated?
questions.explanation: Graves' disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in young women and is caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), which are IgG antibodies that bind and activate the TSH receptor. Exophthalmos (proptosis) is pathognomonic for Graves' disease. Anti-TPO antibodies are more characteristic of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. TSH receptor blocking antibodies cause hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism.

questions.question: A patient with known Graves' disease develops fever (40°C), heart rate 160 bpm, delirium, and vomiting after an elective surgery. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: B. Propylthiouracil, propranolol, hydrocortisone, and potassium iodide
questions.explanation: Thyroid storm is a life-threatening emergency requiring multimodal treatment. Propylthiouracil (PTU) blocks new thyroid hormone synthesis and peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion. Propranolol controls the adrenergic symptoms. Hydrocortisone blocks T4-to-T3 conversion and addresses relative adrenal insufficiency. Potassium iodide (Lugol's solution) is given at least 1 hour after PTU to block hormone release (the Wolff-Chaikoff effect). Radioactive iodine is contraindicated in acute thyroid storm.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman is found to have TSH of 8 mIU/L and positive anti-TPO antibodies. She is asymptomatic. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis) is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. It is characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, positive anti-TPO antibodies (present in >95% of cases), and elevated TSH. Graves' disease causes hyperthyroidism via TSI antibodies. De Quervain (subacute granulomatous) thyroiditis is painful and often follows a viral illness.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has an HbA1c of 9.2%. He is currently on metformin. Which medication class, added to metformin, has the strongest evidence for reducing major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)?
questions.explanation: GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., liraglutide, semaglutide) have demonstrated significant reductions in MACE in patients with established cardiovascular disease in landmark trials (LEADER, SUSTAIN-6). SGLT-2 inhibitors also have strong cardiovascular evidence, particularly for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascularly neutral. Sulfonylureas have not shown cardiovascular benefit and carry a risk of hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A 22-year-old with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs: glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, anion gap 28, serum ketones positive. Potassium is 5.4 mEq/L. After starting insulin infusion, what is the expected change in potassium?
options: A. Potassium will rise further due to acidosis correction
C. Potassium will fall as insulin drives it intracellularly
D. Potassium will normalize without intervention
questions.explanation: In DKA, total body potassium is depleted despite a normal or elevated serum potassium at presentation—due to the transcellular shift caused by acidosis and insulin deficiency. When insulin infusion is started, potassium is driven intracellularly, and serum potassium can drop precipitously, causing life-threatening hypokalemia. Potassium replacement must be initiated before insulin if serum K+ is below 3.5 mEq/L, and continued once <5.0 mEq/L. Close monitoring is essential.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with extreme hyperglycemia (glucose 1,100 mg/dL), altered mental status, and severe dehydration but no significant ketonemia. Serum osmolality is 380 mOsm/kg. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) classically occurs in elderly type 2 diabetics and is characterized by extreme hyperglycemia (often >600 mg/dL), hyperosmolality (>320 mOsm/kg), severe dehydration, and altered mental status without significant ketonemia or acidosis. The absence of ketones is because residual insulin is sufficient to suppress lipolysis but inadequate to control glucose. Mortality is higher than DKA. Treatment centers on aggressive fluid resuscitation and gradual glucose lowering.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio is markedly elevated. CT of the adrenals shows a 1.8 cm left adrenal adenoma. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) due to a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma is best treated with laparoscopic adrenalectomy of the affected side, which can be curative. Adrenal vein sampling is recommended prior to surgery to confirm unilateral secretion. Spironolactone or eplerenone (mineralocorticoid antagonists) are appropriate for bilateral adrenal hyperplasia (the more common cause) or patients who are not surgical candidates. Bilateral adrenalectomy would cause Addison's disease and is not indicated.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman is found to have an ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome. Overnight dexamethasone suppression test fails to suppress cortisol. 24-hour urine free cortisol is elevated. High-dose dexamethasone suppression test does NOT suppress cortisol. MRI of the pituitary is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome with non-suppression on high-dose dexamethasone and a normal pituitary MRI points to a primary adrenal etiology (adenoma or carcinoma). In Cushing's disease (pituitary adenoma), ACTH is elevated and high-dose dexamethasone typically suppresses cortisol by >50% because the pituitary adenoma retains some sensitivity to glucocorticoid feedback. Ectopic ACTH is also ACTH-dependent (elevated ACTH). Adrenal adenomas are ACTH-independent (low ACTH) and autonomously produce cortisol.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with episodic headache, diaphoresis, palpitations, and hypertension. 24-hour urine metanephrines and catecholamines are markedly elevated. CT abdomen shows a 4 cm adrenal mass. What must be done BEFORE surgical resection?
options: C. Start alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin for 10–14 days
D. Initiate medical therapy with metoprolol and amlodipine
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma requires adequate alpha-adrenergic blockade before surgery to prevent hypertensive crisis during tumor manipulation. Phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha-blocker) or selective alpha-1 blockers (doxazosin, prazosin) are started 10–14 days preoperatively. Beta-blockade must NEVER be initiated before alpha-blockade, as this would leave alpha receptors unopposed and precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis. Once adequate alpha-blockade is established, a beta-blocker may be added to control reflex tachycardia.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue, nausea, weight loss, hyperpigmentation of skin creases and buccal mucosa, and a sodium of 128 mEq/L. Cortisol stimulation test (cosyntropin stimulation) shows a blunted response. What additional finding would confirm PRIMARY adrenal insufficiency over central (secondary)?
questions.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) is characterized by destruction of the adrenal cortex, resulting in deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. The low cortisol leads to loss of negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, causing markedly elevated ACTH—which is responsible for the characteristic hyperpigmentation (ACTH stimulates melanocortin receptors). In secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency, ACTH is low or inappropriately normal, and mineralocorticoid function is typically preserved (no hyponatremia from aldosterone deficiency).

questions.question: A 55-year-old man is found to have calcium of 11.8 mg/dL on routine labs. PTH is 95 pg/mL (elevated). He is asymptomatic. 24-hour urine calcium is 350 mg/day. DXA shows osteoporosis at the lumbar spine. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: This patient has primary hyperparathyroidism meeting surgical criteria per current guidelines: osteoporosis (T-score below -2.5) is one of the indications for parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism. Other indications include age <50, serum calcium >1 mg/dL above upper limit of normal, creatinine clearance <60 mL/min, or 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/day. Cinacalcet lowers calcium but does not improve bone density and is reserved for patients who refuse or cannot undergo surgery.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man is found to have calcium 12.5 mg/dL, PTH <5 pg/mL (suppressed), and PTHrP elevated. He has a recently diagnosed lung mass. What is the most likely cause of hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients and is caused by tumor secretion of PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein). PTHrP activates PTH receptors, causing hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is a classic cause. Primary hyperparathyroidism would show elevated PTH. Multiple myeloma causes hypercalcemia via osteoclast-activating factors (elevated PTHrP is less typical).

questions.question: A 62-year-old woman is diagnosed with osteoporosis (T-score -2.8 at hip). She has no contraindications. What is the first-line pharmacologic treatment?
questions.explanation: Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate, zoledronic acid) are first-line therapy for osteoporosis based on extensive evidence for reducing both vertebral and non-vertebral fractures. They are antiresorptive agents that inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption. Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis or treatment failure. Denosumab is also effective but requires continued dosing to avoid rebound bone loss. Raloxifene is used primarily when vertebral fracture prevention is the goal and has limited efficacy at the hip.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with LDL 185 mg/dL and a 10-year ASCVD risk of 18% refuses lifestyle changes. Which medication class should be started?
questions.explanation: According to ACC/AHA guidelines, patients with a 10-year ASCVD risk ≥7.5% and LDL ≥70 mg/dL are candidates for statin therapy. A 10-year risk of 18% places this patient in the intermediate-to-high risk category, warranting high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg) targeting ≥50% LDL reduction. Ezetimibe is added to statin therapy if LDL remains above goal. Fibrates primarily reduce triglycerides. Niacin is no longer recommended for routine LDL reduction.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and parathyroid adenoma. Genetic testing reveals a RET proto-oncogene mutation. Which syndrome does this represent?
questions.explanation: MEN2A (Sipple syndrome) is caused by activating mutations in the RET proto-oncogene and is characterized by medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC, virtually 100% penetrance), pheochromocytoma (~50%), and primary hyperparathyroidism (~20-30%). MEN1 involves the MEN1 gene and causes pituitary adenoma, parathyroid hyperplasia, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (the '3 Ps'). MEN2B includes MTC and pheochromocytoma but instead of parathyroid disease, features mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus. Prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended for RET mutation carriers.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea, galactorrhea, and a serum prolactin of 220 ng/mL. MRI shows an 8 mm pituitary adenoma. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Prolactinomas are the most common functioning pituitary adenomas. Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine due to better tolerability and efficacy) are the first-line treatment for both micro (<10 mm) and macroprolactinomas. They normalize prolactin in ~80-90% of cases and reduce tumor size. Surgery is reserved for patients intolerant of or resistant to dopamine agonists, or those with visual compromise from a macroadenoma. Cabergoline achieves prolactin normalization and tumor shrinkage in the majority of patients.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with acromegaly has a serum IGF-1 three times the upper limit of normal and an MRI showing a 2.2 cm pituitary macroadenoma with no visual field defects. What is the preferred initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Transsphenoidal surgery is the first-line treatment for acromegaly caused by a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, with cure rates of ~80-90% for microadenomas and ~50% for macroadenomas. It offers the best chance of biochemical cure and immediate decompression. Medical therapy with somatostatin analogs (octreotide, lanreotide) is used as adjuvant treatment when surgery fails to achieve biochemical control, or as primary therapy in patients who refuse or are unfit for surgery. Pegvisomant (GH receptor antagonist) normalizes IGF-1 but does not shrink the tumor.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and CKD stage 3b (eGFR 32 mL/min) requires additional glucose lowering. Which agent should be AVOIDED due to risk of lactic acidosis?
questions.explanation: Metformin is contraindicated when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m² due to the risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis. It should be used with caution (and dose reduced) when eGFR is 30–45 mL/min. Sitagliptin can be used in CKD but requires dose adjustment. Insulin is safe in CKD but doses may need reduction. Empagliflozin has reduced efficacy below eGFR 45 mL/min and is generally not recommended for glycemic control below this threshold, though it may be continued for heart failure/CKD benefits.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with a BMI of 42 kg/m² and type 2 diabetes controlled on oral agents presents for bariatric surgery evaluation. Which surgical procedure has the strongest evidence for long-term diabetes remission?
questions.explanation: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) achieves the highest rates of type 2 diabetes remission (60–80%), often occurring before significant weight loss, suggesting hormonal mechanisms (increased GLP-1, decreased ghrelin) beyond caloric restriction. Sleeve gastrectomy achieves ~50–60% diabetes remission. Gastric banding has the lowest remission rates and highest long-term failure rates. Bariatric surgery is recommended for patients with BMI ≥40 or ≥35 with obesity-related comorbidities like type 2 diabetes.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology, classic presentation, and initial management of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
questions.answer: DKA results from absolute or relative insulin deficiency combined with excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, cortisol, epinephrine), leading to hyperglycemia, lipolysis, and hepatic ketone body production. Classic presentation includes polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations (deep rapid breathing to compensate for metabolic acidosis), and fruity breath from acetone. Laboratory findings show hyperglycemia (typically 250–600 mg/dL), anion gap metabolic acidosis (pH <7.3, bicarbonate <18 mEq/L), and ketonemia/ketonuria. Initial management includes IV fluid resuscitation with isotonic saline, insulin infusion (regular insulin 0.1 units/kg/hr after potassium >3.5 mEq/L), potassium replacement, and close monitoring of glucose, electrolytes, and acid-base status every 2–4 hours.
questions.explanation: DKA is a life-threatening emergency most common in type 1 diabetes but can occur in type 2. Precipitants include infection, missed insulin doses, myocardial infarction, and new-onset diabetes. Resolution criteria include pH >7.3, bicarbonate >18 mEq/L, and anion gap closure—not glucose normalization. Overlap with normal glucose DKA ('euglycemic DKA') can occur with SGLT-2 inhibitor use. Cerebral edema is a feared complication particularly in pediatric patients.

questions.question: A patient on long-term glucocorticoid therapy undergoes emergency abdominal surgery. Explain why stress-dose steroids are required and outline the appropriate protocol.
questions.answer: Chronic glucocorticoid use suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis through negative feedback, leading to adrenal atrophy and an inability to mount an appropriate cortisol stress response during surgery. Normally, cortisol secretion increases 3–5 fold under surgical stress; patients with HPA suppression cannot do this and risk adrenal crisis (hypotension, shock, hyponatremia). Stress-dose steroid protocol: for major surgery, administer hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before induction, then 50 mg IV every 8 hours for 24–48 hours, tapering back to maintenance dose once the patient is eating and stable. Minor procedures may require only 25–50 mg hydrocortisone once. Any patient who has received >20 mg/day prednisone equivalent for >3 weeks within the prior year should receive perioperative stress coverage.
questions.explanation: HPA axis recovery after glucocorticoid withdrawal can take up to 12 months. Testing with a cosyntropin stimulation test can assess HPA axis recovery in elective situations. Mineralocorticoid replacement is not needed for stress dosing because high doses of hydrocortisone provide sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. Failure to provide stress doses can result in perioperative Addisonian crisis with cardiovascular collapse.

questions.question: Explain the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.answer: The initial finding is hypercalcemia on routine labs, confirmed by repeat measurement of total calcium or ionized calcium. Simultaneous measurement of intact PTH is the key diagnostic step: an elevated or inappropriately normal PTH in the setting of hypercalcemia confirms primary hyperparathyroidism (HPT). Additional labs include phosphate (typically low in primary HPT), 24-hour urine calcium (elevated in primary HPT; low in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia), 25-hydroxyvitamin D (to exclude concurrent deficiency that could mask HPT severity), and serum creatinine. Imaging with 99mTc-sestamibi parathyroid scintigraphy and/or neck ultrasound is performed when surgery is planned to localize the adenoma.
questions.explanation: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) is a benign condition that mimics primary HPT (elevated calcium, normal/high PTH) but is distinguished by a very low urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio (<0.01). Genetic testing for CASR mutation confirms FHH. DXA scan is important to identify osteoporosis as a complication and surgical indication. 4D-CT or MRI may be used for preoperative localization if initial studies are non-localizing.

questions.question: Describe the features, pathophysiology, and management of Cushing's syndrome.
questions.answer: Cushing's syndrome results from chronic excess glucocorticoid exposure, either exogenous (iatrogenic, most common) or endogenous. Endogenous causes are ACTH-dependent (Cushing's disease from pituitary adenoma ~70%; ectopic ACTH ~15%) or ACTH-independent (adrenal adenoma/carcinoma). Clinical features include central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, hypertension, glucose intolerance, osteoporosis, and easy bruising. Diagnostic workup begins with 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test (cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL is abnormal). Once hypercortisolism is confirmed, ACTH level differentiates ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent disease. MRI pituitary and inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) help localize pituitary vs. ectopic source. Treatment is surgical resection of the causative lesion.
questions.explanation: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (IPSS) with CRH stimulation is the gold standard for distinguishing Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH, with a central-to-peripheral ACTH gradient >3 after CRH indicating pituitary source. Medical therapy (ketoconazole, metyrapone, mifepristone) may be used while awaiting surgery or when surgery fails. Adrenal carcinoma requires mitotane. Nelson's syndrome (post-bilateral adrenalectomy pituitary tumor enlargement due to loss of negative feedback) is a complication of bilateral adrenalectomy.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with no prior cardiovascular disease has LDL 155 mg/dL, HDL 38 mg/dL, and triglycerides 850 mg/dL. He reports recurrent episodes of epigastric pain. What is the most immediate concern?
questions.explanation: Triglycerides above 500 mg/dL, and especially above 1,000 mg/dL, carry a significant risk of acute pancreatitis. The epigastric pain in this patient is a warning sign. Fibrates (fenofibrate, gemfibrozil) are first-line for severe hypertriglyceridemia and can reduce triglycerides by 40–60%. Omega-3 fatty acids are also effective. Statins reduce triglycerides modestly. Dietary fat restriction is also essential. Acute pancreatitis from hypertriglyceridemia can be severe and requires hospitalization and NPO status.

questions.question: A 66-year-old woman on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism has her dose adjusted. Which TSH level represents the ideal treatment target for most adult patients?
questions.explanation: The therapeutic target for levothyroxine replacement in primary hypothyroidism is a TSH within the normal reference range of approximately 0.5–3.0 mIU/L. Supratherapeutic doses causing TSH suppression below 0.1 mIU/L are associated with atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, and increased cardiovascular risk. Higher TSH targets (1–5 mIU/L) may be preferred in elderly patients. Patients with thyroid cancer requiring TSH suppression therapy have intentionally lower targets.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is seeking additional glycemic control. Which medication class offers proven benefit for heart failure outcomes in addition to glucose lowering?
questions.explanation: SGLT-2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) have demonstrated significant reductions in heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular mortality in patients with HFrEF, independent of diabetes status. The mechanism involves osmotic diuresis, reduced preload and afterload, improved myocardial energy metabolism, and possible direct cardiac effects. DPP-4 inhibitors are cardiovascularly neutral but saxagliptin was associated with increased heart failure hospitalizations in the SAVOR-TIMI 53 trial. Sulfonylureas and meglitinides have no heart failure benefit.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes asks about the mechanism and clinical use of GLP-1 receptor agonists. Explain.
questions.answer: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) is an incretin hormone secreted by intestinal L-cells in response to nutrient ingestion. GLP-1 receptor agonists mimic its actions: they stimulate glucose-dependent insulin secretion (reducing hypoglycemia risk), suppress glucagon secretion, slow gastric emptying (reducing postprandial glucose excursions), and reduce appetite via central mechanisms—leading to significant weight loss (3–15% body weight depending on agent). They are administered subcutaneously (semaglutide also available orally). Major clinical benefits include HbA1c reduction of 1–2%, weight loss of 3–10 kg, and, for certain agents (liraglutide, semaglutide, dulaglutide), significant reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with established CVD or high risk.
questions.explanation: The main side effects are gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), especially on initiation, which can be minimized by dose titration. There is a theoretical concern about pancreatitis (rare), and GLP-1 RAs should be avoided in personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 (based on rodent data). Semaglutide 2.4 mg/week is FDA-approved for obesity management (brand name Wegovy) even without diabetes.

questions.question: Describe the classic presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency).
questions.answer: Addison's disease is caused by destruction of the adrenal cortex, most commonly by autoimmune adrenalitis in developed countries (or tuberculosis globally), resulting in deficiency of both cortisol and aldosterone. Classic presentation includes fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, orthostatic hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation of skin creases, scars, and buccal mucosa (due to elevated ACTH stimulating melanocortin receptors). Diagnosis is confirmed by a cosyntropin stimulation test showing a peak cortisol <18–20 mcg/dL, combined with an elevated plasma ACTH level distinguishing it from secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency. Treatment requires lifelong glucocorticoid replacement (hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in divided doses) and mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone 0.05–0.1 mg/day).
questions.explanation: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency presenting with hypotension, hypoglycemia, and circulatory collapse, triggered by illness, surgery, or missed doses. Treatment requires immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours and aggressive IV fluid resuscitation. Patients should be educated to double or triple their steroid dose during illness ('sick day rules') and carry an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit. Medic alert bracelet is essential.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is pregnant (8 weeks gestation). What insulin regimen is safest during pregnancy?
options: A. Oral hypoglycemic agents (metformin and glipizide)
B. Basal-bolus insulin regimen with insulin analogs
questions.explanation: In type 1 diabetes during pregnancy, a basal-bolus insulin regimen using rapid-acting (aspart or lispro—FDA category B) and long-acting (detemir is preferred; glargine is used off-label) analogs is recommended. This provides the best glycemic control with the flexibility to adjust doses as insulin requirements change dramatically throughout pregnancy. Oral agents (sulfonylureas, metformin) are not recommended as first-line in type 1 DM and have varying safety data in pregnancy. Target HbA1c in pregnancy is 6–6.5% (without undue hypoglycemia).

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with MEN1 syndrome is found to have a 2 cm pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with markedly elevated fasting gastrin (800 pg/mL). He has recurrent peptic ulcers refractory to PPI therapy. What is the diagnosis and treatment?
options: B. Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome); treat with high-dose PPI and consider surgery
D. VIPoma; treat with fluid replacement
questions.explanation: Gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) is characterized by markedly elevated fasting gastrin (>1,000 pg/mL is diagnostic; >200 pg/mL with appropriate clinical context suggests it) and recurrent peptic ulcers from hypergastrinemia stimulating excessive gastric acid secretion. It is the second most common functional pNET in MEN1 after insulinoma. Initial treatment is high-dose PPI. In sporadic cases, surgery is curative; in MEN1, surgery is more controversial due to multiplicity of tumors. Secretin stimulation test (paradoxical rise in gastrin ≥200 pg/mL) confirms the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with fasting hypoglycemia, symptoms relieved by eating, and a serum insulin level inappropriately elevated with a low C-peptide. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Exogenous insulin administration causes hypoglycemia with elevated insulin but LOW C-peptide, because exogenous insulin does not contain C-peptide (which is co-secreted with endogenous insulin from proinsulin). An insulinoma would show elevated insulin AND elevated C-peptide. Sulfonylurea abuse would show elevated insulin and C-peptide plus a positive urine sulfonylurea screen. Non-islet cell tumor hypoglycemia is caused by IGF-2 secretion and shows suppressed insulin. This pattern (high insulin, low C-peptide) is diagnostic of surreptitious insulin injection.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks. Her fasting glucose is 98 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial is 145 mg/dL on dietary modifications alone. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: A. Continue dietary modifications and reassess at delivery
questions.explanation: Gestational diabetes management targets fasting glucose <95 mg/dL and 1-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL (or 2-hour <120 mg/dL). Despite being at the upper limit of targets, insulin is the preferred pharmacologic agent for gestational diabetes when lifestyle measures fail, as it does not cross the placenta. Metformin and glyburide are used in some settings but are not FDA-approved for GDM and cross the placenta. Given postprandial values approaching target, close monitoring is appropriate, and insulin is started if targets are consistently exceeded.

questions.question: Describe the differential diagnosis and workup of hypercalcemia.
questions.answer: Hypercalcemia is most commonly caused by primary hyperparathyroidism (in outpatients) and malignancy (in hospitalized patients). The initial step is to check intact PTH: elevated or inappropriately normal PTH points to primary hyperparathyroidism or rarely familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH), while suppressed PTH suggests PTH-independent causes. PTHrP is elevated in humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (squamous, renal, bladder cancers). Elevated 1,25-(OH)2 vitamin D (calcitriol) is seen in granulomatous diseases (sarcoidosis, TB) and lymphoma, as macrophages produce 1-alpha hydroxylase. 25-OH vitamin D toxicity shows elevated 25-OH D. Multiple myeloma causes hypercalcemia via osteoclast-activating factors with a low/normal PTHrP. Milk-alkali syndrome and thiazide diuretics are other causes. Urine calcium-to-creatinine clearance ratio <0.01 distinguishes FHH from primary HPT.
questions.explanation: Treatment of acute severe hypercalcemia (Ca >14 mg/dL or symptomatic): IV normal saline (2–4 L) to restore volume and increase urinary calcium excretion, followed by calcitonin (4 IU/kg IM/SQ every 12 hours for rapid but temporary effect), and bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid for malignancy-related hypercalcemia). Denosumab is used for bisphosphonate-refractory hypercalcemia of malignancy. Glucocorticoids work for granulomatous disease and lymphoma by inhibiting 1-alpha hydroxylase.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is incidentally found to have a 2 cm adrenal mass on CT done for abdominal pain. Describe the evaluation of an adrenal incidentaloma.
questions.answer: Adrenal incidentalomas require evaluation for both hormonal excess and malignancy. Hormonal workup includes: (1) 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test to screen for subclinical Cushing's syndrome; (2) plasma metanephrines or 24-hour urine catecholamines/metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma (must be excluded before any biopsy); (3) plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio if the patient is hypertensive or hypokalemic (to screen for primary hyperaldosteronism). Radiologic characteristics guide malignancy risk: CT attenuation <10 Hounsfield units (HU) is characteristic of a benign lipid-rich adenoma; >10 HU warrants further evaluation with washout protocol CT or MRI. Size >4 cm raises concern for adrenocortical carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Adrenal biopsy is rarely indicated and should only be performed after pheochromocytoma is excluded. If imaging characteristics suggest adenoma and hormonal workup is negative, follow-up CT at 6–12 months is recommended. Masses >4 cm or with malignant imaging features (irregular borders, heterogeneous) should be considered for surgical resection. Adrenocortical carcinoma is rare but aggressive, with 5-year survival ~40% for localized disease. Subclinical Cushing's is the most common hormonal finding in incidentalomas (~5–20%).

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and urine specific gravity of 1.002. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L and serum osmolality is 305 mOsm/kg with urine osmolality of 85 mOsm/kg. After water deprivation test, urine osmolality increases to 600 mOsm/kg following desmopressin (DDAVP) administration. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Central diabetes insipidus (CDI) results from ADH deficiency due to hypothalamic or posterior pituitary pathology. The water deprivation test reveals the inability to concentrate urine, and the robust response to exogenous DDAVP (urine osmolality >50% increase) confirms that the kidneys are intact but lack ADH stimulation. Nephrogenic DI shows a poor response to DDAVP (<50% increase). Primary polydipsia typically shows partial concentration on water deprivation without requiring DDAVP. CDI is treated with intranasal or oral DDAVP.

questions.question: Explain the diagnostic approach to SIADH and list four common causes.
questions.answer: SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion) is diagnosed by demonstrating hyponatremia (Na <135 mEq/L) with inappropriately concentrated urine in a euvolemic patient. Diagnostic criteria include: serum osmolality <275 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg (inappropriately elevated), urine sodium >40 mEq/L (reflecting normal renal sodium handling), and absence of hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, and diuretic use. Common causes include: (1) CNS disorders (stroke, meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage, head trauma); (2) pulmonary diseases (pneumonia, tuberculosis, mechanical ventilation); (3) malignancies—especially small cell lung cancer (secretes ectopic ADH); (4) medications (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, NSAIDs, oxytocin). Treatment depends on severity: fluid restriction for mild/chronic cases, hypertonic saline (3% NaCl) for severe symptomatic hyponatremia, and vaptan (tolvaptan, conivaptan) for refractory cases.
questions.explanation: The rate of sodium correction is critical: correction faster than 8–10 mEq/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), causing irreversible neurologic damage. In severely symptomatic patients (seizures, coma), 1–2 mEq/L/hour correction is acceptable until symptoms resolve, then slowed. Chronic SIADH management with demeclocycline or vaptans is used when fluid restriction fails.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with Hashimoto's thyroiditis on stable levothyroxine develops worsening fatigue and myxedema symptoms. Her TSH has risen from 2.5 to 9.8 mIU/L over 6 months. She recently started a new medication. Which drug interaction most likely increased her levothyroxine requirements?
options: B. Calcium carbonate taken with levothyroxine
questions.explanation: Calcium carbonate, iron supplements, aluminum-containing antacids, and proton pump inhibitors can significantly impair levothyroxine absorption when taken simultaneously. Patients should be instructed to take levothyroxine on an empty stomach 30–60 minutes before meals and separate it from calcium or iron by at least 4 hours. Other drugs that increase levothyroxine requirements include cholestyramine, rifampin (increased metabolism), phenytoin, and estrogen (increased thyroid-binding globulin). Dose increases of 20–30% may be needed when interacting drugs cannot be avoided.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man undergoes workup for osteoporosis. Labs show: calcium 8.4 mg/dL (normal), phosphate 1.8 mg/dL (low), PTH 95 pg/mL (elevated), 25-OH vitamin D 12 ng/mL (low), and alkaline phosphatase markedly elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: B. Osteomalacia secondary to vitamin D deficiency
questions.explanation: This picture—normal calcium, low phosphate, elevated PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism from low vitamin D → low calcium stimulating PTH), severely low 25-OH vitamin D, and high alkaline phosphatase (reflecting increased osteoblast activity and bone turnover)—is classic for osteomalacia. The PTH elevation is secondary, not primary (primary HPT causes hypercalcemia). Alkaline phosphatase is elevated due to defective bone mineralization with increased osteoblast activity. Treatment is vitamin D and calcium supplementation. Paget's disease would show normal calcium and PTH with markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase in a focal distribution.

questions.question: Describe the management of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS).
questions.answer: HHS management centers on aggressive fluid resuscitation, gradual glucose lowering, and electrolyte repletion. Begin with 1–2 L of 0.9% normal saline over the first 1–2 hours to restore hemodynamic stability. Switch to 0.45% saline once blood pressure normalizes, as patients have significant free water deficit. The target is to correct approximately half the free water deficit over the first 12–24 hours. Insulin infusion is started at a low dose (0.05 units/kg/hr) only after adequate fluid resuscitation; early insulin without fluids can cause further osmolality shifts. When glucose reaches 250–300 mg/dL, add dextrose to IV fluids and reduce insulin rate. Potassium replacement is required as with DKA. The goal is to reduce osmolality by no more than 3–8 mOsm/kg/hour to avoid cerebral edema.
questions.explanation: HHS carries a higher mortality than DKA (up to 15–20% vs. 1–5%), largely because it occurs in elderly patients with multiple comorbidities and is often triggered by serious illness (infection, MI, stroke). Unlike DKA, acidosis is minimal or absent. Thromboembolic prophylaxis with heparin is considered due to the hyperviscous state. Neurologic status may be severely impaired at osmolalities >320 mOsm/kg. Identifying and treating the precipitating cause is essential.

questions.question: Which finding on thyroid ultrasound is MOST concerning for malignancy in a thyroid nodule?
questions.explanation: Microcalcifications (punctate echogenic foci) and irregular or infiltrative margins are the ultrasound features most strongly associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma, the most common thyroid malignancy. Other suspicious features include marked hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape, and extrathyroidal extension. Cystic nodules are predominantly benign. Peripheral 'eggshell' calcifications can occur in benign nodules but dense rim calcifications may be associated with malignancy in some cases. A halo sign generally suggests a benign adenoma.
