questions.question: A 50-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has persistent microalbuminuria (albumin-to-creatinine ratio 85 mg/g) on two occasions, eGFR 68 mL/min, and blood pressure 138/88 mmHg. He is on metformin only. What additional treatment should be prioritized?
options: A. Start an ACE inhibitor or ARB
B. Start a calcium channel blocker for blood pressure
C. Refer for immediate nephrology consultation
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors (e.g., lisinopril) or ARBs (e.g., losartan) are the cornerstone of nephroprotection in diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria, regardless of blood pressure. They reduce intraglomerular pressure by dilating the efferent arteriole, slowing progression of diabetic nephropathy and reducing proteinuria. Blood pressure target is <130/80 mmHg in diabetics with CKD. SGLT-2 inhibitors (finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist) also have evidence for slowing CKD progression in diabetes and are now recommended as add-on therapy.

questions.question: Describe MEN1 syndrome: genetic basis, clinical features, and management priorities.
questions.answer: MEN1 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1, Wermer syndrome) is caused by inactivating mutations in the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 11q13, encoding menin. It follows autosomal dominant inheritance. The classic triad involves: (1) parathyroid hyperplasia (>90% penetrance by age 50)—the most common and often first manifestation, causing primary hyperparathyroidism; (2) pancreatic/duodenal neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs)—gastrinomas most common (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), followed by insulinomas, non-functional tumors, glucagonomas, and VIPomas; (3) anterior pituitary adenomas (~30–40%)—prolactinomas most common, followed by GH- and ACTH-secreting tumors. Management: parathyroidectomy (3.5-gland or 4-gland with autotransplantation) for hyperparathyroidism; high-dose PPIs and surgery for gastrinomas; laparoscopic enucleation for insulinomas >2 cm; dopamine agonists for prolactinomas. Surveillance begins in mutation carriers at age 5–10 years with annual biochemical screening.
questions.explanation: Genetic testing of first-degree relatives is essential once a proband is identified. MEN1-related gastrinomas are usually multiple and duodenal, making curative surgery difficult. Pancreatic NETs >2 cm carry significant malignant potential and should be resected. Thymic NETs are a life-threatening but underappreciated manifestation of MEN1. Surveillance CT/MRI every 1–3 years is recommended for pancreatic lesions. The most common cause of death in MEN1 is complications from pNETs or thymic NETs.

questions.question: A 42-year-old woman presents with weight gain, dry skin, fatigue, and a hoarse voice. Her TSH is elevated and free T4 is low. She is started on levothyroxine. When should TSH be rechecked to assess adequacy of therapy?
options: B. 4–8 weeks after starting or adjusting dose
questions.explanation: TSH has a long half-life and reflects the average thyroid hormone concentration over the preceding 4–6 weeks. Therefore, TSH should be rechecked 4–8 weeks after initiating or adjusting levothyroxine therapy to assess whether the target TSH has been achieved. Checking too early (e.g., 1 week) will not reflect the steady-state effect and may lead to unnecessary dose adjustments. Once the dose is stable and the patient is euthyroid, TSH should be monitored annually.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man with Addison's disease presents with fever, hypotension (BP 80/50 mmHg), severe weakness, confusion, and vomiting. He ran out of his hydrocortisone 3 days ago. What is the immediate treatment?
options: A. Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg and IV fluids
B. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours, plus aggressive IV saline
C. IM dexamethasone 4 mg once and observation
D. Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally and IV fluids
questions.explanation: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus, followed by 50–100 mg every 6–8 hours (or continuous infusion), along with aggressive IV 0.9% saline (1–2 L in first hour) and dextrose if hypoglycemic. Hydrocortisone at these doses also provides adequate mineralocorticoid activity (fludrocortisone is not needed acutely). Do not delay treatment for diagnostic confirmation; draw cortisol and ACTH levels before giving steroids if possible but do not wait for results. Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate in a vomiting, hemodynamically unstable patient.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in the United States?
questions.explanation: Graves' disease accounts for approximately 60–80% of all cases of hyperthyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions like the United States. It is an autoimmune condition caused by TSH receptor-stimulating antibodies (TSI). It predominantly affects women aged 20–50 years. Toxic multinodular goiter is more common in older patients and in iodine-deficient regions. Subacute thyroiditis causes transient hyperthyroidism followed by hypothyroidism. Toxic (autonomous) adenoma is a single hyperfunctioning nodule.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman is found to have a serum calcium of 10.8 mg/dL and PTH of 88 pg/mL on two separate occasions. She is otherwise asymptomatic. Outline the criteria for surgical intervention in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.answer: Current guidelines (from the Fourth International Workshop on Asymptomatic PHPT, 2014) recommend parathyroidectomy in asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism when any of the following criteria are met: (1) serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal (>11.0 mg/dL using typical reference range); (2) skeletal involvement: DXA T-score ≤ -2.5 at any site, or vertebral fracture by imaging; (3) renal involvement: eGFR <60 mL/min, 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg/day with elevated stone risk, or nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis on imaging; (4) age <50 years (due to lifetime risk of complications). This patient's calcium is just at or below the surgical threshold, and age 35 (<50 years) itself is an indication for surgery.
questions.explanation: Patients who do not meet surgical criteria can be monitored with annual serum calcium and creatinine, and DXA every 1–2 years. Adequate hydration and avoidance of thiazide diuretics and prolonged immobilization are recommended. Cinacalcet can be used to reduce serum calcium in those who decline or cannot undergo surgery but does not improve bone density. Vitamin D deficiency should be corrected cautiously (avoiding exacerbation of hypercalcemia).

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with a history of hypertension and obesity (BMI 36) presents with fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL on two occasions. Describe the approach to newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes mellitus including initial workup, targets, and first-line treatment.
questions.answer: At diagnosis of type 2 diabetes, initial workup includes HbA1c (to assess degree of hyperglycemia), kidney function (eGFR, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio), fasting lipid panel, liver function tests, blood pressure, and screening for diabetic retinopathy (dilated fundus exam). Cardiovascular risk stratification is essential. Treatment targets: HbA1c <7% for most patients (individualized to 7.5–8% for elderly or those with multiple comorbidities), blood pressure <130/80 mmHg, and LDL <70 mg/dL if ASCVD risk is ≥10%. Lifestyle modification (Mediterranean or low-carbohydrate diet, 150 minutes/week of moderate exercise, weight loss of ≥5–10%) is the foundation of treatment. Metformin is first-line pharmacologic therapy unless contraindicated (eGFR <30), starting at 500 mg once or twice daily with meals, titrating to 1,000 mg twice daily over 4–8 weeks.
questions.explanation: If HbA1c is ≥1.5–2% above target at diagnosis, combination therapy should be considered upfront. Choice of second agent is guided by comorbidities: SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 RAs are preferred in patients with established CVD or high cardiovascular risk, heart failure, or CKD. Comprehensive diabetes care includes smoking cessation, aspirin in high-risk patients, annual foot exams, and vaccination updates. Referral to a diabetes educator and registered dietitian improves outcomes significantly.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a headache and is found to have a random blood glucose of 280 mg/dL and HbA1c of 9.8%. He has polyuria and polydipsia for 3 months. Which statement about HbA1c is correct?
options: A. HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over the past 2 weeks
B. HbA1c is falsely elevated in iron deficiency anemia
C. HbA1c can diagnose diabetes at a cutoff of ≥6.5%
D. HbA1c is accurate in sickle cell disease
questions.explanation: An HbA1c ≥6.5% is one of the four criteria for diagnosing diabetes mellitus (along with fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL, 2-hour glucose ≥200 mg/dL on OGTT, or random glucose ≥200 mg/dL with symptoms). HbA1c reflects average blood glucose over 2–3 months (the lifespan of red blood cells). Iron deficiency anemia can falsely ELEVATE HbA1c (reduced RBC turnover). HbA1c is unreliable in conditions that alter red cell lifespan: hemolytic anemia, sickle cell disease, G6PD deficiency (all cause falsely LOW HbA1c).

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is admitted with recurrent hypoglycemia despite reducing her basal insulin dose. She reports that her hypoglycemia occurs mainly post-exercise. Describe hypoglycemia unawareness and strategies for prevention.
questions.answer: Hypoglycemia unawareness occurs when patients lose the normal autonomic warning symptoms (shakiness, diaphoresis, palpitations, hunger) that precede neuroglycopenic symptoms, often due to prior hypoglycemia blunting the counterregulatory response—a phenomenon called hypoglycemia-associated autonomic failure (HAAF). This creates a vicious cycle where each hypoglycemic episode further impairs the response to subsequent episodes. Prevention strategies include: (1) strict avoidance of hypoglycemia for 2–4 weeks, which partially restores awareness in many patients; (2) less aggressive glycemic targets (HbA1c 7–8%) in patients with unawareness; (3) continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with low-glucose alarms and predictive alerts, which significantly reduces hypoglycemia frequency; (4) structured blood glucose awareness training (BGAT); (5) islet cell or pancreas transplantation in refractory cases with severe hypoglycemia unawareness.
questions.explanation: Post-exercise hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes occurs due to increased glucose uptake by muscles and can be delayed (4–8 hours post-exercise). Strategies include reducing basal insulin by 20–50% on exercise days, consuming carbohydrates before and during exercise, and setting a higher CGM alarm threshold. Closed-loop insulin delivery (artificial pancreas) systems that automatically suspend insulin delivery during predicted hypoglycemia have dramatically reduced nocturnal and post-exercise hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease?
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori infection is the most common cause of peptic ulcer disease, accounting for approximately 70-90% of duodenal ulcers and 70% of gastric ulcers. H. pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa, inducing chronic inflammation that disrupts the mucosal protective barrier. NSAID use is the second most common cause. Eradication of H. pylori significantly reduces ulcer recurrence.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man is diagnosed with a duodenal ulcer and confirmed H. pylori infection. Describe the first-line and second-line eradication regimens, including duration, and explain how eradication is confirmed.
questions.answer: First-line treatment in areas with low clarithromycin resistance (<15%) is clarithromycin-based triple therapy: a PPI (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg twice daily) + clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily + amoxicillin 1 g twice daily for 14 days, achieving ~80% eradication. Where resistance is higher or penicillin allergy exists, bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth subsalicylate + metronidazole + tetracycline for 14 days) or concomitant therapy (PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin + metronidazole) is preferred. Second-line therapy uses levofloxacin-based triple therapy or bismuth quadruple if not used first-line. Eradication is confirmed with the urea breath test or stool antigen test at least 4 weeks after completing antibiotics and 2 weeks after stopping PPIs to avoid false negatives.
questions.explanation: H. pylori eradication dramatically reduces peptic ulcer recurrence from ~80% to <5% at 1 year. Testing for eradication is mandatory after treatment for all peptic ulcer patients. Serology cannot confirm eradication as antibodies persist for months to years. Rising clarithromycin resistance globally is shifting guidelines toward bismuth quadruple or concomitant regimens as preferred first-line treatment.

questions.question: Which symptom pattern is most characteristic of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD)?
options: A. Postprandial epigastric pain relieved by antacids
B. Heartburn and regurgitation worsened by lying down
C. Colicky abdominal pain with alternating diarrhea and constipation
D. Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
questions.explanation: GERD classically presents with heartburn (retrosternal burning) and acid regurgitation, both of which worsen when lying supine or after large meals due to increased pressure on the lower esophageal sphincter. Symptoms are typically relieved by antacids or sitting upright. Postprandial epigastric pain relieved by antacids is more suggestive of peptic ulcer disease. Colicky pain with altered bowel habits suggests IBS, and right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals suggests biliary pathology.

questions.question: A patient with long-standing GERD undergoes surveillance endoscopy and is found to have Barrett's esophagus with low-grade dysplasia. What is the recommended management?
options: B. Endoscopic eradication therapy (e.g., radiofrequency ablation)
D. High-dose PPI therapy only with repeat endoscopy in 5 years
questions.explanation: Current guidelines recommend endoscopic eradication therapy (EET), most commonly radiofrequency ablation (RFA), for confirmed low-grade dysplasia in Barrett's esophagus. RFA eradicates dysplastic tissue and reduces progression to high-grade dysplasia and adenocarcinoma. Surveillance alone (every 6-12 months) may be considered in selected cases after multidisciplinary review, but EET is preferred. Esophagectomy carries significant morbidity and is reserved for intramucosal carcinoma not amenable to endoscopic therapy.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with a history of alcohol use disorder presents with hematemesis. Upper endoscopy reveals esophageal varices with active bleeding. After initial resuscitation, which combination of treatments is most evidence-based for controlling acute variceal hemorrhage?
options: A. IV octreotide + endoscopic band ligation
B. IV vasopressin + emergency surgical shunt
D. Blood transfusion to Hgb >10 g/dL + TIPS procedure
questions.explanation: The combination of a vasoactive drug (octreotide or terlipressin) plus endoscopic band ligation is the current standard of care for acute esophageal variceal hemorrhage. Octreotide reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure. Band ligation mechanically obliterates varices and has fewer complications than sclerotherapy. IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone) should also be given to prevent bacterial infection. Vasopressin is less preferred due to systemic vasoconstriction side effects. Transfusion targets Hgb 7-8 g/dL (restrictive strategy) to avoid portal pressure increases.

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes Crohn's disease from ulcerative colitis?
options: B. Skip lesions and transmural inflammation
D. Increased risk of colorectal cancer
questions.explanation: Crohn's disease characteristically causes transmural inflammation (involving all layers of the bowel wall) and skip lesions (discontinuous areas of involvement separated by normal mucosa). This transmural involvement leads to complications like fistulas, abscesses, and strictures. Ulcerative colitis involves only the mucosa and submucosa and is contiguous, starting from the rectum. Both conditions can cause bloody diarrhea, elevated CRP, and increased colorectal cancer risk, making these non-distinguishing features.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with known Crohn's disease presents with perianal pain and a draining fistula. MRI pelvis confirms a perianal fistula. Which biologic agent has the most evidence for fistulizing Crohn's disease?
questions.explanation: Infliximab (anti-TNF-alpha monoclonal antibody) has the most robust evidence for fistulizing Crohn's disease. The ACCENT II trial demonstrated that infliximab maintenance therapy achieved fistula closure in a significant proportion of patients and maintained response over 54 weeks. Combined surgical (seton placement) and medical management is often required. Vedolizumab and ustekinumab are effective for luminal Crohn's but have less data specifically for fistulizing disease. Natalizumab is no longer preferred due to PML risk.

questions.question: Which of the following is a hallmark feature of ulcerative colitis on colonoscopy?
options: A. Cobblestone appearance with deep linear ulcers
B. Continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum
C. Skip lesions with normal intervening mucosa
D. Small bowel involvement with strictures
questions.explanation: Ulcerative colitis characteristically shows continuous mucosal inflammation beginning at the rectum and extending proximally in a contiguous pattern. Endoscopic findings include erythema, friability, loss of vascular pattern, and pseudopolyps in severe disease. Cobblestone appearance with deep linear ulcers and skip lesions are characteristic of Crohn's disease. Ulcerative colitis does not involve the small bowel (except backwash ileitis in pancolitis).

questions.question: Describe the colorectal cancer surveillance recommendations for patients with ulcerative colitis, including timing, frequency, and risk factors that modify surveillance intervals.
questions.answer: Patients with extensive UC (pancolitis) should begin surveillance colonoscopy 8 years after symptom onset; those with left-sided colitis begin at 15 years; proctitis alone confers no increased CRC risk and follows average-risk guidelines. After the initial surveillance colonoscopy, intervals are every 1-3 years based on risk stratification: high-risk features (stricture, dysplasia on prior biopsy, PSC, family history of CRC <50 years, extensive inflammation) warrant annual colonoscopy; low-risk features allow every 2-3 years. Patients with concomitant primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) have a markedly elevated CRC risk and require annual surveillance colonoscopy from the time of IBD diagnosis. Chromoendoscopy with targeted biopsies is preferred over random biopsies for dysplasia detection. Flat or invisible dysplasia found on biopsy requires multidisciplinary review and often colectomy.
questions.explanation: The cumulative CRC risk in UC is approximately 2% at 10 years, 8% at 20 years, and 18% at 30 years for pancolitis. PSC dramatically amplifies this risk. Adequate bowel preparation and mucosal healing at the time of surveillance improve dysplasia detection accuracy. Dysplasia-associated lesion or mass (DALM) classifications have been replaced by contemporary endoscopic resectability criteria.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with recurrent abdominal pain, bloating, and alternating diarrhea and constipation for over 6 months. Stool cultures, CBC, and inflammatory markers are normal. Which diagnosis is most consistent with these findings?
questions.explanation: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or mixed) for at least 6 months without organic etiology. The Rome IV criteria require recurrent abdominal pain at least 1 day/week for the last 3 months associated with defecation, change in stool frequency, or change in stool form. Normal laboratory and endoscopic findings are consistent with IBS. Celiac disease would show abnormal serologies; microscopic colitis and Crohn's would show histological or endoscopic abnormalities.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with Child-Pugh C cirrhosis presents with confusion, asterixis, and elevated ammonia. His wife reports he has been constipated for 3 days. Which treatment is most appropriate for acute hepatic encephalopathy?
options: B. Lactulose titrated to 2-3 soft stools per day
questions.explanation: Lactulose is the first-line treatment for hepatic encephalopathy. It is a non-absorbable disaccharide that acidifies colonic contents, converting ammonia (NH3) to ammonium (NH4+) which is poorly absorbed, and promotes its excretion. The target is 2-3 soft bowel movements per day. Rifaximin is added for secondary prophylaxis or refractory cases. Protein restriction is no longer recommended as it worsens malnutrition in cirrhotic patients; adequate protein intake (1.2-1.5 g/kg/day) is advised. Neomycin has nephrotoxicity concerns. Flumazenil has limited evidence and is used only if benzodiazepine overdose is suspected.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most sensitive test to diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in a cirrhotic patient with ascites?
options: B. Ascitic fluid PMN count ≥ 250 cells/mm³
questions.explanation: SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count of ≥ 250 cells/mm³, regardless of culture results. This threshold has high sensitivity and allows empiric treatment to be started promptly. Ascitic fluid cultures are positive in only 40-50% of cases due to low bacterial concentrations, making culture alone insufficient for diagnosis. Systemic signs like fever and elevated WBC are non-specific. Early diagnosis and treatment with third-generation cephalosporins (cefotaxime) is critical as SBP carries significant mortality.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis develops tense ascites. Large-volume paracentesis is performed. Which intervention is essential to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction when removing more than 5 liters?
options: B. IV albumin infusion (6-8 g per liter of ascites removed)
C. Oral midodrine after the procedure
questions.explanation: Intravenous albumin infusion at 6-8 g per liter of ascitic fluid removed is recommended to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction (PPCD) when more than 5 liters are drained. PPCD is characterized by splanchnic vasodilation and circulatory compromise that can worsen renal function and increase mortality. Albumin expands the intravascular volume and maintains oncotic pressure. IV saline does not adequately prevent PPCD. Midodrine is used for refractory ascites management, not acute post-paracentesis care. TIPS is considered for refractory ascites requiring frequent large-volume paracentesis.

questions.question: A patient with hepatitis C cirrhosis develops hepatorenal syndrome type 1 (now called acute kidney injury in cirrhosis). Creatinine has doubled to 2.6 mg/dL over 48 hours. Which treatment combination has the strongest evidence?
questions.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is treated with intravenous albumin combined with a vasopressor. Terlipressin (a vasopressin analogue) combined with albumin has the strongest evidence, showing improved renal function and survival in randomized trials. Where terlipressin is unavailable (e.g., United States), norepinephrine combined with albumin is an alternative. Midodrine + octreotide + albumin is a less potent alternative. Furosemide would worsen volume depletion. Hemodialysis is a bridge to liver transplantation, not primary therapy. Liver transplantation remains the definitive treatment.

questions.question: Which serological pattern indicates acute hepatitis B infection with high infectivity?
options: A. HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc IgG positive
B. HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, anti-HBc IgM positive
C. HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative
D. HBsAg positive, anti-HBe positive, HBV DNA undetectable
questions.explanation: Acute hepatitis B infection is characterized by positive HBsAg (surface antigen), positive anti-HBc IgM (which indicates recent infection), and positive HBeAg (e antigen, indicating high viral replication and infectivity). HBeAg positivity correlates with high viral titers. Option A represents past infection with immunity. Option C represents vaccine-induced immunity (no prior infection). Option D represents inactive HBV carrier state or resolved infection with persistent HBsAg.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with fatigue, elevated ALT/AST (3-5x ULN), positive ANA (1:160), elevated IgG, and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) classically presents in young to middle-aged women with elevated transaminases, hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), positive autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM1), and interface hepatitis on biopsy (lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration at the portal-lobular interface). The simplified AIH score or IAIHG scoring system aids diagnosis. Primary biliary cholangitis presents with elevated ALP, anti-mitochondrial antibodies, and bile duct damage. AIH is treated with prednisone +/- azathioprine with excellent response.

questions.question: Which hepatitis virus is transmitted via the fecal-oral route and is a common cause of acute hepatitis in travelers to developing countries?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted via the fecal-oral route, typically through contaminated food or water. It is the most common cause of acute viral hepatitis in travelers to endemic regions. HAV causes self-limiting acute hepatitis and does not progress to chronic infection. The vaccine is highly effective for prevention. Hepatitis B and C are bloodborne pathogens. Hepatitis D requires hepatitis B coinfection and is transmitted parenterally.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever (38.8°C), and jaundice. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct (12 mm) with a stone. Which diagnosis and immediate management is most appropriate?
options: A. Acute cholecystitis — laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours
B. Ascending cholangitis — IV antibiotics + urgent ERCP within 24-48 hours
C. Acute pancreatitis — IV fluids + NPO + analgesics
D. Primary sclerosing cholangitis — ursodeoxycholic acid
questions.explanation: This presentation (Charcot's triad: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice) with dilated CBD and stone is classic for ascending cholangitis. Tokyo Guidelines define severity and recommend urgent biliary drainage. Mild-moderate cholangitis requires IV antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam or ceftriaxone + metronidazole) followed by ERCP within 24-48 hours for stone extraction and biliary decompression. Severe cholangitis with organ dysfunction requires emergency drainage within hours. Delayed or inadequate drainage carries significant mortality risk. Cholecystectomy is performed electively after resolution.

questions.question: A 45-year-old obese woman presents with sudden-onset severe right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder after eating a fatty meal. Murphy's sign is positive. Ultrasound shows gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: C. Ursodeoxycholic acid for stone dissolution
D. IV antibiotics alone and discharge
questions.explanation: This presentation is consistent with acute cholecystitis. Current Tokyo Guidelines and surgical society guidelines recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) as the preferred treatment for acute cholecystitis in appropriate surgical candidates. Early surgery reduces hospital stay, complications, and conversion to open surgery compared to delayed surgery. IV antibiotics are given perioperatively. ERCP is for choledocholithiasis (CBD stones). Ursodeoxycholic acid is for non-surgical candidates with small cholesterol stones and patent cystic duct.

questions.question: Describe the diagnostic criteria for acute pancreatitis, the Revised Atlanta Classification of severity, and the initial management approach.
questions.answer: Acute pancreatitis requires at least 2 of 3 criteria: (1) characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back, (2) serum lipase or amylase ≥3× upper limit of normal, (3) characteristic imaging findings on CT or MRI. The Revised Atlanta Classification defines severity as: mild (no organ failure, no local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure <48h and/or local complications without persistent organ failure), and severe (persistent organ failure >48h, single or multi-organ). CT severity index (Balthazar score) grades pancreatic and peripancreatic necrosis. Initial management includes aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's solution (preferred over normal saline, reducing SIRS), adequate analgesia, early oral feeding as tolerated (not prolonged NPO), and identification and treatment of the underlying cause (ERCP within 24h for biliary pancreatitis with cholangitis; cholecystectomy before discharge for mild gallstone pancreatitis).
questions.explanation: Lipase is preferred over amylase due to higher sensitivity and specificity, and longer elevation window. CT with IV contrast is not routinely needed at presentation but is indicated for diagnostic uncertainty, clinical deterioration, or suspected complications at 48-72h. Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended for sterile necrosis. Early oral feeding reduces infectious complications and length of stay compared to prolonged bowel rest.

questions.question: A 48-year-old man with gallstone pancreatitis is admitted. CT scan on day 3 shows 40% pancreatic necrosis. He remains febrile on day 10. Which management is appropriate?
options: B. CT-guided fine needle aspiration to confirm infection, then step-up approach (percutaneous/endoscopic drainage)
C. Prophylactic antibiotics should have been started at admission
D. Continue supportive care; infected necrosis cannot be treated until 6 weeks
questions.explanation: Management of necrotizing pancreatitis with suspected infected necrosis follows the 'step-up' approach: minimally invasive drainage (percutaneous or endoscopic transluminal) before surgical necrosectomy. CT-guided FNA can confirm infection (gas bubbles on CT are also diagnostic). Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended routinely for sterile necrosis. When infection is confirmed, carbapenem or fluoroquinolone therapy is initiated. Surgical necrosectomy is reserved for patients failing minimally invasive approaches. Walling-off of necrosis (WOPN) typically occurs at 4+ weeks, making intervention easier at that time.

questions.question: A patient presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, and a palpable, non-tender gallbladder. Which diagnosis is most consistent with this presentation (Courvoisier's sign)?
questions.explanation: Courvoisier's sign (palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless obstructive jaundice) suggests malignant biliary obstruction, most commonly pancreatic head carcinoma. The gallbladder dilates because it is not chronically scarred (as it would be in choledocholithiasis where the gallbladder is fibrotic and cannot distend). Pancreatic head cancer compresses the common bile duct, causing conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with dark urine and pale stools. Choledocholithiasis typically causes painful jaundice. Acute cholecystitis presents with pain and fever.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, bloating, and weight loss. IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody is markedly elevated. Endoscopy with duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia. Which dietary modification is the definitive treatment?
options: B. Gluten-free diet (eliminating wheat, barley, rye)
D. Low-fat diet with pancreatic enzyme replacement
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten (found in wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). The definitive treatment is a strict, lifelong gluten-free diet, which leads to symptomatic improvement, normalization of serology, and mucosal healing in most patients. Histological improvement may take 1-2 years. Accidental gluten exposure causes relapse. Low-FODMAP diet is for IBS. Lactose-free diet is for lactase deficiency. Pancreatic enzymes treat exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.

questions.question: Describe the non-invasive and invasive tests available for diagnosing H. pylori infection, their sensitivities/specificities, and when each is preferred.
questions.answer: Non-invasive tests include: (1) Urea breath test (UBT) — patient ingests 13C-labeled urea; if H. pylori is present, urease cleaves it and labeled CO2 is detected in exhaled breath; sensitivity/specificity >95%; preferred for post-treatment confirmation. (2) Stool antigen test (SAT) — monoclonal antibody-based ELISA detects H. pylori antigens in stool; sensitivity/specificity ~94%; alternative to UBT for confirmation. (3) Serology (IgG antibodies) — sensitivity ~85%, specificity ~79%; cannot distinguish active from past infection; not useful for post-treatment testing. Invasive tests (require endoscopy): (1) Rapid urease test (CLO test) — biopsy placed in urea-containing medium; color change indicates urease activity; sensitivity ~90-95%. (2) Histology — gold standard for diagnosis plus assessment of gastric pathology; H. pylori seen on Giemsa or Warthin-Starry stain. (3) Culture — allows antibiotic sensitivity testing; low sensitivity (~70-80%) but essential for refractory cases. PPIs suppress H. pylori and must be stopped ≥2 weeks before UBT, SAT, or rapid urease testing to avoid false negatives.
questions.explanation: Serology is acceptable only for initial diagnosis in treatment-naive patients when other tests are unavailable, or in populations with high prevalence. UBT is preferred for post-eradication testing due to convenience and accuracy. Endoscopy-based testing is preferred when endoscopy is already indicated (ulcer, alarm symptoms). Culture-guided therapy is reserved for multiple treatment failures.

questions.question: At what age should average-risk colorectal cancer screening begin according to the 2021 USPSTF guidelines?
questions.explanation: In 2021, the USPSTF updated its recommendation to begin colorectal cancer screening at age 45 (lowered from 50) for average-risk adults. This change was driven by increasing rates of early-onset colorectal cancer in adults under 50. Screening continues through age 75. Adults aged 76-85 should have individualized decisions. Acceptable screening modalities include colonoscopy every 10 years, annual fecal immunochemical test (FIT), CT colonography every 5 years, or flexible sigmoidoscopy every 5 years.

questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology of hepatic encephalopathy and the rationale for using lactulose and rifaximin in its treatment.
questions.answer: Hepatic encephalopathy results from accumulation of neurotoxic substances, primarily ammonia (NH3), that bypass hepatic detoxification due to liver failure and/or portosystemic shunting. Ammonia, produced by intestinal bacteria and amino acid catabolism, crosses the blood-brain barrier and disrupts neuronal function by impairing astrocyte glutamine synthesis, causing astrocyte swelling, and altering neurotransmitter balance favoring inhibitory GABA pathways. Lactulose is a non-absorbable disaccharide metabolized by colonic bacteria to lactic and acetic acid, acidifying the colon and converting NH3 to NH4+ (poorly absorbed ammonium), while also promoting bowel movements to expel ammonia-producing bacteria. Rifaximin is a non-absorbable rifamycin antibiotic that directly suppresses urease-producing intestinal bacteria, reducing ammonia generation; used as adjunctive or maintenance therapy, it significantly reduces recurrence of encephalopathy.
questions.explanation: Ammonia-centered pathophysiology is central to HE, though other toxins (mercaptans, short-chain fatty acids) may contribute. The gut-liver-brain axis is the therapeutic target. Lactulose targets ammonia elimination; rifaximin targets ammonia production. Both have strong evidence for secondary prophylaxis. Protein restriction is outdated; adequate protein intake is now recommended to prevent sarcopenia, which itself worsens HE prognosis.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis presents with new onset ascites. Diagnostic paracentesis reveals: total protein 1.5 g/dL, albumin 0.8 g/dL, serum albumin 2.4 g/dL. Calculate the SAAG and interpret the result. What are the first-line treatments for this condition?
questions.answer: The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) = serum albumin - ascitic albumin = 2.4 - 0.8 = 1.6 g/dL. A SAAG ≥ 1.1 g/dL indicates portal hypertension as the cause of ascites (accuracy ~97%), consistent with cirrhosis, congestive heart failure, or Budd-Chiari syndrome. In this context, alcoholic cirrhosis with portal hypertension is confirmed. First-line treatment includes sodium restriction (< 2 g/day dietary sodium), diuretic therapy with spironolactone (starting 100 mg/day, titrated to 400 mg/day) combined with furosemide (40 mg/day, titrated to 160 mg/day) in a 100:40 ratio to maintain normokalemia, and abstinence from alcohol. Large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement is indicated for tense or refractory ascites.
questions.explanation: SAAG accurately distinguishes portal hypertensive from non-portal hypertensive ascites better than the exudate/transudate classification. Low-SAAG (< 1.1) suggests peritoneal carcinomatosis, tuberculosis, nephrotic syndrome. The cornerstone of portal-HTN ascites management is reducing sodium intake and promoting renal sodium excretion with aldosterone antagonists. Terlipressin or midodrine may be added for hepatorenal syndrome. TIPS is considered for refractory ascites in appropriate candidates.

questions.question: Describe the diagnostic criteria and endoscopic features that distinguish ulcerative colitis from Crohn's colitis.
questions.answer: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is characterized by continuous mucosal and submucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum and extending proximally without skip areas; endoscopic features include diffuse erythema, granularity, friability, loss of vascular pattern, pseudopolyps (in chronic disease), and mucosal ulcerations. Crohn's colitis demonstrates discontinuous ('skip') lesions with normal intervening mucosa, transmural inflammation causing deep serpiginous or longitudinal ulcers ('bear claw'), cobblestoning from submucosal edema, and may involve any segment from mouth to anus. Rectal sparing and perianal disease (fistulas, skin tags, abscesses) favor Crohn's. Histologically, UC shows diffuse crypt architectural distortion and cryptitis, while Crohn's shows non-caseating granulomas (pathognomonic when present) and transmural lymphoid aggregates. About 10% of colitis cases remain 'indeterminate' when features overlap.
questions.explanation: Accurate distinction guides therapy: UC limited to rectum and colon is potentially curable with colectomy, whereas Crohn's recurs post-surgically. Serological markers (p-ANCA favors UC; ASCA favors Crohn's) and imaging (small bowel involvement on MR enterography) provide supporting data. Indeterminate colitis poses therapeutic challenges, particularly regarding restorative proctocolectomy.

questions.question: Explain the Child-Pugh scoring system for cirrhosis severity, including the parameters used and clinical significance of each class.
questions.answer: The Child-Pugh score assesses cirrhosis severity using five parameters: (1) serum bilirubin, (2) serum albumin, (3) prothrombin time (INR), (4) presence and severity of ascites, and (5) degree of hepatic encephalopathy. Each parameter is scored 1-3 (normal to most abnormal), giving a total score of 5-15. Class A (5-6 points): compensated cirrhosis, 1-year survival ~95%, no restrictions on surgery. Class B (7-9 points): significant functional compromise, moderate risk for procedures, used to identify transplant candidates. Class C (10-15 points): decompensated cirrhosis, 1-year survival ~35-45%, high procedural mortality, priority for liver transplantation. The MELD score has largely replaced Child-Pugh for transplant organ allocation due to better prediction of 90-day mortality.
questions.explanation: Child-Pugh remains clinically useful for quick bedside assessment and surgical risk stratification. Its limitations include subjective components (grading ascites and encephalopathy) and inability to capture acute-on-chronic liver failure. MELD-Na (incorporating serum sodium) is now the primary transplant allocation score in the United States.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with massive hematemesis. He is hemodynamically unstable (BP 80/50, HR 120). Describe the initial resuscitation approach and the steps for managing presumed variceal hemorrhage.
questions.answer: Initial resuscitation includes securing 2 large-bore IV access, initiating crystalloid fluids to maintain hemodynamic stability, and crossmatching for blood transfusion targeting hemoglobin 7-8 g/dL (restrictive transfusion strategy — overtransfusion raises portal pressure and worsens outcomes). Airway protection with endotracheal intubation should be considered given hematemesis and encephalopathy risk. Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus followed by 50 mcg/hour infusion should be started immediately to reduce splanchnic blood flow. IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily (or norfloxacin) prophylaxis reduces bacterial infections and improves survival. Urgent upper endoscopy within 12-24 hours (after stabilization) is performed for diagnosis and band ligation. If bleeding is uncontrolled, balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) as a bridge to TIPS is used. TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) is indicated for refractory variceal bleeding. Non-selective beta-blockers and prophylactic band ligation are used for secondary prevention.
questions.explanation: The 5-day mortality from acute variceal hemorrhage remains 10-20% in modern series. Pharmacological therapy (octreotide/terlipressin) + endoscopic band ligation + antibiotics is the evidence-based triad. Pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours in high-risk patients (Child-Pugh C or B with active bleeding) reduces rebleeding and mortality. Vasopressin alone is avoided due to systemic vasoconstriction.

questions.question: Describe the differential diagnosis of lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB) in adults and outline the initial evaluation and management approach.
questions.answer: Common causes of LGIB by frequency: diverticulosis (30-40%, painless brisk bleeding), angiodysplasia (ectatic mucosal vessels, typically cecum/ascending colon, often in elderly or CKD patients), ischemic colitis (crampy pain + bloody diarrhea, watershed areas at splenic flexure/sigmoid), colorectal cancer (occult or intermittent bleeding, associated symptoms), hemorrhoids (bright red blood per rectum, painless unless thrombosed), and IBD. Initial evaluation includes hemodynamic assessment and resuscitation, CBC, coagulation studies, and type and screen. Risk stratification (Oakland score or BLEED criteria) identifies patients safe for outpatient management. For hemodynamically stable patients, colonoscopy after bowel preparation within 24 hours is preferred — both diagnostic and therapeutic (epinephrine injection, coagulation, clips). CT angiography (CTA) is indicated for brisk active bleeding when colonoscopy is not immediately feasible or when bleeding source is not visualized; it can detect bleeding rates as low as 0.3-0.5 mL/min. Nuclear medicine tagged RBC scan is sensitive for intermittent low-rate bleeding (0.1 mL/min) but poor localization. Mesenteric angiography with embolization is therapeutic for active arterial bleeding.
questions.explanation: LGIB stops spontaneously in 80-85% of cases. Re-bleeding risk is highest with diverticular and angiodysplastic sources. Urgent colonoscopy (within 24h) improves diagnostic yield but requires adequate preparation. CTA has largely replaced nuclear medicine scans at most centers given superior speed and localization. Patients with massive LGIB should have nasogastric lavage or upper endoscopy to exclude an upper GI source presenting as hematochezia.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with coffee-ground emesis and melena. Nasogastric lavage returns bloody fluid. His Blatchford score is 14. Which action is most appropriate?
options: A. Outpatient management with oral PPI and repeat labs in 48 hours
B. Admission, IV PPI, and urgent endoscopy within 24 hours
C. Admission, observation, and elective endoscopy within 72 hours
D. Immediate surgical consultation for exploratory laparotomy
questions.explanation: A high Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS ≥ 7) identifies high-risk patients with upper GI bleeding who require hospital admission and urgent endoscopy. A GBS of 14 is very high-risk, indicating need for urgent intervention. IV PPI (pantoprazole 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour infusion) reduces the rate of high-risk stigmata and need for endoscopic therapy. Endoscopy within 24 hours is standard for significant UGIB; it allows for diagnosis and hemostasis (epinephrine injection, thermal coagulation, hemoclips). Low GBS (0-1) identifies patients safe for outpatient management.

questions.question: Describe the Forrest classification of peptic ulcer hemorrhage stigmata, including rebleeding risk for each category and corresponding management implications.
questions.answer: The Forrest classification stratifies endoscopic findings by rebleeding risk: Ia — active arterial spurting (rebleeding 55-100%); Ib — active oozing (10-27%); IIa — non-bleeding visible vessel (43-55%); IIb — adherent clot (22-33%); IIc — flat pigmented spot (7-10%); III — clean-based ulcer (<5%). High-risk stigmata (Ia, Ib, IIa) require immediate endoscopic hemostasis using combination therapy: epinephrine injection (1:10,000) plus a second modality (thermal coagulation, hemoclip, or fibrin glue). Combination therapy is superior to epinephrine alone. After hemostasis of high-risk lesions, high-dose IV PPI infusion (80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) reduces rebleeding by maintaining intragastric pH >6, stabilizing clot formation. Adherent clot (IIb) management is debated — cold water irrigation to attempt clot removal followed by treatment of underlying vessel is recommended by some guidelines. Low-risk stigmata (IIc, III) require only oral PPI and can be discharged early if otherwise stable.
questions.explanation: The CURE trial and multiple meta-analyses established combination endoscopic therapy superiority. Second-look endoscopy is not routinely recommended but may be considered after suboptimal initial hemostasis. Rebleeding after successful endoscopic therapy occurs in 10-15% of high-risk ulcers; repeat endoscopy is first-line; surgical or angiographic intervention is reserved for failure of two endoscopic attempts.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and peripheral edema. D-xylose absorption test is abnormal. Small bowel biopsy shows PAS-positive macrophages containing Tropheryma whipplei. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: C. Ceftriaxone 2g IV daily for 2 weeks, followed by trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 1 year
questions.explanation: Whipple's disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, a gram-positive actinobacterium. Classic presentation includes malabsorption, diarrhea, weight loss, arthralgias, and CNS involvement (oculomasticatory myorhythmia is pathognomonic). PAS-positive macrophages on small bowel biopsy are diagnostic. Treatment requires ceftriaxone 2g IV daily for 2 weeks (to treat CNS disease) followed by oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for at least 1 year to prevent relapse. Untreated, Whipple's disease is fatal. Gluten-free diet treats celiac disease. Pancreatic enzymes treat exocrine insufficiency.

questions.question: A 72-year-old woman on long-term NSAIDs develops a duodenal ulcer with active bleeding. After endoscopic hemostasis, what is the most appropriate strategy to reduce ulcer recurrence while she continues NSAIDs for arthritis?
options: A. Switch to a selective COX-2 inhibitor and add high-dose H2-blocker
B. Test for and eradicate H. pylori, then use daily PPI with continued NSAID use
D. Sucralfate 1g four times daily is sufficient gastroprotection
questions.explanation: When NSAIDs must be continued after peptic ulcer bleeding, the strategy is: (1) test for H. pylori and eradicate if positive (H. pylori + NSAIDs synergistically increase ulcer risk), (2) use a PPI continuously (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg/day) for gastroprotection. If possible, switching to a COX-2 inhibitor reduces GI risk but does not eliminate it, and still requires PPI co-therapy after UGIB. Discontinuing NSAIDs is ideal but may not be feasible. Sucralfate alone is insufficient for high-risk patients on NSAIDs. Misoprostol is an alternative gastroprotective agent but is limited by GI side effects.

questions.question: Which serum marker is most useful for monitoring response to treatment in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)?
questions.explanation: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the primary serum tumor marker used in HCC surveillance and monitoring. AFP > 400 ng/mL is highly specific for HCC in a cirrhotic patient with a liver mass. After curative resection or ablation, AFP should normalize; persistent elevation or re-elevation suggests residual tumor or recurrence. AFP alone is insufficient for screening (sensitivity ~60%), so it is used in conjunction with ultrasound every 6 months for HCC surveillance in high-risk patients (cirrhosis, chronic HBV). CA 19-9 is for pancreatic/biliary cancers. CEA is for colorectal cancer. CA 125 is for ovarian cancer.

questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology and management of hepatitis C infection, including current antiviral regimens and goals of therapy.
questions.answer: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is a single-stranded RNA flavivirus transmitted primarily via blood exposure (IV drug use, needlestick, blood transfusion before 1992). HCV infects hepatocytes and evades innate immunity through multiple mechanisms, causing chronic hepatitis in ~75-85% of acutely infected individuals. Chronic inflammation and fibrosis progression leads to cirrhosis in 15-20% over 20-30 years, with subsequent risk of HCC (~1-4%/year in cirrhotics). Current treatment uses direct-acting antivirals (DAAs): NS3/4A protease inhibitors, NS5A inhibitors, and NS5B polymerase inhibitors. Preferred regimens include sofosbuvir/velpatasvir (pangenotypic, 12 weeks), glecaprevir/pibrentasvir (pangenotypic, 8 weeks for non-cirrhotic treatment-naive), and ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. Sustained virological response (SVR, undetectable HCV RNA 12 weeks post-treatment) is the goal and is achieved in >95% of patients, representing functional cure and significantly reducing fibrosis progression, HCC risk, and all-cause mortality.
questions.explanation: The HCV treatment revolution has transformed care from interferon-based regimens (40-50% SVR, significant toxicity) to oral, well-tolerated DAA regimens. Testing HCV genotype was essential historically but pangenotypic regimens have simplified this. Cirrhotic patients require longer treatment and post-SVR HCC surveillance. Reinfection is possible as immunity is not sterilizing. Universal screening for HCV is recommended for all adults 18-79 years by USPSTF.

questions.question: Describe the diagnostic approach to a patient presenting with jaundice, distinguishing between pre-hepatic, hepatic, and post-hepatic causes.
questions.answer: Jaundice (icterus) results from hyperbilirubinemia (>2.5-3 mg/dL) causing yellow discoloration of sclera and skin. The approach begins with fractionating bilirubin. Pre-hepatic jaundice (unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia) results from excessive red blood cell destruction (hemolysis) or impaired conjugation (Gilbert's syndrome, Crigler-Najjar); labs show elevated indirect bilirubin, normal liver enzymes, normal urobilinogen in urine, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin. Hepatic (hepatocellular) jaundice shows mixed or predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with markedly elevated AST/ALT (hepatitis pattern) and bilirubin in urine; causes include viral hepatitis, alcoholic hepatitis, autoimmune hepatitis, DILI. Post-hepatic (cholestatic/obstructive) jaundice shows predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with elevated ALP/GGT, bilirubin in urine, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus; causes include choledocholithiasis, cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic cancer, PSC, PBC. Imaging (ultrasound, MRCP) is key to detecting biliary obstruction. Liver biopsy may be needed for hepatocellular causes.
questions.explanation: A systematic fractionation approach prevents premature closure. Gilbert's syndrome is the most common benign cause of isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 polymorphism). Elevated ALP with elevated GGT (not bone origin) confirms hepatic cholestasis. MRCP is the preferred non-invasive imaging for biliary anatomy. ERCP provides both diagnosis and therapy for bile duct obstruction.

questions.question: Describe the Milan criteria for liver transplantation in hepatocellular carcinoma and the management approach for patients who do not meet these criteria.
questions.answer: The Milan criteria define the standard transplant candidacy threshold for HCC within cirrhosis: single tumor ≤5 cm, or up to 3 tumors each ≤3 cm, with no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Transplantation within Milan criteria achieves 5-year post-transplant survival rates of 70-75%, comparable to transplantation for non-malignant indications. Patients beyond Milan criteria but within extended criteria (UCSF criteria: single ≤6.5 cm or ≤3 tumors with largest ≤4.5 cm and total ≤8 cm) may still be considered at experienced centers. For patients outside Milan criteria, downstaging using locoregional therapy (transarterial chemoembolization/TACE, radiofrequency ablation) can achieve tumor regression to meet Milan criteria; successful downstaging with sustained response (>3 months) allows listing for transplant. Systemic therapy with sorafenib or lenvatinib is used for advanced/metastatic HCC not amenable to curative or locoregional therapy.
questions.explanation: The Milan criteria remain the gold standard despite evolving evidence supporting extended criteria in select patients. Locoregional therapies serve dual roles: bridging therapy to prevent progression on the waitlist, and downstaging to transplant eligibility. AFP response to locoregional therapy is a key prognostic marker. Microvascular invasion on explant pathology significantly increases recurrence risk even within Milan criteria.

questions.question: A patient with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and ulcerative colitis is found to have a dominant biliary stricture on MRCP. Which complication must be immediately excluded?
questions.explanation: Cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer) is the most feared complication of PSC, occurring in 10-15% of patients over their lifetime, with a lifetime risk ~10 times higher than the general population. A new dominant stricture in PSC should always raise suspicion for cholangiocarcinoma. ERCP with brush cytology/FISH analysis and CA 19-9 levels are used for evaluation. Cross-sectional imaging (MRCP, CT) and PET scan may help. The prognosis of cholangiocarcinoma complicating PSC is poor, and early detection through regular MRCP surveillance (annually) is critical. PSC patients with UC also have markedly increased colorectal cancer risk requiring annual colonoscopic surveillance from diagnosis.

questions.question: Describe the clinical features, diagnosis, and management of chronic pancreatitis, including its complications and the approach to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.
questions.answer: Chronic pancreatitis is irreversible inflammatory destruction of the pancreatic parenchyma, most commonly caused by chronic alcohol use (70%) and smoking, followed by genetic mutations (PRSS1, SPINK1, CFTR), idiopathic, autoimmune, and obstructive causes. Clinical features include recurrent or chronic epigastric pain radiating to the back (hallmark), steatorrhea (malabsorption from exocrine insufficiency — typically occurs after >90% loss of exocrine function), diabetes mellitus (endocrine insufficiency), and weight loss. Diagnosis: CT imaging shows parenchymal calcifications (pathognomonic), ductal dilation, and atrophy. MRCP/EUS are more sensitive for early disease. Fecal elastase-1 <200 μg/g confirms exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI). Management of pain: abstinence from alcohol/smoking, analgesics (stepwise), antioxidants, endoscopic therapy (ERCP for ductal stones/strictures), and surgery (Puestow procedure — lateral pancreaticojejunostomy) for refractory pain. EPI is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with meals and snacks (lipase ≥40,000-50,000 units/meal), taken with food. Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation (A, D, E, K) and monitoring for diabetes are essential.
questions.explanation: Chronic pancreatitis carries significant morbidity: 5-year mortality ~20%, largely from cardiovascular disease, malnutrition, and malignancy. Pancreatic cancer risk is 5-15x elevated. Autoimmune pancreatitis (IgG4-related, type 1) is a reversible mimicker of chronic pancreatitis and cancer — it responds dramatically to corticosteroids and must be distinguished before surgery. EUS-guided celiac plexus block provides temporary pain relief in refractory cases.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic extraintestinal manifestation of inflammatory bowel disease?
questions.explanation: Extraintestinal manifestations (EIMs) occur in 25-40% of IBD patients. Erythema nodosum (tender, raised nodules typically on the anterior shins) is the most common skin manifestation of IBD and correlates with intestinal disease activity. Other EIMs include: pyoderma gangrenosum (skin), primary sclerosing cholangitis (liver), episcleritis and uveitis (eyes), peripheral and axial arthropathies (joints), and aphthous mouth ulcers. Some EIMs (erythema nodosum, peripheral arthritis) parallel intestinal activity, while others (uveitis, PSC, ankylosing spondylitis) run an independent course.

questions.question: Explain the evaluation and management of acute severe ulcerative colitis (ASUC), including the criteria used to identify it and indications for escalation to surgery.
questions.answer: Acute severe ulcerative colitis is defined by Truelove and Witts criteria: ≥6 bloody stools/day plus at least one systemic feature: temperature >37.8°C, HR >90 bpm, hemoglobin <10.5 g/dL, or ESR >30 mm/hr. All patients require hospital admission, IV corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 60 mg/day or hydrocortisone 300-400 mg/day), thromboprophylaxis, bowel rest with nutritional support, and daily clinical assessment. After 3 days of IV steroids, non-responders (stool frequency >8/day or CRP >45 mg/L on day 3 — Oxford index) should receive salvage therapy with infliximab (5 mg/kg) or cyclosporine (2 mg/kg IV). If salvage therapy fails within 4-7 days, or if there is clinical deterioration, toxic megacolon (transverse colon >6 cm on AXR), perforation, or hemorrhage, urgent colectomy is required. Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is the procedure of choice to remove the diseased colon while preserving ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) as a future option.
questions.explanation: The 'steroid-responsive vs. steroid-refractory' decision point at day 3 is critical to prevent prolonged futile corticosteroid use. The Oxford criteria (day-3 predictor) have ~85% accuracy for colectomy. Infliximab and cyclosporine have equivalent efficacy for salvage (~50% response), with choice guided by prior biologic exposure and center experience. Delayed colectomy increases surgical mortality; earlier surgical consultation in ASUC improves outcomes.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with known alcoholic liver disease presents with confusion and is found to have a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L. He is treated with hypertonic saline. Two days later he develops progressive quadriplegia and difficulty swallowing. What complication has occurred?
questions.explanation: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), formerly called central pontine myelinolysis, results from overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia. When hyponatremia has been present for >48 hours, brain cells adapt by losing intracellular osmolytes. Rapid sodium correction depletes cerebral osmolytes faster than they can be replenished, causing osmotic injury to the myelin sheath — particularly in the pons and extrapontine regions. The maximum correction rate is 6-8 mEq/L per 24 hours (no more than 10-12 mEq/L in any 24-hour period). Clinical features include dysarthria, dysphagia, locked-in syndrome, and quadriplegia. This is particularly relevant in cirrhotic patients who are malnourished and often chronically hyponatremic.

questions.question: Outline the pharmacological treatment options for IBS-D (diarrhea-predominant IBS) and IBS-C (constipation-predominant IBS), including mechanisms of action and key safety considerations.
questions.answer: For IBS-D: Loperamide (mu-opioid agonist) reduces stool frequency and urgency but does not improve abdominal pain and is used symptomatically. Rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic, 550 mg TID x14 days) is FDA-approved for non-constipated IBS; it modulates gut microbiota and reduces luminal bacterial overgrowth, improving global symptoms and diarrhea in ~40% of patients. Alosetron (5-HT3 antagonist) is approved for severe IBS-D in women who have failed conventional therapy; it slows colonic transit and reduces visceral sensitivity but carries a rare risk of ischemic colitis and severe constipation, requiring REMS enrollment. Eluxadoline (mixed mu-agonist/delta-antagonist) reduces bowel contractions and pain; contraindicated in patients without a gallbladder (risk of sphincter of Oddi spasm) or with alcohol use disorder. TCAs (amitriptyline 10-25 mg nightly) provide visceral analgesia and slow gut transit, useful for pain-predominant IBS-D. For IBS-C: Lubiprostone (ClC-2 chloride channel activator) increases intestinal fluid secretion; approved for IBS-C in women ≥18. Linaclotide and plecanatide (guanylate cyclase-C agonists) increase intestinal secretion and reduce visceral pain; first-line for moderate-severe IBS-C. Tegaserod (5-HT4 agonist) is available under restricted access for IBS-C in women <65 without cardiovascular risk factors.
questions.explanation: The gut-brain axis and visceral hypersensitivity are central to IBS pathophysiology, explaining why both gut-directed and centrally acting agents (TCAs, SSRIs, cognitive behavioral therapy) have efficacy. Low-FODMAP diet reduces fermentable carbohydrate load and improves symptoms in ~50-70% of IBS patients regardless of subtype. Psychosocial comorbidities (anxiety, depression) are present in up to 60% of IBS patients and should be addressed.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B (HBeAg-negative, HBV DNA 8,000 IU/mL, ALT 2x ULN) and F3 fibrosis on liver biopsy. Which antiviral treatment is most appropriate?
options: A. No treatment required; observe and repeat labs in 1 year
C. Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) or entecavir long-term
questions.explanation: This patient has HBeAg-negative chronic hepatitis B with detectable viremia, elevated ALT, and significant fibrosis (F3), meeting AASLD criteria for antiviral treatment. First-line agents are tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), tenofovir alafenamide (TAF — preferred in renal/bone disease), or entecavir due to their potent viral suppression, high barrier to resistance, and excellent safety profiles. Treatment reduces hepatitis, prevents cirrhosis progression, and decreases HCC risk. Lamivudine has a high resistance rate and is no longer recommended. Pegylated interferon is an alternative for select patients (young, elevated ALT, low viral load, HBV genotype A/B) seeking finite therapy but is poorly tolerated and less effective.

questions.question: Describe the diagnostic evaluation and management of acute cholecystitis, including the role of imaging and the Tokyo Guidelines severity criteria.
questions.answer: Acute cholecystitis is inflammation of the gallbladder, most commonly caused by gallstone obstruction of the cystic duct (calculous, 90%) or by ischemia/sludge without stones (acalculous, 10%, in critically ill patients). Diagnosis requires clinical features (RUQ pain ≥24h, Murphy's sign, fever, nausea), laboratory findings (leukocytosis, mildly elevated transaminases/bilirubin), and imaging. Abdominal ultrasound is first-line imaging (sensitivity ~80-90%): findings include gallstones or sludge, gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy's sign. HIDA scan is the most sensitive test (~97%) when ultrasound is equivocal. The Tokyo Guidelines (2018) stratify severity: Grade I (mild, no organ dysfunction, responds to medical therapy), Grade II (moderate: leukocytes >18,000, symptom duration >72h, marked local inflammation), Grade III (severe: organ dysfunction). Management: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cephalosporin + metronidazole), and early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 72h) for Grade I/II. Grade III patients require ICU support, biliary drainage (percutaneous cholecystostomy if high surgical risk), and delayed cholecystectomy.
questions.explanation: Early cholecystectomy (within 72 hours) is superior to interval cholecystectomy (6-8 weeks) in suitable patients, with reduced conversion rates and hospital stay. Delayed surgery risks recurrent attacks (18-20% within 6 weeks), common duct stone complications, and Mirizzi syndrome. Acalculous cholecystitis in ICU patients requires high clinical suspicion and early percutaneous drainage given prohibitive surgical risk.

questions.question: Interpret the following liver function test pattern and propose the most likely diagnosis: AST 520, ALT 480, ALP 180, GGT 210, total bilirubin 8.2, direct bilirubin 6.1, albumin 2.8, INR 1.9, platelet count 88,000.
questions.answer: This pattern shows markedly elevated transaminases (AST/ALT ratio ~1.08 — relatively equal, which differs from alcoholic hepatitis where AST:ALT >2:1), suggesting significant hepatocellular injury, along with conjugated (direct) hyperbilirubinemia. The mildly elevated ALP and GGT suggest some cholestatic component. Low albumin (2.8 g/dL), prolonged INR (1.9), and thrombocytopenia (88,000 — suggesting hypersplenism) indicate significant hepatic synthetic dysfunction and likely underlying cirrhosis/portal hypertension. The combined picture of acute hepatocellular injury (elevated aminotransferases) superimposed on chronic liver disease (low albumin, coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia) is consistent with acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) or an acute decompensation of cirrhosis. Differential includes acute viral hepatitis on cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis with underlying cirrhosis, drug-induced liver injury, or ischemic hepatitis ('shock liver') superimposed on cirrhosis. Further evaluation: viral hepatitis serologies, alcohol history, medication review, acetaminophen level, autoimmune markers, liver imaging.
questions.explanation: The AST:ALT ratio provides clues: >2:1 favors alcoholic hepatitis; equal elevations favor viral or DILI. Thrombocytopenia in this context likely reflects hypersplenism from portal hypertension. Albumin and INR together assess synthetic function better than transaminases. ACLF carries a 28-day mortality of 30-60% depending on the number of organ failures — early liver transplant evaluation is critical.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive dysphagia for solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and weight loss. Barium swallow shows a 'bird's beak' appearance at the gastroesophageal junction. Esophageal manometry confirms aperistalsis with incomplete LES relaxation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax with swallowing and absence of normal esophageal peristalsis, due to loss of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus. Classic presentation: progressive dysphagia to both solids AND liquids (distinguishing it from mechanical obstruction), regurgitation of undigested food (no acid taste, as food pools in esophagus), and weight loss. Barium swallow: dilated esophagus with distal 'bird's beak' tapering. Esophageal manometry confirms the diagnosis. Treatment: pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy, or peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM). Must exclude pseudoachalasia from malignancy at the GEJ.

questions.question: Describe the MELD score, how it is calculated, and its clinical applications in hepatology.
questions.answer: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is an objective, laboratory-based scoring system that predicts 90-day mortality in patients with chronic liver disease. It is calculated using three variables: serum creatinine, serum bilirubin, and INR, using the formula: MELD = 3.78 × ln[bilirubin (mg/dL)] + 11.2 × ln[INR] + 9.57 × ln[creatinine (mg/dL)] + 6.43. MELD-Na incorporates serum sodium (which independently predicts mortality, particularly from ascites and HRS): MELD-Na = MELD + 1.32 × (137 − Na) − [0.033 × MELD × (137 − Na)]. Clinical applications include: (1) organ allocation for liver transplantation in the United States (UNOS uses MELD-Na; higher scores receive priority), (2) prognosis assessment and identification of patients requiring ICU-level care, (3) selection of candidates for early TIPS in variceal hemorrhage (MELD >10-15), and (4) risk stratification before hepatic procedures. Scores >15 generally indicate transplant consideration; >25 indicates significant short-term mortality risk.
questions.explanation: MELD replaced the Child-Pugh score for transplant allocation in 2002 because it is objective, reproducible, and better predicts 3-month waitlist mortality. Exceptions and points can be granted for complications not reflected in lab values (HCC, hepatopulmonary syndrome). MELD ≤9: 1.9% mortality; MELD 10-19: 6% mortality; MELD 20-29: 19.6% mortality; MELD 30-39: 52.6% mortality; MELD ≥40: 71.3% 3-month mortality.
